The record detail, 8a — build target

This specifies the supplied composition; it does not revise it. Every number below is read off the drawing, rounded onto the grid or onto the scale where the drawing sits between two legal values, and the rounding is named where it happened. Where the supplied composition contains a conflict — two instances at 72, an artist set twice — the conflict is stated and resolved in one direction, because a build cannot hold both. Every entry in that list is resolved — that is what the list is for — so an entry is not struck because the drawings below apply its resolution, which is the normal state of one. The artist clause was struck for exactly that reason and is restored: the redrawing setting the artist once is the resolution this list promises, not evidence the supplied drawing never doubled it. Membership is the test, not exit: an entry is a conflict internal to the supplied composition — something the artwork itself asserts twice or two ways — and such a conflict is a permanent fact about the artwork, so no entry ever leaves. The contrast-floor clause left because it was never one: it was a conflict between the supplied drawing and a rule this file introduced, so it was miscategorised rather than exited, and its departure is not a precedent for striking anything. Which is also why it does not come back now that the clamp is reinstated (§5.2, §11.4): the fill clears at the reinstated clamp — 6.32:1 against ink, never below 5.4:1 across the band — and §5.2’s rule moved the 11px label off a base-step ground altogether, so there is no conflict left to file on either list. Only the chroma floor stays withdrawn. An earlier version of this passage gave a single exit condition — the rule that made it a conflict being withdrawn — and then struck an entry by a second one it never stated. §7 lists what the drawing cannot answer.

Three standing rules on measurement, placed first because §17, §19, §20 and §22 were spent on a constraint one measurement would have dissolved (§23). One: any ruling that changes a figure another drawing depends on reports the measured before and after against the supplied render, with its threshold named — derived numbers are not a substitute. Two: any change to a cell or band dimension names its delta in the section that makes it; §2.1 named two adjustments and omitted the 77px one that mattered, and that omission is checkable. Three: a reading of the render is cited only if it was measured, with the threshold stated — reading it by eye produced 480 and 452 in §23, both wrong. A derivation inside the file and a measurement of the render are different acts, and only the second can tell the file it has drifted.

1 · The composition, drawn at 1440 × 900

Redrawn on the grid and the scale, at true size, shown here at 0.5722. The identity band’s isometric is one record’s generated arrangement (§5.4’s split marker, on §5.1’s licence); the matrix solid and the sleeve are placeholders — see §5.4, whose two halves differ on exactly this point. This is the richest state: every module populated. One record of seventeen renders it.

Differences from the supplied raster, all of them roundings onto an existing constraint and all of them listed: the artist line measures ~28 and takes 40, the only legal neighbour (§4.2); the fill ships as sampled, the lift into the withdrawn clamp having gone with it (§5.2, §11); cell edges are rounded to the nearest column (§2.1); and the supplied raster draws every mark at one value, where §5.5's ladder puts the disc and the three edge fields at the tint step — so the ground marks here are mixed 34% toward paper and the raster is not the reference for colour. Both drawings carry reissue qualifying the release-year label on the record that is one; the second mono pressing run is withdrawn (§8.1) and plant, weight and colour stay below the fold by the identify/describe rule. The pressing block anchors to a reserved floor 140px above the cell floor, and the corner triangle owns the corner below it. Anchoring the block to the cell floor put it inside the triangle's box, where the 11px Pressing label measured 2.95:1 and the second mono run 3.82:1 against a 4.5:1 requirement. Three things could give and only one of them was free: darkening the type would make a tint mark the page's second type-bearing mark and drag §5.2's whole lightness derivation with it, since that floor is argued from the year field being the only one; moving the field out of the corner keeps the contrast and loses the ground work in the lower left, which is what the field is for. So the block's floor moved instead — §4.2 anchors the pressing block to a floor, not specifically to the cell's edge, and the gap mechanism is unchanged with the floor 140px higher. The triangle shrinks from 186 to 140 tall to make the reserve fit, which is the smaller cost. The larger one: the reserve was subtracted from the same content box the title→pressing gap lived in, so it did not come out of the void — it was the void, and that is what withdrew §8.1's second pressing run. The gap fell from 112px to 3.7px with the run in the stack; with it withdrawn, and the tail's 47px moved into the identity band (§2.1), the gap measures 43.1px — which does not absorb a third title line by itself. The corner reserve yields the balance at three lines and the rest at four, and measured on the real route the give closes with 27px to spare, so no record in the collection collapses its genres run — the collapse is a guard with a stated condition (§4.2) rather than a case the page draws. §4.2's standing check is satisfied by naming that subject, not by geometry: one record of seventeen loses its corner field and one line of genre, and that is the whole cost of the longest title in the collection.

The anchoring §4.2 rules is now drawn — the identity cell is a column with the pressing block pushed to the floor, so the void falls between title and pressing and a growing title closes it rather than pushing the block into a clipped edge. What remains undrawn is §8.1's cost claim: the titles here take one line and two — Meddle one, The Hurdy Gurdy Man two — so neither shows the five-line case where the corner track reaches zero. The run does not drop on it — §4.2's measurement closes with 27px to spare — and that claim is ruled and unverified. And one non-rounding: this drawing fails §5.5's mark floor and is not to be read as conforming. One mark fails it: the construction, at 0.42% counting only its base faces, which reaches the remedy already named — grow the coloured faces, not the disc. Nothing else is in breach, and this count has been wrong in three successive revisions of this note (one mark, then two, then two with the wrong members), each time because a mark was tested against a floor that does not govern it. The journal edge and the sleeve bar are linear and run their full edge. The three edge fields are tint-step ground, which the floor does not reach at all — and §5.1 fixes their extent rather than capping it — an edge field’s extent follows its height, the corner triangle at 268 × 140 — so they are neither in breach nor available as somewhere to add colour. This cited §5.4, which is the paragraph that declines to give the ornament marks any geometry, so the exemption rested on a claim its source denies. The earlier version of this note cited a 65%-against-40% ceiling that §5.5 has since withdrawn — the ceiling was unreachable by any composition, and the drawing failing it was evidence against the rule rather than against the drawing. The floor it is replaced by, the drawing also fails, and that failure is a real finding: the construction's coloured faces are too small to read as the page's colour arriving again. Where drawing and §5.5 disagree, §5.5 governs.

2 · The grid

2.1 · Twelve columns, zero gutter, full bleed, three fixed bands

Twelve equal columns across the full viewport, gap: 0, no page margin. At 1440 that is a 120px column. The page bleeds: the nav rule, the band rules and the colour marks all run to the viewport edge, and there is no centred container — up to the 1728 cap; beyond it the grid centres and the bleed becomes paper margin (§7). Rules are drawn as borders on the cell that owns them, never as a background showing through a gap.

Upper band: 4 / 4 / 4 — corrected by §23; this read 4 / 3 / 5, and the paragraph below is the original measurement, which rounded the construction cell from 437 to 360 without naming the loss. Upper band (original): 4 / 3 / 5. Lower band: 3 / 2 / 2 / 2 / 3. Measured off the raster the upper dividers fall at 451 and 888 against the grid's 480 and 840, and the lower five cells measure 310 / 262 / 291 / 259 / 318 against 360 / 240 / 240 / 240 / 360. The drawing is not on a twelve-column grid and the build is. The rounding is stated rather than hidden because it is visible: the identity cell gains 29px, the figures cell loses 51. The proportions — widest at both ends of the lower band, the two narrow interior cells flanking the figures — survive the rounding, and those are what the composition is doing.

Band heights are fixed, not content-derived: 53 nav · 547 identity · 300 record = 900, and there is no tail. The tail's 47px went to the identity band because the give §4.2 needed had to add height rather than reallocate it — 140px of corner reserve cannot absorb a five-line title's growth on its own, and no redistribution inside 500px closes that arithmetic — the 47px is what buys the 27px the built stack now clears by. The fold now lands on the record band's closing rule instead of on empty paper: a band boundary is a composition edge too, and it is the edge every other band ends on. The nav is 53 because the built AppHeader is 53 — the drawing showed 56, and a spec that restates a measurable component's height wrongly is worse than one that omits it. The three pixels go to the tail, the only band with nothing in it; identity and record are unchanged, because both carry content measured against their exact heights (§7). This is the whole no-scroll budget at 1440 × 900 and it is spent. An empty module changes nothing about the geometry — the lower band is 300px whether five cells carry text or one does, which is what makes §6 a question about marks rather than about reflow. The tail is paper, not a footer; nothing is drawn in it.

3 · Rules

One ink weight, one colour weight, and one inset hairline that is not a cell edge

1px, oklch(0.72 0.004 80) — every structural edge. Under the nav, under the identity band, and on the right of every cell but the last in each band. There is no heavy rule anywhere in this composition, which is the sharpest difference from 7a: ranking is carried by the colour fields and by the 72, so the rules only have to divide. A build that reintroduces a 6px structural vertical has imported a device from a layout this one replaces. Stated as the reversal it is: this deletes the three 6px verticals already built and tested for 7a. Intended, not an omission — 7a ranked its bands with rule weight because it had no colour field to rank with, and this composition has two 72s and eight colour marks doing that work. Keeping both ranks the page twice.

2px, derived colour — the journal's right edge, and nowhere else. It is the only rule on the page that is not grey and the only edge that is 2px. It marks the one cell whose content the owner writes rather than records, and it must not be applied to a second cell: two of them and the weight is a tier rather than a mark. When the colour falls back to ink (§5.3) this rule falls back with it — 2px ink, still the only 2px edge.

Two inset hairlines are rules about type, not about cells. The one under the identity block runs 372px — the text measure, not the 480px cell — and the one over Images runs 220px. They stop short deliberately: an inset hairline separates two things inside one module, a full-bleed one separates modules. The failure mode is an implementer extending either to the cell edge, which silently promotes a paragraph break into a division.

The active nav item carries a 2px ink underline, 7px below the baseline. Ink, not colour — nav state is the same on every record and nothing that is constant across records may be drawn in a colour that varies with the record.

4 · Type

4.1 · The inventory, richest state — 72 × 2 · 40 × 2 · 13 × 9 · 11 × 14 · 10 × 2

72 appears twice, and the composition can hold two because they never share a band. The title sits in the identity band as ink on paper; the year sits in the record band as ink on the colour field. Same size, opposite ground, 500px apart vertically — they read as one claim each rather than as a tier. The obligation is the separation, not the count: a third 72, or either one moved into the other's band, and the page has a display tier instead of two display events.

40 appears twice: the artist and the market figure. Both are single instances in their own band, and the market 40 keeps the property 7a gave it — the one number on the page the owner does not control.

Adjacency, as in 7a §4, and it holds in three places here. 11px mono label directly above the 72 in the release-year field; 11px label directly above the 40 market figure; 72 title directly above the 40 artist with nothing between them. Small first, large beneath, no intervening element. The identity block is the one pairing that runs large-to-small, because there the 72 is the subject and the 40 is its qualifier.

11 carries the entire label system and there are fourteen of them. Five nav items, one wordmark, one eyebrow, five field labels, and two action lines (Add entry, Images / Manage). Mono, uppercase, .10em tracking — .12em in the nav strip only. Field labels are muted oklch(0.44 0.008 70); the label inside the colour field is full ink, and actions are full ink because an action is not a field name. 10 is reserved for the two dated meta lines. 13 is every piece of prose and every mono data line; nothing on this screen is set at 15, 12 or 9. One value is added to the scale below the fold and nowhere else: 16, for the typed line of an input only (§9.3). It is a correctness requirement rather than a type choice, and it is bounded to text the user can place a cursor in.

Mono against sans is the data/prose split, not a decoration. Catalogue line, matrix line and every label are mono; titles, artist, provenance, journal, about and note are sans. The format line — Vinyl, LP, Album — is sans 500, because it is a description rather than an identifier.

4.2 · Two roundings and one deletion, all forced by the scale

The artist line measures ~28 in the raster and the scale forbids 16 to 39. It takes 40. 15 was the other legal neighbour and it is the wrong one: at 15 the artist joins the label tier and the identity block becomes a single display object with a caption. At 40 it is the second-largest thing on the page, which is what the drawing shows it to be.

No clamp, no size change, and the break is balanced. The five-line title is a bad break, not a long title. Measured, the worst case fits — 498 of 500 — so every clamp option on the table pays real characters of a record's name for a problem correctness does not have. What is actually wrong is the shape: On The / Radio: / Greatest / Hits Vol. 1 & / 2 orphans a digit, and an orphaned volume number reads as a rendering fault rather than as a long title. So: text-wrap: balance and hyphens: none on the 72 block. Five lines stay five lines, evenly measured, no orphan — the artefact goes and nothing is spent. Balance is the one repair that costs neither a character, a size off the scale, a column, nor the tail.

The 2px is coincidence and is not treated as margin. One character, a fallback face before the webfont lands, a different rounding — and it overflows. The guard is structural, not a clamp: the pressing block anchors to a reserved floor 140px above the cell edge (§1) and the title block flows from the top, so the two can never push each other. Title overflow spends the gap between them, and that gap measures 43.1px at two title lines. It is not the third coincidence-standing-in-for-a-margin, because nothing is measured to fit inside it: the failure mode is defined and what it consumes is ornament. The 40.5px, answered once: it was a missing element, not a different edge. Genres moved into the pressing block under §8.1's identify/describe rule and neither drawing rendered it — a 13px mono run plus its 9px lead is 28.5px. The build's number is the real one: 71.6 − 28.5 = 43.1px at two title lines. The first version of this sentence subtracted the whole 40.5px discrepancy from the gap and reported 31.1 — double-counting the very figure it was explaining, since 28.5 of that 40.5 is the drawn run and the balance sits in leads elsewhere in the stack, not in the gap. The genres run is now drawn in both. This is the last question about the identity cell — the frame stands as it is, and §8 already settled that it does not need to absorb anything further.

The mechanism, because a ruling that yields needs one: the identity cell is a two-track grid — content at 1fr, ornament at minmax(0, 140px) — so the corner field is a track that shrinks by exactly what the content takes. Reserve and field were previously a fixed padding-bottom and a fixed absolute height, two independent numbers with nothing coupling either to remaining space, and overflow flows through padding regardless. Three things give, in order, and the arithmetic closes only once the third is counted. First the gap: 43.1px at two title lines. Then the reserve: the track resolves to 115.4px at three lines, 47.7px at four, and 0 at five. Those figures are the drawing's and the drawing has drifted: measured on the real route, the longest title in the collection is absorbed by the ornament track with 27px to spare at every viewport from 1280 to 1728. The drawn two-line base stands about 69px taller than the built stack, so the give order's arithmetic — 183.1px of give against 203.1px of growth, 20px short — is computed against a stack that does not exist. The build's measurement is authoritative here and the drawing is the defect, for the same reason as the acquisition date (§8.1): a text stack's height is a measurement, not a decision, and the drawing is a hand-set approximation of type the route sets for real. §0 makes the drawing the specification for the composition; it was never the authority on what 72px/0.94 in Inter Tight actually occupies. Recorded rather than silently corrected, because the 69px is a real divergence and the raster above still carries it. The ornament track must keep its automatic min-content minimum for any of that to happen — a min-height:0 on the content item pins the 1fr track at its base 376px and the content simply overflows the ornament instead of displacing it, which is the same ruling-without-a-mechanism defect one layer down. The field shrinks on two records and vanishes on one, which is most of what the 547px band bought: at 500px the drawn stack was 67px short and the built stack now clears by 27px. So the arithmetic closes by geometry and the collapse fires on no record in the collection today — which changes what the threshold is, not whether the mechanism exists. Stated as a condition rather than a line count: the genres run collapses when the ornament track has resolved to 0 and the remaining growth still exceeds the gap. The line count was a proxy, and "five lines" is the granularity defect §9.2 records arriving in §4.2 — the rule named lines when its reason is about height, so it fires wrongly the moment the type stack or the measure moves. Under the condition, the five-line record does not collapse and a record whose facts run one line longer does. The build asserts what the build does; a test written to the drawing's threshold would have asserted the drawing against the build, which the §8.1 sweep caught twice. The mark is specified for when it fires: §8.1 ranks it the frame's least specific line — true of the work rather than of this pressing, so the only line whose collapse costs no distinguishing information at all — which makes it the line whose loss costs least, and collapsing it frees 28.5px — enough for any shortfall the condition admits. What replaces it is a count on the format line: Vinyl, LP, Album · 3 genres, underlined, opening the editor that holds every other pressing fact. The count costs no height because it appends to a line already set, which is the only reason a mark is affordable at all in a cell that has run out of give — a second line would cost the 28.5px the collapse just recovered. This is the page's second use of a count for a fact that exists and is not shown — the first is the Images 4 Manage → line — and §6 requires absence to be visible rather than silent in any case. That precedent was withdrawn for one round and restored: the line was drawn and not built, so citing it asserted that the build matched the drawing where it did not, and the resolution was that the drawing was right. The collapse is affordable either way, because the count appends to a line already set. A reader on that record sees that the record has three genres and that this cell will not show them, which is the difference between a fact withheld and a fact lost.

Undrawn, and stated as such: the drawings above carry a one-line title and a two-line one, so neither shows the collapse, the count, or the zero-height corner track — and no record in the collection renders them either, since the condition is unmet on all seventeen. The collapse is a guard with a stated trigger rather than a case the page currently draws. Ornament yields first and completely, then the weakest fact; the first needs no external licence, because this section’s own two-track mechanism supplies it — ornament at minmax(0, 140px) is a track that shrinks by exactly what the content takes. This clause cited §5.4 and then §5.1, and both were wrong in opposite directions: §5.4 gives the ornament no box at all, and §5.1 fixes the triangle at 268 × 140, which is an immovable extent rather than one in the layout’s gift. The two are compatible because §5.1 fixes the ratio and the track fixes the height available, so the mark keeps its shape while yielding its size, and this names the second in advance instead of leaving overflow:hidden to pick. No title is truncated and nothing overlaps at any line count — on one record of seventeen, one line of genre is gone.

The cell is not too narrow, and the alternative is refused on the construction's behalf. A wider identity cell takes columns from the construction, which is the only element on the page whose value depends on having room — the probe's whole finding was that spread and a 6:1 size band are what give it something to read. Trading the construction's legibility on all seventeen records for the wrapping of one is the wrong trade, and it would also be made on the evidence of a single compilation title with a colon in it.

The artist is set twice in the supplied drawing and must ship once. Pink Floyd appears as the second line of the 72 block and again at 40 below it. The 72 block holds the title only — it is the record's name, and the composition's second line is the title wrapping demonstrated on a record whose title does not wrap. The 40 line is the artist. This is drawn correctly in §1, §6.1 and §10’s composite — no 72 block in the file contains an artist name. §1 reproduced the supplied form until the strike that resolved it; the sentence describing the two drawings as deliberately split — faithful here, correct there — outlived the split by one round. The clause above about the supplied drawing’s second line still describes what was supplied, not what §1 draws.

5 · Colour

5.1 · Eight marks, one value, derived per record

One derived value fills every colour mark on the page, at one of the three steps of §5.5 and never at an opacity variant. The marks, in the order the eye takes them: the release-year field (the only one that carries type), the bar right of the sleeve, the flat triangle in the identity block's lower-left corner, the disc behind the rendered still, the quarter-circle in provenance, the quarter-circle in About, the journal's 2px edge, and the construction's coloured faces — eight drawn regions, one value. Two vocabularies, divided by the frame, and the rule is mechanical: a mark that touches a page edge is a flat plane of the derived colour; a mark that does not is an isometric solid. No judgement, nothing to infer, and it needs no appeal to what a mark is for — a build can check it.

An edge field's extent follows its height, not its cell: the corner triangle is 268 × 140, a width-to-height of 1.91. The width was unspecified and the build had picked 180, so the file needed the number — but the first attempt at this sentence derived one, giving 182 from the projection's box ratio, and that is a rule this file is not allowed to make: §0 says every number is read off the drawing, and the drawing has said 268 in all three instances since it was made. A derivation that lands 86px from the drawn mark is not a tighter statement of it, it is a second mark. The general form, which this project has now hit seven times: a number arrived at by reasoning is a proposal, and in a file whose premise is measurement it has to be checked against the drawing before it is written, not after. Tying extent to the cell remains the wrong term — the host cell is span 4 at 480px, and a 480px triangle is a band across the block rather than a corner mark — but the alternative to a cell-relative width is a measured one, not a derived one. Both other edge fields take their extent from the drawing the same way. The division is legible at the surface because the two kinds behave differently where it matters most, at the frame: a plane that continues past the view reports that the view is a window, and an object with a slice taken out of it reports that something went wrong. Nothing else on this page is cropped, so a cropped object has no company and reads as damage.

This retracts a ruling made one turn earlier, and the retraction is the more useful record. That ruling withdrew the flat marks entirely and extended the isometric vocabulary to the edges, on the argument that a flat edge mark is a division of labour no reader can see. Drawn side by side, the opposite held — which is the sixth time in this project that a decision taken on an argument was reversed by a drawing, and the second time in this section. The part that survives is the part that was tested by looking: a mark inside a cell is an isometric solid, because a small circle floating in a cell belongs to no system while a small solid belongs to this one. The rule now covers the tested case and the frame case separately, which is what it should have done first. And this one was caught by drawing it before the build rather than after — every earlier instance in this project was found by measuring something already assembled, which is the same correction arriving at the price of work already done. Two compositions differing in three marks cost less than one implemented ruling, and that is the transferable part: when a ruling extends a tested decision into an untested case, draw the extension rather than arguing it. The black block at the sleeve's edge is no longer an exception: it touches an edge and it is flat. Settled by looking rather than by argument — for marks inside a cell, which is the only case that drawing tested: the matrix solid reads as belonging to this page and a circle floating in a cell reads as a shape that could be on any page. The quarter-circles below are not that case; they touch an edge, and the frame rule sends them the other way. A circle is not part of any system here; a box at 30° is the page's own alphabet, and an ornament drawn in it is the construction appearing small rather than a decoration appearing near it. The construction is one mark however many of its faces carry colour (§5.5), and it is a separate entry from the disc behind it — one object visually, two entries here, because the faces are base step and the disc is tint. Two black marks sit against them, both fixed at ink and neither derived: the block at the sleeve's right edge and the square in About.

Only one of the eight carries type, and after §5.2's amendment it carries only the 72. The derivation clamps the value (§5.2) and the clamp is what guarantees the field its headline allowance; the separate constraint is that no 11px type sits on a base-step ground (§5.2 — tint is admitted as ground under type, with a contrast test on the type), so the release-year label sits on paper above the field and the field holds the 72 alone, ink, at 6.32:1 against a 3:1 allowance — and at no worse than 5.4:1 anywhere in the clamp band.

5.2 · The derivation — clamped base, and one rule about what may sit on it

Sample the cover's dominant chromatic value and clamp it: lightness into 0.62–0.74, chroma to at most 0.09, hue kept as sampled. The clamp was withdrawn for one round and is reinstated (§11.4). The withdrawal's reason was that the wall rendered the same value raw and a clamp on both screens compressed the axis the wall exists to display; the wall at rest is now monochrome, so no second screen reads the value and nothing outside this page constrains it. What the clamp is for, stated without reference to the wall: the field behind the 72 must clear its headline allowance on every record, and a band guarantees that in advance rather than testing it per record. At the null-spine record the unclamped value put the 72 at 1.00 against its own ground. A test on one cell rides with it: the release-year field has an 11px mono label on it, and 11px type needs 4.5:1 — the 72 is not the binding constraint, since headline-scale type has a 3:1 allowance the field never reaches for. Re-derived at the reinstated ground, and the numbers no longer force the rule: at the clamped 0.66 0.05 the field reads 6.32:1 against ink, and across the whole band ink never falls below 5.4:1. The figures that first produced the rule were measured at the sampled 0.55 0.038 — 4.05:1 ink and 2.93:1 paper, neither clearing 4.5 — and that ground is now drawn nowhere, so the claim that the per-record flip "has no answer on the record every raster shows" is withdrawn: at the clamped ground the answer is ink, on every record. The rule survives for a reason independent of the ratios, which is the honest version of it: the field is ground for one figure. An 11px mono label on it makes the field read as a labelled swatch and the 72 as its caption — the field stops being the thing the eye lands on, which §5.1 says is its whole job — and a per-record contrast flip would also reintroduce exactly the per-record test the clamp exists to remove. So it is stated at base step: no 11px type sits on a base-step ground. Base-step grounds carry headline-scale type only, which the 72 clears at 6.32:1 against its 3:1 allowance. Tint is admitted as ground under type of any size, with a contrast test on the type rather than a ban on its size — §9.4's full fill exists precisely to be ground under content, and a rule written "derived ground" captured it, which is the coarser-than-its-rationale shape one layer out from §9.2's. Over the fill at 0.791 0.016 the muted grey reads 2.6:1 and fails outright: its 11px date takes ink at 8.3:1 and its placeholder takes 0.34 at 5.1:1, which is the test doing the work the size ban was standing in for. The release-year label moves off the field onto paper — a 30px strip above a 120px coloured block, the band's 150px unchanged — and the field holds the 72 alone. That is the granularity finding once more and in the useful direction: the constraint belongs to the 11px label, so it is discharged by moving the label rather than by moving every record's colour.

Chroma is clamped down only. The floor is withdrawn, and the sampler is the reason. MIN_REGION_CHROMA at 0.04 is a rejection threshold: a cover with no qualifying region returns its linear-light mean precisely because there was no chromatic region to trust. Lifting to 0.045 at the sampled hue would therefore assert a hue the sampler explicitly declined to identify, on five of sixteen records — and an invented hue is worse than no hue, because nothing downstream can tell it from a real one. So: lightness clamped into the band, chroma clamped down only, no chroma floor — the floor is the one part of the clamp that stays withdrawn, and it is withdrawn for a reason about the sampler rather than about contrast. #bc4889 at 0.164 and #44946b at 0.101 keep their chroma, where the withdrawn ceiling brought them down. #9b9b9a at 0.001 and #363129 at 0.016 ship as near-greys at their own lightness — a warm or cool grey at the right value, which is what those covers are.

§5.5's ladder is what makes that survivable, and it is why this is the answer rather than the other one. Tint and shade derive from base, so a near-grey base gives near-grey steps: those five records render in grey and ink with a faint warm or cool cast, the construction still reads as an object because its three tones are lightness steps and not hue steps, and nothing looks broken — it looks like a record whose sleeve has no colour. The cost, stated plainly: on five of sixteen every mark is a near-grey, so §5.5's floor is met in area and empty in effect — the marks are there at full size and none of them is carrying a hue. That is the honest version of "keyed to nothing", and it is a statement about the derivation rather than about the layout, which is why no area rule was ever going to express it. This sentence has now been rewritten three times, twice because the unit it was expressed in was deleted underneath it; it is stated in marks and hues this time because those are the things §5.2 actually controls. That figure read six until the build corrected it, and the correction is in this argument's favour. Six was measured against the averaged derivation; the resampling moved Bridge Over Troubled Water from 0.019 to 0.055, which clears the rejection threshold, so it keys. Eleven records keyed, five quiet. Same class of defect as the A62 re-measure — a figure cited as evidence, correct when written, superseded by a derivation change nobody re-checked it against — and worth stating here because the accepted cost is the thing this section is arguing about. Those records are quiet, not faulty, and quiet is a state this layout already has a vocabulary for. The alternative was a lie about the sleeve.

Four covers. Upper swatch sampled, lower swatch clamped and shipped — the lower is what every raster in this file draws:

5.3 · The record with no cover

No cover means no derivation, and the fallback is ink for all eight marks, the construction included — filled, not outlined, not omitted. The release-year label and figure reverse to paper; the journal's 2px edge goes ink. The marks must not be dropped: omitting them would let a missing image change the composition's structure, and a structure that differs between records for a reason the reader cannot name is the wallpaper rule inverted. The sleeve slot itself takes the placeholder rule already settled elsewhere — a frame at paper luminance, never a filled rectangle at cover size — so on that one record the ink marks are the page's only dark mass and the slot reads as awaiting rather than as empty.

5.4 · The two rendered stills are fixed assets

Superseded for the identity band’s still, and standing for the matrix solid — the two halves of this paragraph must not be withdrawn together. The construction generator built since (licensed by §5.1, its arrangement ruled by §20) hashes the record id for the arrangement, tones the faces from the ladder, and was tested against the seventeen real ids, so the identity still is generated per record and its base-face area is a per-record quantity §5.5’s floor measures. The matrix solid stays exactly as written — record-independent, fixed grey — and §13 depends on it: it is the one place the ladder must not reach. This paragraph was written when both were placeholders. The original: The isometric still in the identity band and the small solid in Matrix are record-independent artwork, not generated per record. They are the same image on all seventeen. Only the disc behind the large one takes colour, at the tint step (§5.5); the still itself does not recolour. The small solid in Matrix is the same artwork at small scale and therefore takes no derived colour at all — fixed grey, like the two black marks are fixed ink. A mark in the record's hue cannot be the same image on all seventeen, which is what this paragraph requires of it. Both are placeholders in every drawing in this file — their content is an asset question, and nothing in the layout depends on what they depict. That last clause is the one §17 overturns for the large still: §5.5’s floor is measured on the base faces the arrangement depicts, so the layout now depends on it precisely.

Decoration does not decorate an absence. The three edge fields are ornament: they carry no data and answer to no field. When the cell they sit in is empty, they are suppressed — §6 — because a decorated empty cell reads as a designed state rather than as a gap the reader can fill.

Superseded in part by §5.1, which gives the corner triangle 268 × 140 on the rule that an edge field’s extent follows its height — the build had picked 180 and the file needed the number. The two black marks and the quarter-circles stand as written, and §4.2’s give order and §5.5’s floor exemption both cite §5.1 for extent rather than this paragraph. The original: The five ornament marks have no geometry here and will not be given any. The three edge fields are flat planes of the derived colour, outside the projection by §5.1's frame rule, and their shapes are the render's: a corner triangle and two quarter-circles. The two black marks are flat and fixed at ink. None of the five is the construction generator's output — that was true for one turn, under the withdrawn isometric ruling, and is not true now; the generator owns the construction and the cell-contained solid in Matrix, and nothing that touches a page edge. Three edge fields, black block, black square — this file gives them a count, a value, a step (§5.5) and a suppression rule, and stops. Specifying vertices would fix by hand the exact thing the generator exists to derive, and would need re-specifying the moment the slot set changes. What the layout owes them is a box each — the cell, the inset, the corner they anchor to — and what they owe the layout is to stay inside it. Shapes, sizes and the disc's radius come from the hash. That makes them the generator's problem, and the generator has a probe. The two black marks are the exception in value only: fixed ink, never derived, because they anchor the construction rather than being its subject.

5.5 · Colour as a system, and where it stops

The page is keyed to one derived value, and being keyed is a set of relationships rather than a quantity of colour. The difference between a system and three placements is not how much there is — it is whether a reader can say what the colour means in each place without being told. Three rules do that; the fourth part is what protects them. This amends §5.1, which specified the marks and not their relationship.

One value, one ladder, three steps. The raw derivation of §5.2, then tint at 34% toward paper, base, and shade at 26% toward ink. No fourth step: three is the most a reader holds as distinct positions, and a fourth makes lightness look like it encodes something. Every coloured pixel on the screen is one of those three values.

The panel conflict, confirmed as the build resolved it, with the rule restated so it stops conflicting. Accent placement and tone derivation are two systems and the conflict came from reading one rule as governing both. Tone derivation is unchanged: top lightest, left base, right darkest, on every form. Placement is separate — an accent-bearing face takes the base step whichever face it is, so the panel, whose largest projected face is its right, carries base there and has no shade face. That does not breach the rule below; it means the rule below describes derivation and never placement. And the face is chosen by projected area, not by shape units — "top is the largest visible face" is true for beam, slab, cube and plate and false for the panel by seven times, which is what produced a 92.3/7.7 split in a path that was supposed to be traced between two ends.

The residual 87.7% worst case is not repaired, because the ratio is the wrong target — same finding as the budget, one level down. Two accent faces do not need to be equal; they need each to be findable. So the requirement on them is a floor apiece, not a ratio between them, and cube-with-plate at 2.10 against 7.84 passes if both clear it. The archetype set is left alone: changing it to equalise a ratio would be tuning the wrong axis, and the cube is small by design because the 6:1 band is what stopped the compositions reading as orderly.

The step says what kind of thing the mark is, and that is the system. Base is for marks that carry or frame the record's own material: the release-year field, the bar down the sleeve's edge, the journal's 2px edge, and the construction. The construction is one base mark however many faces carry colour — the coloured form's three plus the two accent tops are one object seen from three sides, not five marks, and every rule here that counts or sizes a mark counts it once and sizes it by its faces' combined area. The unit of counting belongs in this mapping rather than only in the enumeration below, which is where two later rules picked up the ambiguity. Tint is ground — the disc behind the construction, and the three flat edge fields — the corner triangle and the two quarter-circles. Shade is a face and never a shape: it exists only as the darkest side of a coloured form, which is the right-hand face on every archetype but a panel carrying an accent, where there is no shade face at all. A reader who notices that the strong marks always touch the record and the pale ones are always behind something has read it correctly, and there is nothing else to read.

Each band carries exactly two base marks. Identity band: the sleeve bar, and the construction — the same unit the mapping defines, counted once and including its accent tops. Record band: the year field, and the journal edge. This is the relationship §5.1 was missing — the same colour at the same strength in both halves of the page is what makes it one composition rather than a coloured lower half with accents above it.

Where it stops — five exclusions, and they are the restraint. No type is ever coloured, so no contrast floor on this page depends on the derivation. No grid rule is coloured but the single 2px journal edge — the structure is grey on every record. The paper is never tinted: one warm white on all seventeen, which is what lets the keyed marks read as keyed instead of as a theme. Nothing constant across records takes colour — nav, actions, labels, the two black blocks. No second hue and no gradient, because a derived hue plus anything is two claims about one record.

The area budget is withdrawn. It was authored, not measured, and it measures the wrong axis. This paragraph specified 12–18% of the page and asserted the budget was spent. Measured on the assembly it is 10.55% richest, 9.23% modal, 9.10% emptiest — under the floor on every record, re-measured this round because moving the 11px label off the year field cut the page's largest mark from 240 × 150 to 240 × 120 and took 1.56 points off every total (the pre-split figures were 12.11 / 10.79 / 10.66; a mark's area changing is exactly the event that makes an area figure stale, and this file has now had that class corrected in §5.2 and §4.2 as well) — which by its own wording puts almost every record in the state it names as the failure. But the figure being wrong is the smaller half. releaseYearField alone is 6.26% — 59% of all colour after the label split, 7.82% and two-thirds before it — everything else is under 1.5%. A page can hit any area target with one big rectangle, so an area percentage cannot tell a keyed composition from one large mark plus rounding, and 9.23% concentrated in a single cell is exactly the latter.

This is the general form again, and its most expensive instance: a constraint defined over an axis correlated with the signal rather than over the signal itself. The signal §5.5 is about is distribution — colour arriving at the same strength in both halves of the page — and total area is merely correlated with it. Same shape as the mean over a cover when the signal was hue, the fit over an arrangement when the signal was size, the shuffle over assignment when the signal was position. The tell is the same each time: the number moved and the thing it was meant to govern did not.

The 40% ceiling is withdrawn too — one turn after it was written, because it is the same defect a fifth time and I wrote it. A share-of-coloured-area ceiling is a ratio, and a ratio moves when either term moves: the emptiest record measures 68.8% against the richest's 59.3% not because any mark grew but because the edge fields suppress when their cells empty. Both figures are post-split — 73.4% and 63.6% before the 11px label moved off the field — and the pair moving together while the rule's subject did not is the clearest statement of why a ratio was the wrong instrument. The rule tightens hardest on the records with the least colour, which is the opposite of what it was for, and the arithmetic confirms no composition can satisfy it — reaching 40% needs total colour at 15.65% against a measured 10.55%, which would make the construction 56% solid colour and dominate the band the remedy was meant to protect. A ceiling no composition can reach is not a rule.

What replaces it is a floor on the small marks, not a ceiling on the large one, and that inverts the diagnosis. The year field at 59% is not the defect: it is the page's anchor, the one mark guaranteed on every record (§6), and the ground the 72 sits on. The defect is that the other marks are too small to be read as the same colour arriving again — the construction's coloured faces at 0.42% are the clearest case. So: every base-step mark must clear a floor, measured in the mark's own dimension. The year field is exempt, once and for this reason: it is the anchor, the one mark guaranteed on every record (§6), and a floor on it would be a floor on the thing that is never the problem. Tint marks are outside the floor entirely — the disc and the three edge fields are ground, and ground that is too small to find is ground doing its job. The count is already settled above at exactly two base marks per band; this adds a size and nothing else.

Two kinds of base mark, two measures. A field mark — in this layout, the construction — occupies area, and its floor is 0.5% of the page. A linear mark — the journal's 2px edge, the bar down the sleeve — is a line, and a line's findability is its length and its contrast, not its area: a 2px edge running a full cell height is instantly findable and will never reach 0.5% of anything. Their floor is extent: a linear mark runs the full length of the edge it marks, end to end, with no inset. Both currently pass it.

This is not the year field's exemption granted twice more, and the difference matters. The journal edge and the sleeve bar are not exempt from anything — they are measured on the axis that governs them, which is the sixth appearance of the same correction in this file: a rule defined over an axis correlated with the signal rather than over the signal itself. Area correlates with findability for a block and not for a line. The alternative readings both fail on inspection: widening the journal edge to ~20px makes a second rule weight at a thickness §3 does not have and destroys the "only 2px edge" that marks the one owner-written cell; widening the sleeve bar eats the cover, which §5.5 calls the source rather than a mark. A rule that can only be satisfied by breaking two other settled rules is measuring the wrong thing, not discovering two exceptions.

One consequence to carry into the build: the disc is tint and does not count toward the construction's base area. With it the construction measures 1.43% and clears; without it, 0.42% and fails. The failing number is the real one — a mark's floor is measured in its own step — and it reaches the remedy already named: grow the coloured faces, not the disc.

A floor is per-mark and absolute, so it does not move when the page empties, cannot be satisfied by one large rectangle, and cannot be gamed by suppression. Of the three ways out, this is the third — the year field does not shrink and the construction does not become a colour field; the construction's coloured faces, the one base field mark the floor governs, are where the page was actually failing. Total area may then land anywhere; nothing is keyed to it, and "more colour" is no longer a quantity anyone can argue about.

7 · What this file cannot answer

The fixed band heights are a bet against long content. 300px of record band holds the journal entry drawn in §1 and roughly forty more characters. There is no measured longest entry, no clamp specified, and no scroll available. Either the journal cell clamps with a more affordance or the no-scroll constraint is wrong; this file does not decide it, and it is the first thing the build will hit.

The construction crosses the rule into the title's cell, and that is the one thing on the page that makes the grid interesting rather than merely visible. Everything here obeys its box, so the grid is legible and inert; a visible grid becomes interesting only once something ignores it. Exactly one element crosses, it is the construction, and it crosses one edge — the rule between the sleeve cell and the identity cell — reaching into the identity band's lower void. The rule stays drawn at full strength underneath: a rule a form crosses still divides, and a rule deleted where the form passes is a hole rather than a crossing. One crosser is the whole of the licence — a second makes crossing the convention and the grid stops being ignored, it stops existing. This also answers the identity void without cutting the band, because what fills it is the construction reaching across rather than a new mark invented to occupy it.

The two voids are ruled together, once, and the ruling is to keep both bands at their heights. They are one lever with the colour budget — a shorter band with the same marks is a higher percentage — so ruling on them separately would rule twice on one number. The budget being withdrawn removes the reason to cut, and each band then has to justify its own height on its own content. Identity: the cell is over-constrained rather than voided. It holds the title stack, one mono pressing run and a 140px reserved corner field in 547px, which leaves 43.1px between title and pressing at two lines (§4.2) — so there is no void between them, and the empty region is the reserved corner band itself, which is a field's box rather than slack — cutting it breaks the only record that needs it, and a band sized to the modal case cannot hold the collection. Market: the void is the diagonal's box, and 7a §1.4 retired field-level diagonals for failing an area floor, so a 60% empty half is the mark doing its job on fourteen of seventeen records. Neither void is slack; both are the richest and the sparsest case sharing one geometry, which §2.1 chose deliberately.

The diagonals read as intended, and the reason they look wrong is §2.1 working. A diagonal is corner-to-corner so its extent equals its box; the grid is full-bleed with rules only where §3 puts them; so where two cells meet with no rule at that boundary, a mark filling its box has no visible edge to stop at. That is the page's own logic, not a defect in the mark or the cell — and the fix, were one wanted, would be a rule at every cell boundary, which §3 refuses for stronger reasons than this. Kept as drawn.

All eight marks are drawn; an audit that found five was counting data attributes. The release-year field is a cell background, the journal edge is a 2px border, and the construction's faces are generated SVG — none of the three carried one. A mark implemented as a property of a cell is still a mark — worth stating because the same blindness would have hidden the concentration finding above, the largest mark on the page being precisely the one with no element of its own.

Long titles: measured, and this paragraph was wrong in both directions. It claimed the 38-character title takes three lines and overflows. It takes five — the break orphans a digit — and it does not overflow: 498 of 500 at this file's exact spec, so the band holds every real title in the collection. Both halves of the error came from estimating a wrap instead of setting one, and the underestimate is the more instructive half: the number was low enough to make the problem sound like a height problem, which is the one thing it is not. §4.2 now decides it — balance the break, anchor the pressing block, no clamp. What remains genuinely open is a title longer than any that exists, for which there is 2px and no plan.

The derivation is specified and unmeasured, and one record now shows how. A predominantly green cover derives terracotta, so the sampler returned a minority accent rather than the dominant field. The share floor could not be checked: it is not in the repository at the read ref — record-colour.ts takes the dominant region as already-stored input and owes nothing to the choosing of it, so whatever picks it is not committed under src/. What is confirmed there: NEAR_GREY_CHROMA = 0.04, and lightness moved with chroma held — which is §5.2 as written. The open question is sharper than "unmeasured": whether a region qualifying on chroma and area can still lose to a smaller, more saturated one, because that is the behaviour the green cover exhibits and no floor on share alone prevents it. "Dominant chromatic value" names an intent, not an algorithm — no handling of covers with two strong hues, and no run against the seventeen stored images. The clamp's numbers are defensible; the input to them is not yet real.

Nothing below 1440 is specified. A twelve-column full-bleed grid with a 300px fixed band and two 72s has no stated behaviour when the columns stack, and the adjacency pairs in §4.1 are what break first.

The cover is fitted, not cropped, and the cell gives way rather than the artwork. A square sleeve in a wide short cell under object-fit: cover shows a horizontal slice — 83% of the artwork at 1440, 47% at 2560 — of the element §5 calls the page's entry point and the source of its colour. Nothing else on this page is allowed to be the least faithfully rendered thing on it. So the sleeve draws whole at its natural aspect, sized to the cell's height, and the cell's surplus width becomes paper beside it rather than more crop. The colour marks that sit on the sleeve's edge anchor to the image, not to the cell — the bar runs down the artwork's right edge — because a bar floating in the paper beside a cover is marking nothing.

Above 1440 is now specified, and the reason is the cover rather than the type. Measured: the 72 occupies 85% of its cell at 1440, 87% at 1728, 91% at 2560 — it gets more dominant as the page widens, not less, so the wide-viewport adjacency worry — the one raised in review, not the below-1440 one the paragraph above states, which still stands — was reasoning from the cell doubling without measuring the figure inside it. What does degrade is the sleeve: 83% of a square visible at 1440, 47% at 2560. Less than half the artwork on the element §5 calls the page's entry point and the source of its colour — which is the case for a cap, and it is a case about the image and not about the grid. The page caps at 1728 and centres, with the paper running full-bleed beyond it. The grid is unchanged below the cap; above it the columns stop growing and the bleed becomes paper margin, which §2.1's bleed sentence is amended in place to say. The title's fixed 412px measure and the flattening diagonals are real and are both consequences of the same widening; the cap bounds all three at once and eliminates none of them. At 1728 the identity cell is 576px and the title measure is still 412px, the diagonals have already flattened as far as the cap allows, and the cover has already dropped from 83%. What the cap buys is a worst case rather than a fix — the page at 1728 is partway degraded on all three axes and stays there.

The year field has 1px of slack at 1440, and that is a coincidence rather than a margin — the second on this page. A four-digit 72 measures 203px in a 240px cell with 36px of padding. A wider fallback face before the webfont lands, or any padding change, overflows the largest mark on the page, and the 900px frame has no give to absorb it. The figure filling its field is intended; one pixel of proof is not. The repair is to make the fit a property of the cell rather than of the glyph widths: the year sets in a box the cell reserves for it, and the padding yields before the figure does. That is not drawn here — and after the 498-of-500 title this file has now found the same shape twice, which makes it a thing to check rather than a thing that happened: for every mark measured to fit, name what gives when it does not.

This file specifies no interaction, and did not notice. Searched: disclosure, Manage, upload, Images — zero occurrences of each before this paragraph. Six things the record detail does are absent from every section above: the image uploader, the journal form, the snippet generator, the live market fetch, tags, and four pressing facts — plant, weight, colour, reissue. They were not deferred, because a deferral would be listed here. §2.1 through §6 describe a composition of facts and nothing else: every band height, every empty-state rule, every mark floor was measured against a field that renders a value. The claim made in earlier turns that the uploader and the note were "answered by moving them into cells" is withdrawn — no cell in §1 holds either, and the file has never held a control of any kind.

Field values are plausible, not real, except title, artist, year, label and the Donovan sleeve. Matrix strings, market figures and both About texts are illustrative, and no record in the collection has been confirmed to carry a matrix value at all — which is why §6 lists that row as unmeasured rather than giving it a count.

8 · The frame is the top of a longer page

The no-scroll constraint narrows to what it was always measuring: the record's facts fit one screen. Nothing is given up by saying so, because nothing in this file was ever spent on an interaction. The 900px budget in §2.1, the fixed bands, the one-diagonal rule, the mark floors, the title measure — every one was taken against a field that renders a value, and all of them survive the narrowing unchanged. A constraint scoped to what it measured is not a weakened constraint; it is a constraint that has stopped claiming territory it never surveyed.

The alternative is refused on this file's own evidence. Absorbing a file picker, a textarea, a live fetch and a price list into the frame means growing it or hiding four interactions behind modals — and the frame has 1px of slack at the year cell and 2px at the longest title (§4.2, §7), both already recorded as coincidences standing in for margins. Adding six controls to a frame that is exactly full would make that three, and the third would be the one that broke. It would also require specifying six interactions this file has never addressed, on a page whose every measurement was taken on facts — which is the extension-without-a-drawing failure this project has recorded seven times.

The fold is a composition edge, not a cut. The frame ends where §2.1 ends it — on the record band's closing rule, the tail having gone to the identity band — so the first screen closes on the same 1px edge every band closes on and the page below begins after a division rather than mid-band. No mark, rule or field may straddle 900, and the one element licensed to cross a rule (§7's construction) crosses a vertical inside the identity band and never the fold.

Below the fold takes this file's type, ink and grid, and not its band heights. Inherited: the scale with nothing between 40 and 15, mono uppercase labels at 11 with .10em tracking, 1px hairlines at oklch(0.72 0.004 80), the paper, the ink, the twelve-column full-bleed grid with its 1px cell verticals, and §5.5's ladder — every control label is a label, so the sections below are typographically this page. Not inherited: fixed band heights, and nothing else. Those exist because of a budget, and below the fold there is no budget — height is content-derived, sections stack, and a form that grows pushes the page down instead of overflowing a band. The grid stays because bands are height and columns are alignment (§9.1), so dropping the budget drops the height only. The derived colour crosses the fold at the base step and nowhere else: a base mark on four of the eight sections, selected by the rule in §9.4, plus ornament at the tint step (§9.2), and no construction — that stays the identity band's. The earlier version of this sentence barred ornament below the fold, which is what made the region read as correct rather than designed: a colour bar under a label is a compliance mark, and a page whose decoration stops at 900px is a composition with a document under it.

8.1 · No fact lives below the fold

The frame holds the facts that identify which record and which pressing this is; below the fold describes the copy — its manufacture and its condition. That is the line, and a build applies it without judgement: a fact that would let you tell this pressing from another pressing of the same title goes above the fold; a fact that only describes the object in your hands goes below. Label, catalogue number, country, year, format and matrix identify the pressing. Plant, weight and pressing colour describe the copy. Genres describe neither — they describe the work, and that is the third case the test needs, because the frame holds the record and only the region below holds the object. A genre is true of every pressing ever made of this title and of the music itself, so it cannot sort by a test about telling pressings apart; it belongs with title and artist, which are also facts about the work, and those are the frame's first two lines. The rule in its complete form, and scoped to what it was derived for — the pressing block, and nothing else: of the facts that would otherwise sit in that block, those true of the work or of the pressing stay above the fold, and those true only of the physical copy go below. Plant, weight and colour would differ on another copy of the same pressing; label, catalogue number, country, year, format, matrix and genres would not. The test has no jurisdiction outside that block, and the first version of this sentence claimed it did — "nothing in the frame is true of this copy alone" is false on the drawing in three cells, and a build applying it would have moved provenance, the note and the journal below the fold, emptying three of the record band's five cells, retiring three rows of §6's empty-state table, leaving §3's only 2px edge with nothing to mark and §5.5's record band with one base mark against a required two.

The owner's material is in the frame because it is copy-specific, not in spite of it. Provenance, the note and the journal are the only facts on the page that exist nowhere but here — a catalogue holds the pressing facts and Discogs holds the market, and none of them holds where this copy was bought or what it sounds like. That is what makes this a collection page rather than a catalogue entry, which is the argument §3 already makes when it spends the page's only 2px edge on the journal cell. A rule that sorted them below the fold would be sorting out the reason the page exists. Provenance and §9's Acquisition section are therefore one fact in two places and the frame's copy is the canonical one — the section below is its editor. The frame's cell is NOTE and §9's section is ABOUT THIS RECORD. Both surfaces said About this record and they hold different columns — the cell is record.notes, the owner's own sentence; the section is record.snippet, generated. The frame's labels are field names — PRESSING, PROVENANCE, MATRIX / RUNOUT — and NOTE is the register of its neighbours, which a sentence-shaped label is not. Attribution is not the label's job: the section's own Written by Claude line carries it, so MY NOTE would buy nothing and would be the only possessive label in a frame that belongs to the record rather than its owner. ABOUT THE MUSIC was the other candidate and it repeats what the section's provenance line already says.

The cost, accepted: the cell keeps notes, so its diagonal fires on most of the collection. That is §6 working — an empty note is a fact absent, and the diagonal is the page's mark for one — and it is the right trade against a cell holding generated text under a field name.

Three of §9's eight sections edit a fact the frame shows — Acquisition for provenance, Market for the median, Images for the count. The remaining five stand alone.

The test, because the same measurement was about to retire four other things: a constant is retired when no field exists for the values that would vary it, and kept when the field exists and is unfilled. The first is a fact about the app; the second is a fact about today's data. A rule that reads texture from an unfilled field is measuring the owner's backlog rather than the design — and the defect in the earlier refusal was not the measurement, which was true, but the inference drawn from it.

What the correction reaches, checked rather than assumed: the count returns to the frame; §4.2's citation of it is sound again and restored; §9.4 still marks Images, now on a true ground; and the gallery's two empty states and Images' control-only rendering on sixteen of seventeen are correct today and expire as the collection fills — each describes one image per record, which is a state the app expects to leave, so none may harden into a rule. The date is unaffected and stays struck: the build was right and the drawing wrong, the first divergence in this file to resolve that way, which §0 makes worth naming as the exception.

7a §1.4 retires a mark that is constant across the collection, and the two candidates here split on why they are constant. purchase_date is constant because the app abandoned the field — nothing will ever write it, so the mark can only be texture, and its appearance in the drawing as April 2019 was that retirement not having reached the drawing. The image count is constant because the collection is unphotographed: the schema carries four types — cover, gatefold left, gatefold right, back — so one image per record is a backlog, not a ceiling. The frame therefore draws Images 4 Manage → and does not draw the date — the first time in this file that the divergence has resolved that way, and worth saying plainly because §0 makes the drawing the specification.

Which means provenance is three facts and not four: paid, store and condition. Acquisition stays unmarked either way, but "the frame shows provenance in full" claimed a completeness the field set cannot support, and a ground that overstates is the same defect as one that is false — it just fails later.

Two of seven grounds false on the sweep's first run, in a file read many times, and the two share a cause worth more than the rate: both described something the drawing shows and the build does not. A ground of the form "because the frame shows X" is not a claim about the frame — it is a claim that the build matches the drawing at X, which nothing in this file checks. The grep finds the clause and cannot tell you which side moved, so the review step is two-sided: find X in the build, and if it is absent, rule whether the drawing or the build is the error before touching the ground that cited it. This sentence said three, and all three of its other clauses were false in the same way: Images edits the Images 3 Manage count, which the frame has never drawn; Snippet edits "the text in the journal cell", which drew record.notes and not the snippet (§9.4); and Journal was the target of the frame's Add entry trigger, which the frame no longer carries. Images edits the count and not the sleeve: §8.3 took the cover out of that gallery as a correct de-duplication, so the sleeve cell has no editor below the fold and pairing them here would re-add the cover and reinstate the No images yet falsehood on all seventeen records. And the frame's journal cell shows the snippet, not an entry — §9's Snippet section is generated from the journal, so the cell's prose is the snippet's and its editor is Snippet, which is why Journal is a target rather than an editor. Tags is the clearest of the four that stand alone, on this section's own ruling: a tag is a control and not a fact, so the frame deliberately holds nothing for it to edit. Price history is the other kind — the frame carries the median, and a history is a different fact rather than that one's editor. A section is an editor only where the frame already shows the thing it edits; otherwise it is where the fact lives. §8's claim therefore holds in its exact form, and "some of them" is answered by naming the kind rather than by moving everything.

This withdraws the previous ruling, which moved all four into the frame as a second mono pressing run — it was unbuildable against the cell it was written for. The identity cell holds the title stack and a 140px reserved corner field in 500px, and the second run took the title→pressing gap from 112px to 3.7px, moving the drop threshold to three title lines and the cost to three records of seventeen. A ruling whose price is three records losing facts, paid to keep two facts off the far side of a fold, is on the wrong side of its own trade. The run is withdrawn from both drawings and the gap returns to 43.1px. Reissue stays in the frame — it identifies the pressing rather than describing the copy — and it costs no height at all: it joins the 11px mono label above the 72, which reads Release year · reissue. Not a new line under the figure: §4.1 licenses small-above-large and spends its one large-to-small exception on the identity block, so a mono line beneath the 72 would be a second exception introduced by citation rather than by ruling — and a separate line above it would put an intervening element in a pairing §4.1 requires to have none. Qualifying the existing label breaks neither clause. The word is absent, not false, on an original pressing.

The cost is now paid in ornament rather than in facts, which is the trade this file should have made first. §4.2 anchors the pressing block to a reserved floor 140px above the cell edge and flows the title from the top, so the gap takes the extra line — 43.1px at two lines, which is a whole third line of title. Beyond that the corner reserve yields and the triangle shrinks with it: 115.4px at three lines, 47.7px at four, gone at five. On the supplied distribution (8 at one line, 6 at two, 2 at three, 1 at five) two records have a smaller corner field, and the one five-line record loses its corner field and keeps its genres as a list, since §4.2's collapse condition is unmet on all seventeen (§4.2) — the count is what the layout would withhold, and it would say so where it withholds it. Ornament gives first and completely; a fact gives only after ornament is exhausted, and only the weakest one. That ordering is the rule, not the fact-drop — the page has one element carrying no information and it is spent to zero before anything that carries some is touched.

Tags stay below and the section is renamed Tags, because a tag is a control and not a fact. The test that decides it: a tag's value is that it groups this record with others, which can only be read in a list. Genres describe the record and belong in the frame, where they now are; tags describe the owner's filing and belong with the controls. Filed under was a heading over two different things and stops being one.

One route to the collection, and it is the chrome's. Navigation is constant across records (§3), so it lives in AppHeader and nowhere else; the 10px ← Collection is deleted. The identity cell's Collection eyebrow stays and is not a link — it is the band's label, which is why it is set in the label system rather than as a control.

One Add entry, and the cell's is the control. A label announcing a control 900px below it is the seam in one element. The journal cell's Add entry becomes the trigger — it opens the form below and takes the reader there — and the section below loses its own trigger and becomes the target, keeping the form's submit (§9.3) — a target without a submit is a dead end, and a submit is not the trigger that reached it. Every other control pair below the fold goes to the label system: Edit / Delete and the snippet's pair at 11px mono uppercase in ink, which ends two vocabularies inside one pair; destructive actions take no colour, since §5.5 excludes anything constant across records. Cover and Back lose their uppercase sans — the only uppercase-sans on the page — for the same 11px mono. The snippet's two explanatory lines go from 10 to 13: 10 is reserved for dated meta lines (§4.1) and those are prose.

8.2 · The two shared-surface rulings

MarketPanel converts, and the reach beyond this page is the reason to do it rather than the reason not to. Its tokens map onto the scale without a judgement call — text-xs to 11px mono uppercase where it labels and 13 where it reads, text-sm to 13, text-muted-foreground to oklch(0.44 0.008 70) — so the conversion is a narrowing onto one scale and not a restyle. A shared component on a different type system is how the seam reappears on every screen that mounts it, and the market figure at 40 in the frame is already this file's; the panel below carrying a second market vocabulary is the same fact in two voices.

The sparkline is ink, not the derived colour, because a series is not a mark. Price history's base mark is the bar in its rail (§9.4), so the series has no colour work to do — and it could not do it: forty plotted points are a mark only by fiat, which is not true to what a sparkline is. It is drawn in the rule vocabulary instead — 1px ink, the hairline weight of §3 — which is what a line of data should be on a page whose structure is hairlines. Market carries no mark at all, its figure being drawn in the frame as well (§9.4), so neither section asks a series to be one.

8.3 · A shape worth keeping: removing a duplicate can install a falsehood

Taking the cover out of the gallery — a correct de-duplication, since the frame already shows it — made a cover-only record indistinguishable from a record with no images, so the gallery read No images yet with the cover six columns wide on the same screen. On seventeen of seventeen records, because every record in this collection has exactly one image and it is always the cover. The shape: a de-duplication removes a value from one surface and that surface goes on rendering the state the value used to rule out — the duplicate was not redundant, it was the only evidence distinguishing two cases. Same class as the defects this file keeps recording, with the sign flipped: those were operations defined over an axis merely correlated with the signal; this is a removal justified by an axis merely correlated with redundancy. Two empty states now exist, and a test asserts the two cases stay distinguishable at the grouping layer, so the repair sits where the information is rather than where the symptom appeared.

The same twelve columns as the frame, with row heights derived from content. Drawn at 1440, shown at 0.5722, richest state. The label rail is a column span rather than a separate structure, so every section aligns with the bands above it.
