9.1 · Twelve columns, content-derived rows

The same repeat(12, 1fr) as §2.1, gap 0, full bleed, 34px padding inside every cell — and row heights derived from content instead of fixed. This replaces the 216px label rail, which was the wrong repair. The argument for it was that the twelve columns exist for a budget that does not apply below the fold — but that is an argument against the fixed bands, not against the columns. Bands are height and columns are alignment; dropping the budget only requires dropping the height. A rail aligned to nothing above it made the page a grid with a document stapled under it, and the frame's own record band is already what this region needed to be: twelve columns whose cells hold different things.

The rail survives as a span, not as a structure: the label occupies the first two columns of every section. Same reading — a label on the left, content to its right — and now its x is a column edge rather than an invented one, so it lines up with the identity cell above it. The colour bar sits under the label inside that span, which keeps §9.3 exactly as ruled.

Three content splits and no more, which is what stops each section inventing its own: the ten columns right of the label divide 10, or 5 + 5, or 6 + 4. The section picks by the shape of what it holds — 10 for one continuous thing (tags, thumbnails), 5 + 5 for two comparable things (pressing pairs, source/date, figure/action, series/rows), 6 + 4 for a body with an action beside it (snippet, journal). Four content shapes, three splits, no fourth pattern: label-value pairs and list rows both take 5 + 5 because a date-and-price row and a plant-and-value row are the same object, and a form takes the same 5 + 5 as the pairs it edits. A section needing a fourth split is a section whose content has not been identified yet.

Vertical rules return, because there are cells again: 1px oklch(0.72 0.004 80) on the right of every cell but the last, exactly as §2.1 draws them. That is the second thing the rail could not do — a rail has one edge and a grid has as many as it has cells, and the region now divides horizontally the way the frame does. Section boundaries stay as ruled: the full-bleed hairline of §3 running to the composition's edge while cell padding keeps content at 34px, which is the distinction §3 makes load-bearing and the one thing about the rail version that was right.

Height is derived at every level and nothing is reserved. A row is as tall as its tallest cell, a section as tall as its row, the region as tall as its sections; a form that grows pushes everything below it down. An empty section is not rendered at all — no diagonal, no label, no cell — and §6's one-diagonal rule still does not cross the fold, for the reason it did not before: above, absence must be drawn because the geometry is fixed; below, drawing it would be inventing content. A section with a control renders with the control alone.

9.2 · How an ornament gets a box when the box is not known until render

The frame's ornament rules assume a geometry this region does not have — every mark above the fold sits in a cell of stated height, and below it a cell is 40px on one record and 300px on another. The answer is that ornament here is sized by width and gated by height, because width is the one dimension the region inherited as fixed. Twelve columns at 120px are known before any content renders; heights are not. So an in-cell solid is sized at 0.62 × its section's height — 0.627 of the cell it sits in, the two differing because the section carries the 1px border-top — its width follows the archetype rather than a fixed ratio, and it is placed against the cell's bottom-right corner bleeding past it. This sentence read “0.62 × its cell's height” and “width follows from that height by the projection (h / 1.06)” until now; both are corrected later in this section, which left the first sizing rule a reader meets stating the superseded base and the withdrawn constant. On the four carrying cells that is 79, 72, 76 and 94 tall — height is the primary term and width is derived from it, which is the opposite of the withdrawn rule and the reason the ruled value survives a round trip: the first implementation of this computed height, derived width, then re-derived height from that width, inflating every solid by a pixel and drawing 0.63 where the rule says 0.62. Height rather than width, and that is §10.3's ruling applied here rather than described elsewhere: the earlier rule said half a column, which is a width, and in cells eleven times wider than tall the dimension carrying presence is height — the granularity finding below, arriving one level out. A prior correction in the same term is worth keeping because it is the reason the rule is stated relatively at all: at a fixed 120px a solid is 127px tall, and once the gate and the control clearance are both applied there is exactly one cell in the region it can legally occupy. A rule permitting one position is not a rule about where ornament goes.

Two shapes recorded, both from this subsection's four rounds. The first is new and is not the derived-from-a-set defect §9.4 carries: a rule whose parameters make it vacuous, where every attempt to fix the rule is working on the wrong term. The tell is a rule that keeps needing loosening and keeps not converging — four rounds amounting to relaxing a gate and a clearance that were both correct, against a size that was not. Check the parameters before the predicate when a rule will not settle.

The second explains the other two restatements and is the more transferable: a rule stated at a coarser granularity than its rationale excludes cases the rationale permits. The gate named the solid's total box when its reason is about how much of the solid a reader sees, and the bottom bleed is deliberate — so no one-column solid could pass. The clearance named cell membership when its reason is competition with a hit target, and a cell can be 600px wide and hold a 44px button — so it barred a solid 200px clear of it. The check is whether the thing the rule names is the thing the reason is about: distance rather than membership, visible height rather than total box, and the unit a parameter is set in rather than a unit it merely resembles. No ornament is ever measured against a height it cannot know.

The gate is a ratio, measured on the solid's visible height: a solid renders only where the part of it inside the cell is at most two-thirds of the cell's height, and suppresses entirely above that. Visible, not total, because the bottom bleed is deliberate — an earlier version of this sentence gated the cell at 1.5 × the solid's whole box, which no one-column solid can ever satisfy (127px box needs a 190px cell; the tallest non-control cell in the region is 175px), so the rule as first written permitted zero positions while the drawing showed two. The ratio is also the right thing to measure: the gate exists so ornament does not dominate the cell it decorates, which is a proportion rather than a clearance. Under a height-relative size the gate binds at one value: the solid is 0.62 × its section's height, which is 0.627 of the cell it sits in, against a ceiling of two-thirds. Section, not cell, and the two differ: the section carries the 1px border-top and its cells resolve sub-pixel, so a cell is about 1.2px shorter than the section it belongs to — 126.4 against 127. The rule names the section because that is the height a build has before the cells lay out, and the gate's ceiling is checked against the cell, which is the box the solid is clipped by.

One mechanism note, recorded here rather than at the call site, because the next reader of "0.62 of the section's height" will reach for the same thing: do not use container-type: size. It expresses the rule with no measurement at all, which is why it is the obvious choice, and it collapses the layout — size containment removes a cell's contents from its own height calculation, so a 140px section renders at 69 and the solid at 0 × 0. A percentage height with aspect-ratio for the width does the same job without the circularity and keeps the component server-side.

The archetype varies and the source is the cell, not the record. All four solids being the same cube is a defect — the frame's generator has six archetypes and §9 was using none — but the fix has to survive the size rule, which describes a cube and nothing else. So height stays the governed term at 0.62 of the section, and width follows the archetype rather than a fixed 1.06: a beam at 0.8 × 0.8 × 7.6 draws wide and shallow, a plate at 2.8 × 2.8 × 0.28 draws wide and flat, an upright panel draws narrow. Height carries presence, so fixing height is what preserves the rule; h / 1.06 was never the rule, it was the cube's instance of it. It was not even that by the time it was written: the redrawn cube is 66 × 76, a ratio of 0.87. So the constant was not a rule over-generalised from one case — it was a rule over-generalised from a case that had since moved, which is worse, because a reader checking it against the drawing would have found it wrong for the member it names.

The gate takes no archetype and that is deliberate. It asks what fraction of the cell's height the solid occupies, and height is governed at 0.62 for every archetype — so the answer cannot depend on which one is drawn. Threading an archetype through it would imply it could, which is a worse defect than the redundancy it removes. A fifth archetype needs a width relationship and nothing else.

Which archetype a cell gets is fixed per section and written down: Pressing detail the beam, Snippet the plate, Market the cube, Price history the panel — drawn at 115 × 79, 113 × 72, 66 × 76 and 48 × 94, one height rule and four silhouettes. The first version of this rule derived the archetype from the cell's proportion — beam for a wide cell, cube for a square one — which is a better rule and is vacuous here: the four carrying cells measure 4.75, 6.27, 4.92 and 4.00 : 1, so every one of them is "wide" and the rule yields one archetype for all four, plus no verdict at all at exactly 4.00. A rule that derives variety from an axis the real set does not vary along produces none — the shape §9.2 already records twice, arriving a third time in the round that cites it. The assignment is therefore a decision rather than a derivation, which is also the honest description of what it is.

Not per record, and that is the same ruling §9.4 made for the bars. A hashed or per-record archetype makes the region's ornament encode which record you are on — and the page already has a thing that does that, deliberately and at scale: the construction in the frame. The frame's ornament is the record's; the region's is the page's. The region is an index, and an index whose decoration changes per entry is asking to be read as data. Two marks encoding identity in two vocabularies would also undo the one-vocabulary ruling by the back door. That is the gate doing the work it was written for rather than passing trivially — at the withdrawn fixed size the four cells measured 0.40, 0.39, 0.43 and 0.32, so no placement could ever have failed it. 0.62 rather than something nearer the ceiling is a rounding margin, not a maximum: 0.65 passes a two-thirds gate too, but cell heights are sub-pixel and the solid's is an integer, so a value that close crosses the ceiling on some cells and not others — and a gate that fails by rounding is the coincidence-for-margin defect the title band and the year field each produced once. The drawn ratios are 0.627 on three cells and 0.623 on the fourth. One test, one number, applied per cell at render — not a whitelist of sections with a content floor, which was the other candidate and is the enumeration defect §9.4 records: a section's height varies by record, so a rule naming sections decides on the schema what only the record can answer. The gate is also why suppression is safe here, and §5.4 agrees rather than forbidding it: “decoration does not decorate an absence” requires the edge fields to suppress when their cell is empty, on the identical ground — ornament carries no data — so a record whose Acquisition cell is one line short simply has no solid there. What forbids suppression is §6, and only for a fact: an absent fact must be visible rather than silent, which is why a diagonal fires where a solid does not. An earlier version of this sentence had §5.4 forbidding it, which is the reverse of its source and would have told a build the file’s ornament-suppression rule was a prohibition.

Flat edge fields attach to the region, not to a cell, and bleed off the composition's bottom edge. That is the one place below the fold where a height is known — the region's own end — and it is also what §5.1's frame rule requires: a mark touching a page edge is a flat plane, a mark not touching it is an isometric solid. So the division of labour is exactly the frame's, re-derived from what each kind can be measured against: solids go in cells because a column width is enough to size them, and planes go on the region's edges because a cell's edge is not the composition's.

Everything is tint step and nothing is base. The three faces of a solid are three lightnesses of the one tint value, not three hues — which is §5.3's argument that a form reads as an object because its tones are lightness steps. That keeps §9.4's base-mark count at four and untouched: ornament is ground, the bars are the record's colour arriving, and a reader can still tell which is which because one kind sits in the label column and the other never does.

One per section, and no solid may intersect a control's box or come within half a column of it — the same unit the solid is sized in. The constraint is proximity, not cell membership — an earlier version of this sentence said "never in the same cell as a control", which is coarser than its own reason: a cell can be 600px wide and hold a 44px button, so cell membership bars a solid 200px clear of the thing it is meant to protect. The reason is that a solid behind or beside a file picker or a submit is decoration competing with a hit target, and §9.3's controls are the one thing in this region a reader must find first — which makes the test a distance, measured against the control's box. A ruled input fails it at any distance, because the field spans its cell's full inner width — so Acquisition carries no solid in either cell, which is where the first version of this drawing put one, painting over 120px of the Date field's underline. The uploader and the textarea fail the same way by filling their cells, so Images and Journal carry none, and Tags is excluded by its + add chip. The four that remain are the cells holding only type: Pressing detail's pairs, Market's figure, Snippet's prose, Price history's series. Drawn here: half-column solids in Pressing detail, Market, Snippet and Price history, and two quarter-circles on the region's bottom edge. Ornament is a layer, and the layer is structural rather than a set of z-indexes on the elements that happened to collide. Every cell carries position: relative; isolation: isolate; overflow: hidden — relative to be the containing block, isolate to be a stacking context so a negative index cannot escape to an ancestor, hidden to clip what bleeds — and every ornament sits at z-index: -1 inside it — behind all of the cell's content and in front of the cell's own background, with nothing lifted and nothing enumerated. Controls, ruled fields, chips, uploaders, textareas and type runs are above ornament because they are in flow, not because each was named: the first implementation of this lifted elements by matching their heights and missed the textarea, the uploader and the tag chips — the enumeration defect, inside the paragraph that disavows it. The three declarations are stated here rather than left to the build because a paragraph forbidding per-element lifts has to say what replaces them, and this defect has now occurred twice: three patches in the frame, eleven lifts here.

One note on how the gate was tested, because the distinction survives as prose while the code does something else. A test named for measuring the solid's visible part passed against a gate written on its total height: the two differ only where the cell is shorter than the solid, and there both reject anyway, so no test of the gate's boolean can distinguish visible from total. The distinction is real and lives in the ratio, which is where it is asserted. A test that exercises a rule's output cannot check a premise the output is insensitive to — assert the intermediate value, not the verdict. The frame needed the same fix and it failed there first as three patches, which is why it is stated as a layer here: a per-collision z-index is correct until the next placement moves, and a layer is correct for placements nobody has drawn yet.

9.3 · Controls, which 8a had never drawn

One control vocabulary: 44px tall, 1px ink box, no fill, no radius, 11px mono uppercase ink label — and box-sizing: border-box, so the authored height is the rendered one. The box is §3's hairline weight at ink rather than grey, which is the smallest possible difference that says pressable on a page built from hairlines; a filled button would be the only solid non-derived mass on the page and would read as a colour mark. 44px satisfies the hit-target floor and is also 4× the label's 11px, so the control's height is on the type scale rather than beside it.

Inputs are ruled fields, not boxes: a 1px ink underline under a 16px line, 34px tall — sans where the field takes prose, mono where it takes data, which is §4.1's split applying to entry exactly as it applies to display, so Source is sans and Date is mono. Text entry belongs to the type system, and a box around a line of type is a second frame around something the cell already framed.

16px, not 13, and the conflict is with §4 rather than with A67. A67 is a correctness rule with a named browser failure — Safari zooms a focused input under 16px — and a type-system claim does not outrank a browser that moves the page. But the honest statement of the cost is not "3px larger": it is that 16 is not on the scale at all, which §4.1 states as nothing between 40 and 15. So this is a scale amendment and is written as one: the scale admits 16 for the typed line of an input, and for nothing else. Not for labels, not for prose, not for a heading, not for the field's label above it, and not for read-only data that happens to sit in a field-shaped box. The scope is exactly "text the user can put a cursor in", which is the scope of the browser behaviour that forces it — a size introduced to satisfy a rule must be bounded by that rule's own reach, or the next value with a good reason arrives at 14 and the scale is a suggestion. Geometry is unaffected and the drawing carries it: at 16px/1.9 the line is 30.4px inside a 34px border-box field with a 1px bottom border. The three typed lines above — Source, Date, the journal placeholder — are the whole scope of the 16 in this composition, and they are drawn at it rather than described at it, because this file is the build reference and a build reads the drawing.

Three exceptions, each for a reason the vocabulary cannot cover. The journal textarea takes a full 1px grey box, because it is a region of text rather than a line and a region with only a baseline has no shape at all. The uploader is a dashed 1px grey square at the thumbnail's exact size — same footprint as what it will become, which is §6's sleeve-placeholder rule applied to a control. Tag chips are 30px rather than 44px, because a chip is a value with an affordance attached and not a control; the + add chip is the same box at 1px dashed muted.

Destructive actions are identical to constructive ones. §5.5 excludes anything constant across records from taking colour, and Delete is on every record — so it cannot be red here without red becoming a second non-derived hue on a page keyed to one. The confirmation carries the weight instead, which is where it belongs: a button cannot be dangerous, only an action can.

A form's submit is not the trigger that opened it, and the two never share a label. The frame's journal cell carries Add entry as the trigger (§8.1); this region's Journal section carries Save entry, which is the submit. Drawn with the trigger's label it would be the same seam §8.1 removed — one control announced in two places 900px apart — and a reader who has already pressed Add entry is not adding anything by pressing it again.

9.4 · Where the colour goes, and the floor that does not apply

One base-step mark per qualifying section, in the label span under the label: a 44 × 10 bar. The full fill is admitted, once per region, and it is tint — which means it is not a mark and does not displace one. Base was the tempting answer and it is wrong twice: it would put a second mass at the record's colour, and §5.2's lightness derivation depends on the year field being the only base mark carrying type. The objection to tint — that ground is too weak to anchor — mistakes how the two anchor: a mark anchors by contrast, ground anchors by area, and a tint plane at cell scale has forty times a bar's area. That is why it can be the region's floor at a step the bars would be invisible at. It fills the last section's widest cell, one per region rather than one per section, and the bar in that section stays — a mark and its ground are different objects, so no count is affected. Last, because §10.3 orders the region by density and a page thinning downward needs something to stop on. It sits there because the label span is the constant — a mark at the label column's x sits on the one line the reader has already learned, so it reads as the colour arriving again rather than as a new mark, which is what §5.5's distribution rule asks of the frame and what no single large mark can do.

One test applied to all eight: a section carries the mark when it holds a fact that appears nowhere above the fold. Marked — Pressing detail (plant, weight and colour are drawn in no frame cell), Images (the frame shows a count, never the images), Price history (the frame shows one figure, never the series), Journal (the frame shows no entry at all), Snippet (§10b's generated text is a column of its own and no frame cell has ever drawn it). Unmarked — Acquisition and Market, because the frame draws provenance’s three facts and the median and those sections only edit and refresh them; Tags, because a tag is a control and not a fact (§8.1). Five of eight, and the test decides each section without reference to any other.

Two of those grounds were false statements about the build and they moved the verdict in both directions. Snippet was unmarked because "its text is exactly what the frame's journal cell draws" — the cell drew record.notes, the owner's own text, and the snippet is record.snippet, a separate generated column the frame has never shown. Snippet was always marked under this predicate; the file said otherwise for four rounds. And Journal was marked because "the frame's journal cell shows the snippet, not an entry" — the cell drew an entry, above the note, so the verdict was right and the reason named neither of the two facts the cell actually held.

The shape, and it is not one of the seven §9.2 records: a correct predicate correctly applied to a false fact about the build. Nothing in the chain fails — the rule is sound, the application is sound, the input is wrong — so it survived four rounds of review of the rule it justifies. A predicate gets checked against its cases and the cases against each other, while the sentence asserting what the build draws sits outside both loops. The check is mechanical and belongs in review: for every ground of the form "because the frame shows X", find X in the frame. And what exposed it was a change rather than a review — removing the journal cell forced the question of what that cell had shown, which four readings of the predicate never asked.

Five is what the rule yields, not a target. Four was an observation of the output when the output was wrong, and this paragraph states no minimum and no maximum: a predicate that decides each section on its own cannot also promise a count.

The predicate is evaluated against the schema, not against the record — a section carries the mark when the kind of fact it holds appears nowhere above the fold, whether or not this record has one. So Images, Journal and Price history are marked on all seventeen, including the sixteen where Images and Journal are control-only. The decisive argument is that the alternative makes the mark encode data. A bar that appears when a record has images and vanishes when it does not is an indicator of that fact, and nothing on this page encodes anything — §4 refuses a third 72 for that reason, §5.3 refuses to drop the coverless record's marks for it, and the construction fixes its form count for it. A mark whose presence is information is a different kind of object from a mark that says which record you are looking at.

The measurement makes this load-bearing rather than a detail: on the modal record only four sections render and all four are control-only, so on sixteen of seventeen records the marked set is Images and Journal alone. Evaluating per-record would give the modal page zero marks, which retires the repetition the floor exemption rests on and leaves the region with no derived colour at all on almost the whole collection. Two marks at a constant x is the real repetition this region ships — the drawing's four is the richest record only, and the argument below is made at two.

A mark beside a control-only section is not a mark beside nothing. A section renders when it has content or a control (§9.1), and a control-only Images section is still where this record's images go — the bar says the record's colour reaches that place, not that something is in it. This is §5.3's ruling one region out: there the coverless record keeps all its marks because a missing image may not change the composition's structure, and here an imageless record keeps its label-span mark for the same reason.

A mark on every section would be texture, which §5.5's reasoning retires. And the repetition case is positional rather than numerical — an earlier version of this passage put it as a count, four repetitions being the minimum that reads. That was smuggled in from thinking of the bars as standalone marks, and it would mean the region falls below its own floor on the sixteen records that ship two, which is the opposite of what the exemption exists for. The label column is what repeats; the bars only have to sit in it. Two marks far apart at an x the reader has met in eight labels are the same event as four, because the thing establishing the position is the column and not the marks. No minimum count is specified, and none should be implemented.

§5.5's 0.5%-of-page floor does not govern below the fold, and the reason is the floor's own argument. It exists because a mark too small to find in a fixed composition is not arriving at all — findability inside one screenful. Below the fold the marks repeat in a column, and position does the work area did above. A 44 × 10 bar is 0.02% of the region and findable because it sits in the label column — the one x this region trains the reader to read down, and the same x whether a record ships two bars or four. Measuring it against the frame's floor would be the same defect this file has recorded seven times — applying a rule across an axis it was never derived over.

Recorded as its own shape, distinct from the six this file already carries: those were operations defined over an axis merely correlated with the signal; this is a rule derived from a set, which will always fit that set and may fit nothing else. The tell is that it cannot be applied to a member you have not already decided — the test for any rule stated over an enumeration is to hand it a section the drawing does not contain. Three versions of the mark rule failed that test before the drawing changed instead of the rule.

§10 · The page as one composition

The richest record, frame and region together, uncropped at 57.4% — every drawing until now showed one region at a time, which is why the two rhythms were never visible in the same view.

10.1 · Two rhythms, and what the whole view shows

The two rhythms are real and the measurement names them, read off this view: the frame's cells run 1.1 : 1 height to width — 1.14, 1.52, 0.91 across the upper band and 0.83, 1.25, 1.25, 1.25, 0.83 across the record band, with three of the eight wider than tall — against the region's sections at 11 : 1 width to height, ranging 4.3 to 15.9. An earlier version of this sentence said 1.8 : 1 and 1 : 3.5, both estimated rather than measured and the second inverted; the corrected figures make the break larger than the wrong ones claimed, which is the argument rather than a qualification of it. Same twelve columns, boxes above and rows below, and the cause is the ruling — bands are height, columns are alignment, so dropping the budget dropped the height only.

Seen whole, though, the break is not at the fold. It is at the point the content thins, which is four sections down on the richest record and immediately on the modal one. The frame reads as boxes because it holds eleven facts in 847px; the region reads as rows because most of its sections hold one line. A rhythm built for thin content is what thin content should look like, and forcing a minimum row height would reintroduce the void the frame spent six rounds removing — in a region with no budget to justify it.

So it stands, with the alignment doing the work, and one thing added rather than changed: the region's first section is the one that has to bridge. Pressing detail is the fullest section and it sits directly under the record band — at 5 + 5 with four pairs a side it is nearer a frame cell than a row, and it is the only section that reads as continuous with what is above it. That is the argument for ordering the region by density rather than by kind: fullest first, so the page thins downward instead of stepping.

What the whole view also settles: nothing below the fold is taller than the band above it, so the frame remains the composition and the region remains its index. That was asserted throughout §9 and never once looked at in the same frame as the thing it was claimed against.

§10.2 · Ornament at 11 : 1 — three sizes of answer, drawn

The region at 57.4%, stacked at full width so nothing is clipped — an earlier version of this drawing put the three side by side at 39.8% and hid 47.8% of each, which is the half the ornament sits in. Ornament only varies here; Everything else — splits, rules, labels, controls, edge fields — identical across the three.

10.3 · Which, and the rule that replaces half a column

A is the answer, and the reason is the granularity finding arriving one level out: half a column is a width, and in a band eleven times wider than tall the dimension that carries presence is height. The rule was stated in the unit the frame's roughly-square cells made indifferent, and the region's cells are not indifferent to it. So an in-cell solid is sized at 0.62 × its section's height — 0.627 of the cell — with width following the archetype (this read “0.62 × its cell's height, width following from that height by the projection” until now, in different words from §9.2's, which is why correcting §9.2 left it standing) — 79, 72, 76 and 94 tall on the four cells that carry one, against 64 for all four before. The gate is unchanged and is now doing real work rather than passing trivially: 0.627 visible against a two-thirds ceiling is the binding constraint it was written to be.

B fails on the thing it is trying to fix. Three marks at the drawn size read as a row of specks rather than as one mark — it converts a presence problem into a pattern, and a repeating motif at the bottom of every wide section is a texture, which §5.1 excludes for the same reason the constant provenance diagonal was removed: a mark that appears at a fixed interval stops being a mark. The one-per-section cap holds.

C is the strongest of the three to look at and it breaks the rule that earned its place by looking. A flat field crossing the band is a plane arriving from outside the frame, and these fields arrive from inside it — the section has a left and right edge that are the composition's edges only at the ends. Flat means crossing the page edge; a flat field stopping mid-page is the second vocabulary the matrix solid settled against. It stays available for the region's bottom edge, where it already is, because that edge is the composition's.

What changes in §9.2: the size term only. 0.62 × section height, 0.627 of the cell, replaces half a column; the gate, the half-column clearance from controls, the one-per-section cap, the tint-step ruling and the four carrying sections are all unchanged. Vocabulary is unchanged too — same projection, same three lightnesses, same corner, same bleed — which is what keeps the region's marks reading as the frame's at a size the frame never needed.

11 · The wall, and what the pull is for

The wall at rest is line, ink and paper: no derived colour anywhere in the drawing. Colour arrives with the pull. A record on the shelf is one of seventeen outlines; pulled, it becomes itself and takes its own colour. So the pull is not only motion — it is the transition from the collection to a record, and colour is what marks the transition. Every other surface keeps colour and ornament; the wall at rest is the exception, and the exception is what gives the pull its meaning.

This also settles what A62 measured and could not act on: the fills read as texture rather than identification, and a monochrome shelf stops asserting an identification the fills were never making. Withdrawn with it: the two-screen colour defect, the two collisions, 5b’s four-candidate ink pick at rest, and the whole clamp question on the wall side — all four were arguments about which colour a spine takes, and a spine at rest takes none. The earlier §11 ruled the spine’s raw value canonical and withdrew this page’s clamp to match it. That is reversed: nothing on the wall reads the value at rest, so nothing constrains this page, and the clamp is reinstated as §5.2 states it. The drawings are re-derived back to the clamped base and its three ladder steps — the same 132 literals, moved twice now, which is the cost of a ruling on one screen reaching into another’s rasters.

11.1 · What distinguishes a spine at rest

Position orders, width textures, the label identifies. Position carries the collection’s order rather than the record’s identity; the label identifies exactly, and only at reading distance; width is texture across the shelf and distinguishes nothing. An earlier version of this paragraph made width the channel the eye uses before reading, on the ground that it is the only one of the three derived from the record — spineWidth hashes the id. The next paragraph is why that is wrong.

Width is not a difference channel at any size, and the 200-record drawing measures it rather than predicting it: spineWidth yields eight integer values, so at two hundred each is shared by about twenty-four records and a 1px step between neighbours does not read at all. At seventeen sixteen records already share a width with another — so the seventeen case was never passing on width; it was passing on the label, and the width channel was carrying nothing the whole time. That is sharper than "not enough at two hundred" and it retires the sentence above: width is derived from the record, which made it look like the identifying channel, and being derived is not the same as being distinguishable.

So the label is the only channel that distinguishes, and the open work is keeping it readable rather than adding a second mark. A truncated label is the one failure that removes identification outright, which makes pitch, wrapping and the cap the density work rather than ornament. No truncation count is quoted here, and the reason is narrower than the one first given: the budget did not move — 37 stands (§11.6) — so Wall Density's count is invalid for the reason it always was, that it was gathered at 36 against a code value of 37. It needs re-gathering at 37 or dropping, and those are different reasons for the same action. The general form still holds and is worth keeping: when a parameter does move, a count derived from it is not stale pending re-measurement — it is not evidence at all until someone re-gathers it, and an argument that can stand on arithmetic should not wait for one. A difference rule over widths would be a rule over a channel that does not read; and colour at rest returning as a distinguishing device would spend the ruling above on a density problem it was not addressing. The honest summary of the rest state: position orders, width textures, the label identifies.

11.2 · When the colour arrives

The clock and the single curve are withdrawn for the pull: the span is 1600ms out and 860ms back (§11.21) and the phases overlap (§11.19), so the colour fade runs the full out-span rather than 1000ms. Left at 1000 it would reach full colour 600ms before the record lands. What survives is this section’s actual subject — that colour arrives across the gesture rather than at either end of it — which is a ruling about when, and independent of how long. The single curve also still governs every motion that is one motion; §11.16 lifts it for the pull alone. What follows is the withdrawn clock.

Across the gesture, on the same curve, and not as a fourth property of it. The motion is one 1000ms ease-out cubic driving translation, scale and shear together, and the single curve is load-bearing: if scale finished first the grown rectangle would untilt and read as it turned rather than it came off the shelf. Colour joins that curve as a fade from paper to the record’s clamped base, over the same 1000ms, starting at 0.

The alternatives are worse for stateable reasons. Colour at the end reads as confirmation — the record lands, then lights up — which makes the colour a response to the motion rather than part of it, and puts an event on a curve whose whole argument is that it has none. Colour at the start reads as the shelf changing before the record moves. Across it, the record is becoming itself while it comes toward you, which is what the pull means.

One consequence, because it is a reversal on the same curve: the return is not the pull played backwards for colour. Colour leaves on the same fade, since a record going back becomes one of seventeen again — but the fade to paper must complete before the spine reaches the shelf, or a coloured spine sits in the rest state for the last frames and the exception leaks.

11.3 · What the pulled record shows

The cover, with the record’s colour as the field behind it rather than a wash over it. The cover is the record’s own material and §5 already calls it the entry point and the source of the colour — so the pull arriving at the cover is the pull arriving at the thing the colour was derived from. A field of derived colour alone would be the pull arriving at a swatch, which is the identification A62 found the fills were not making.

And it is a cover at its own aspect, not cropped: the record screen shows 83% of a square sleeve at 1440 and 47% at 2560, a cost paid for a fixed band, and the pulled record has no band to fit. The pulled state is the one surface in the app that can show a whole sleeve, so it shows one.

The record with no cover arrives at type, not at a swatch. §11.3 as first written ruled the covered case and left the seventeenth record arriving at a #3a3a3a square — precisely the swatch the section forbids. With no cover the record's material is its text, so the pulled state sets title and artist large on ink — not on a colour field. An earlier version of this sentence put them on “the same clamped base every other record fades to”, which has no referent when the sample is null (§11.8): §5.3 owns the fallback and §5.3 says ink, and the honest reading is that colour arrives with the pull because it comes from the cover, so a record without one has none to arrive with. The absence takes §6's diagonal across the empty sleeve area, so the pull says no cover rather than showing a grey rectangle and leaving the reader to infer it.

11.4 · The record screen’s contrast findings, which are independent

With the clamp reinstated, the 72’s failures go with it: Grave New World at 1.43, Loss Of Life at 1.77 and the null-spine record at 1.00 were all consequences of withdrawing the clamp, and Super Rich at 3.03 returns inside the band. That is the clamp’s actual job, now stated correctly — it exists so the field clears its headline allowance on every record, not so two screens agree.

The 11px label finding is independent and was true before any of this: fourteen labels reading 3.88:1 against paper, below 4.5. Fixed rather than ruled around — mono label ink moves from oklch(0.48 0.008 70) to oklch(0.44 0.008 70), which reads 4.62:1 and keeps the label below body text in the ink hierarchy. It is one value in 158 places, and the reason it survived this long is that contrast is checked against the ground a mark is drawn on, and these were checked against nothing — paper is the default, so the failure had no site to be noticed at.

11.5 · Which paper the ratios are measured on

The drawing's 0.925 is the page's paper and the app should paint it; --background at 0.985 is the value that moves. Not because the drawing outranks the build — §11.4 has just been corrected the other way — but because every other value in this system was chosen against 0.925: the 0.72 hairline, the 0.18 ink, the 0.44 label, and the ladder's tint step, which is literally derived as a fraction toward paper. Repainting the ground at 0.985 rescales all four relationships at once, and the hairline is the one that cannot survive it — §3 spends its whole argument keeping a rule at the threshold of visible, and that threshold is a contrast, not a lightness.

The general rule, which is the part worth keeping: a contrast ratio is measured on the ground the app paints, so the two numbers have to be one number. The 3.88:1 label finding was measured on 0.925 and the app's label actually read 4.64:1 on 0.985 — the fix stands at 0.44 because it clears both, but it was ruled against a ground the page does not have. That is the coincidence-for-a-margin shape once more and the fourth instance: two values agreeing closely enough that nobody asked which one was being measured. So paper is one token, named in both places, and every ratio in this file is measured against it — and the four ratios derived this round (6.32, 5.4, 4.62, 2.6) are measured on 0.925 and stand only once the app paints it.

One item confirmed in scope rather than left to be inferred: §5.2's release-year label strip is a build item, not a drawing-only refinement. The 30px paper strip above a 120px coloured block is drawn in every raster and is not built, and the rule behind it — the field is ground for one figure — does not depend on the contrast figures that first produced it. And the null-spine 1.00 was live rather than a consequence of the withdrawal: recordLadder(null) is null under any clamp, so §11.4 cited it as evidence for the clamp when it was evidence for §5.3's fallback. Fixed on the rendered route, and the citation is corrected here.

11.6 · Scale, the empty run, and the label threshold

D2's figures are ratios and 5b's 240 is the scale — Code's reading is confirmed. The reason is the 9px floor: 150 × 12 at 1:1 sets a 9px label across a 12-unit spine, so the drawing would specify a label wider than the face it sits on. Adopting the ratios at 240 lands every D2 number where the build already is — thickness 19.2 inside the hash's 17–24, the 6.5 label at 10.4 against the built 10.39. Stated as the rule so the 1.6× is not read as drift: D2 specifies proportions, 5b specifies the unit, and a figure in D2 is only a number once multiplied. The two exceptions are the ones that do not scale — the 9px floor is an absolute in text-micro, and the character budget is 37, derived from the face at either scale, and it is spine-text.ts with a test on the derivation rather than the answer. Face less the baseline inset, over the measured advance: floor(232 / 6.235) = 37 at 5b's unit, and floor(145 / 3.9) = 37 at D2's. The two agreeing is the check, and it is what a transferable budget looks like.

This was withdrawn for one round on arithmetic that used the wrong advance, and the error is worth stating because it is the narrowest one in this file. The withdrawal computed 260px against a 240 face using an advance of 7.03 — D2's 6.5px size plus its 0.5px letter-spacing — which is the estimate the same round had just conceded was wrong, applied at the other scale. The measured advance is 0.6em and nothing else: 6.235px at 5b's 10.39 label. So checking a spec figure against the face is not sufficient; it has to be checked with the measured advance, and the measured advance is the one number here that was read off a rendered label rather than derived. D2's 30 is the superseded figure and its letter-spacing is removed, since the advance the cap divides by has to be the advance the label is set at.

A run with no seated records still has a shelf. The plane was built from shelfRuns, which drops an empty run, so a shelf holding one pulled record lost the plane the record was pulled from — and §2 does not address it because §2 describes arrangements rather than the absence of one. The rule: the plane is a property of the shelf, not of its occupants, so it spans the seated arrangement whether or not anything is seated in it. A record pulled from a shelf is still pulled from somewhere, and the plane is what says so.

And the threshold is D1's answer rather than a scaling rule: the wall never fits the collection into the viewport. §5 removes labels below 1:1 and never shrinks them, which is right — but §11.1 makes the label the only channel that identifies a record, so a wall below 1:1 is a wall of unidentified outlines, and at 200 records on a 1440 viewport that is the whole shelf. So the wall renders at 1:1 and pans; it does not scale to fit. The overview at 200 is a different view with a different job, not this one shrunk — which is also why the 24px-pitch comb read as structureless: it was this drawing asked to do the overview's work. The label switch stays built as specified, as the guard for viewports narrower than one record, not as the mechanism for showing the collection.

The paper divergence is now visible against the app chrome, which is §11.5 working rather than a new defect: the composition paints 0.925 and the app paints 0.985, and §11.5 rules the app is what moves. The visible seam is the measurement — a ground that reads as a panel against the chrome is what a wrong paper looks like, and it will close when --background does.

11.7 · The plane’s extent, and where the panel sits

One plane, one width, every row — the wall’s width, with the records inset inside it. Spanning each run’s seated extent gives four planes of 456, 433, 434 and 430, ragged by 26px, and a shelf whose length is a function of what is on it is not a shelf — it is a platform per arrangement, which is why the rows read as islands with the pitch measured correct at 1.272 against D2’s 1.271. The width is the pan extent — the plane runs the full width of the wall and off both edges of the viewport (§11.8). An earlier version of this sentence made the width a capacity, on the ground that a width derived from the fullest row moves every plane when one record joins that row; the ground holds and the answer did not, because a capacity is still a count, and forty per shelf leaves the collection an eighth full while sixteen is wrong at the eighteenth record. A fixture must not be sized by a count at all, and the thing being drawn is a fixture rather than a measurement of the collection. So the plane is the wall and the collection sits in it — which is also what makes an empty run’s plane (§11.6) unremarkable rather than a special case.

And §2’s section breaks are marks within the plane, not the plane’s ends. They currently coincide because each plane stops where a section does, so the break is being read off the fixture’s edge — the same defect one level out: a division of the collection expressed as a division of the furniture. A break is a rule across the plane at the seat boundary, and the plane runs on past it.

The panel is kept and §10b’s content is its content — the ruling is where it sits. §11.3 rules what the object shows, D2 rules how it arrives, and neither mentions text; §10b rules that every fact leaves the object for a panel beside it. Those agree rather than conflict, and the panel is what the gesture arrives at, so: it sits in the plane of the page, not in the projection — flat, on paper, at the record screen’s type and rules. Nothing in the panel is sheared. Where exactly is withdrawn to §11.9: this section placed it to the right of the pulled record and aligned to the cover’s top edge, which positions a destination against a moving object, and §11.9 gives it a fixed framed region in the page’s left column instead. What survives is everything in this paragraph that is not a position. The projection is what the collection is drawn in; the record’s facts are read, and §4.1’s split already says reading matter is set flat.

Two consequences worth stating rather than leaving to the build. The first is withdrawn: this section derived the panel’s width from the cover’s projected width so that record and facts would occupy one measure — and called that pair “two columns”, which is not §11.9’s two columns and would now name the same phrase for two different structures. Under §11.9 the panel’s width is its column’s and the record takes the drawing region entire. And Turn over survives, because it is about the record rather than about which face is toward the reader: the pulled state shows the sleeve’s front on the right face, and turning it over shows the back on the same face. A control that flips the artwork does not depend on the face carrying it.

The no-cover record arrives at type, and §11.3’s own sentence forces it: the pull must not arrive at a swatch, and one record of seventeen has no cover, so the covered case is not the general case. With no cover the record’s material is its text — title and artist set large on ink, on the face where the cover would be — and §6’s diagonal crosses the empty sleeve area so the state says no cover rather than showing a grey square and leaving the reader to infer it. That is the one place text enters the projection, and it does so because it is standing in for artwork rather than being read as fact.

The frame defect is worth recording for its shape: the extent was computed over planes and front faces while the top faces stand D·sin30 above them, so the top row ran off the viewport. A bounding box taken over a subset of the geometry it is meant to bound — and the subset was the faces that existed before the top face was added, which is the enumeration shape §9.2 records, arriving in the frame calculation.

11.8 · The accessibility contract, the fork, and two contradictions

The spines are anchors inside the SVG, not a list beside it. Five specs the lit wall met — a spine is a link and works without JavaScript, it names its record by role, the wall shows what its heading says, every record carries its full title, and a keyboard can walk the wall and open a record — are a contract the swap cannot drop, and they are ruled here because the panel is what those links open. The list was the lit wall’s mechanism and it would put a second representation of the collection on the page; §11.1 already makes the label the only identifying channel, so a parallel list is the identifying channel drawn twice, in two vocabularies, with nothing saying which is the wall. An <a> wrapping each spine’s faces keeps one representation: the href is the record’s route, so it works with JavaScript off, and the full title goes in the accessible name where the face carries the truncated one — which is the only place in this design where truncation is not a loss.

The one thing that has to be checked rather than asserted: SVG has no z-index, so paint order is document order, and document order is what a keyboard walks. Those could disagree — a drawing painted back to front and read left to right is two orders over one list. They do not, and the reason is worth recording: within a row the seats vary only along x, so the back-to-front sort by x + y is already seat order, and shelves run top to bottom in both. So one order serves the painter and the reader, and no tabindex is needed — which is the check to keep, because the day a row’s seats vary in depth the two orders separate and the drawing silently gets a wrong reading order.

The no-cover field is ink, and the other two candidates fail on their own terms. #3a3a3a is a default colour, which SPEC §4 says never renders — a value invented to fill a null is exactly the fill that section forbids. §11.3’s “the same clamped base every other record fades to” has no referent when the sample is null, so it is not an answer but a sentence written without the null case in view. §5.3 owns the fallback and §5.3 says ink, so the pulled state of a record with no cover is type on ink with §6’s diagonal — no colour, which is also the honest reading: colour arrives with the pull because it comes from the cover, and a record with no cover has none to arrive with.

The size is fitted to the square rather than taken from the scale, and that is not an exception to the scale — it is the scale not applying. §4 governs type that is read; this type stands in for artwork, so it is a drawn element and its size is derived from its box, which is what the 72 does in the year field and what §9.2’s ornament does in its cell. Five lines of headline type in a 188px square is a paragraph, and no size on the scale fixes that, because the defect is that a size was chosen at all. The fit: the title sets to the largest size whose longest word fits the square’s measure, at most three lines, anchored top so a clip takes the tail rather than the head — floored at the scale’s 15, below which it truncates at a derived cap like the spine label (§11.6) rather than shrinking further, since type too small to read stands in for nothing. The artist sits above it at LABEL, which is read rather than drawn and therefore does take a scale size.

The fork at 820 is withdrawn with the premise it rested on. This paragraph argued the overlay from the panel competing with the projection for width; under §11.9 it never does, at any viewport, because it has a column of its own. So the narrow-viewport question is now whether the two columns stack, and it is deferred rather than answered — a stacked facts-over-drawing page is a different composition from the one §11.9 rules, and A32’s collapsed panel was an answer to an overlap that no longer happens. The projection does not reflow: the wall renders at 1:1 and pans (§11.6), so a narrow viewport shows fewer records rather than smaller ones, and whatever the stacked composition turns out to be, the projection inside it is unchanged — which is the one thing the deferral does not defer.

Arrows between pulled records are kept as the old screen has them — wall order, absent at the ends, a slide at the same depth. §11 never mentioned them, and the omission is the shape this file keeps finding: §11.2 ruled the gesture from the shelf and nothing ruled movement between two records already off it. The slide holds depth because the record is already pulled: changing depth would be a second pull, and the arrows are movement along the collection rather than into or out of it.

Capacity is withdrawn as the plane’s measure — the plane is the wall, and the wall is the pan extent. Forty per shelf leaves the collection an eighth full and reads as a fixture waiting to be stocked; sixteen fits today and becomes wrong at the eighteenth record. Both are the same defect the ragged plane had: a fixture sized by a count. The plane runs the full pan extent and therefore off both edges of the viewport, and a fixture that ends inside the view is what reads as a platform — which is what §11.7 was reaching for in saying the records sit in the plane rather than the plane under the records. At seventeen the wall is a shelf the collection sits at the left of, and that is a true statement about the collection rather than an empty fixture.

11.9 · Two columns, and where the pull lands

The page is two columns: facts left, drawing right, with the rule between them running the full height. The left column carries COLLECTION and the count at its head, and below a hairline a framed region that is empty at rest and holds the panel when a record is pulled — §10b’s content, flat on paper, at the record screen’s type. That fixes the panel to a region rather than positioning it against a moving object, which is what every previous attempt was doing and why each one needed a new rule: §11.7 sized it against the cover, §11.8 overlaid it below 820, and both were answers to “where is the object now”. A destination does not move, so it needs no scrim, no lightness step and no overlap ruling, and the left third stops being empty at rest — it is a region that is waiting rather than a margin that is unused.

The record lands in the drawing’s region and takes it entire — the largest parallelogram at the wall’s angle the region holds, over the wall it came from. An earlier version of this sentence made it the largest square, unsheared; §11.10 withdraws both — what survives is that it takes the region entire rather than sharing it. §11.2’s single curve was built for exactly this and the geometry is exact: the right face is the cover, so the face already toward the reader is the one that grows — and it stays sheared through the pull, then turns: §11.10 withdrew the straightening and §11.14 restores the square as a second phase’s end rather than as this phase’s geometry. A face resolving to zero shear is geometrically a face meeting the reader, and it lands as an axis-aligned square with no relationship to the drawing beneath it. It takes the whole region rather than sharing it with the panel, because the panel has a column of its own; an earlier proposal made it the larger of two equal columns, which was still sizing the object against its facts.

No lightness step behind it. The step was proposed when the panel sat over the drawing and needed separating from it; with the panel in the left column the only thing over the wall is the record, and a record in front of a wall reads as in front of it because it is larger and its seat is empty — two differences, and the second is the stronger one because it is a change in the wall rather than in the record. This paragraph first cited square and unsheared as two of three differences, and §11.10 withdrew both, so the step is refused on scale plus the empty seat. A step would be a scrim by another name, and §11 spent its whole argument on the wall at rest being line, ink and paper.

The count stays at the column’s head and the panel fills the region below it. COLLECTION and the count are the collection’s identity, not the record’s, and the wall is still there behind the pulled record — a panel that replaced the whole column would say the collection had been left, which is the opposite of what the pull is. The hairline between them is already drawn at rest, so nothing moves when the panel arrives.

The arrows belong with the record, not the panel. They move along the collection and the record is the thing that slides, so an arrow against the panel is a control placed with the facts rather than with the object they describe — the same misplacement the panel itself had, one level down. Wall order, absent at the ends, at the record’s edges in the drawing’s region.

Rows are a fixed length, not filled to the view, and §11.8’s no-reflow rule extends to wrapping. §11.10 sets that length from the unit’s proportion rather than as a capacity; the reasoning below is why it is fixed at all. It was written about sizes and the reason reaches further: a record that changes shelf when the window narrows has a position that is a fact about the viewport rather than about the collection, and §11.1 leaves position carrying the collection’s order. The plane still runs the pan extent — that is what stops the fixture reading as a platform (§11.8) — but the seats per row are fixed, so the wall is a shelf the collection sits at the left of and the plane runs past it. A row’s length and a plane’s length are different quantities, and conflating them is what produced both the ragged plane and the empty one.

11.10 · The unit, the pull in projection, and two views

The wall is a fixed unit of four shelves joined at their ends, and the collection fills it left to right, top to bottom. Capacity 40 produced one row of seventeen running off the right edge, and the diagnosis is the one this file keeps making: capacity is a count per row, and what makes a shelf read as a shelf is the shape of the stack. Those are different axes, so the parameter could not reach the property — at seventeen records nothing stacks, and the wall becomes furniture only at the forty-first. The row length is therefore set from the unit’s proportion rather than from the collection: four shelves and a row length that make a unit taller than it is wide, which is what the reference is and what §11.8 was asking for in saying a fixture must not be sized by a count.

The shelves are joined at their ends and nowhere else. 5b rules out a carcass because a box around the collection competes with the records standing in it, and that holds — but four planes with nothing joining them is not a shelf either, and the reference gets its solidity from the stack rather than from a box. So: the four planes, plus the vertical members at their ends that make them one unit. No back, no front, no top. The empty shelves draw — §11.6 already rules an empty run keeps its plane, and at seventeen records three empty shelves are the fixture rather than a gap in it. Above one unit’s worth the wall gains units, and the pan extent is what holds them, so the row never lengthens to fit the collection.

The pulled record stays in the projection for the whole of the pull: it slides forward along the depth axis and grows, and it does not straighten while it is coming out. §11.14 adds the phase after it — once clear of the row the record turns and squares up, so this section governs phase one and the flat square is phase two’s end state rather than a withdrawn answer. §11.9’s “the face straightens and grows” is withdrawn. It was geometrically true — the right face is the cover, so a shear resolving to zero is that face meeting the reader — and the result is a flat axis-aligned square with no relationship to the drawing it sits on, which reads as an image pasted over a line drawing. The whole argument for the isometric was that everything on the wall is one drawing, and the pull was the one place that argument was being spent. So the cover arrives as a parallelogram at the wall’s own angle — large, unmistakably the cover, and still part of the same drawing.

And the seat empties. A record cannot be in the row and in front of it, so the pull leaves a gap at its seat — which is what a record off the shelf looks like, and it is also the return path drawn: the gap says where it goes back. That the spine stayed put was the same defect one level down: the pull was adding an object rather than moving one.

D1 reopens and the answer is two views, because the earlier ruling was stated over the wall when its reason was about reading. “A sub-1:1 wall is a shelf of anonymous outlines once the label is the only identifying channel” is true and it is an argument about identification — which is the near view’s job and not the far view’s. The far view answers how much there is and how it is arranged; identification there is not failing, it is not being attempted. The comb was this drawing asked to do the overview’s work, and the row is the overview asked to do this drawing’s — one view failing two jobs in both directions, which is the granularity shape §9.2 records arriving at the top level of the screen.

So: a far view of the whole unit with no labels, and a near view at 1:1 that pans and reads. Labels are absent in the far view rather than shrunk — §11.6’s threshold already says type too small to read stands in for nothing, and it is the same ruling as the sleeve fit. Movement between them is the same gesture as the pull, one step out: the far view zooms to the near view at the point addressed, so the sequence is collection, then shelf, then record, and each step is the same motion at a different scale. What must not happen is a third drawing — the far view is this unit seen whole, not a diagram of it.

11.11 · The three drawings, and the figures they fix

§11.10 made three claims about how something reads and none of them had been drawn. Every claim of that kind in this project has needed drawing before it was true — the corner triangle, the comb, the islands — so these are here before the build rather than after it. The polygons are the measurement and the prose is written from them, which is the opposite of how the first version of this section was assembled and the reason it disagreed with itself in five places.

Far view, 17 records — one unit, top shelf occupied, three shelves empty, labels absent. 442 × 1047 units, 1 : 2.37.

The empty shelves hold. Three vacant planes joined at their ends read as a fixture with room on it rather than as a gap, and the reason is visible: the uprights carry the vertical interval, so an empty shelf is a measured space rather than an absence. The unit projects to 442 × 1047 at 1 : 2.37, taller than wide as §11.10 requires. That figure is read off the boxes the drawing actually emits rather than enumerated by hand, which is what got it wrong twice: the uprights are emitted from z = −PT with height UH, so their top is at UH − PT and not UH, and a hand enumeration over z ∈ [−PT, UH] double-counts one shelf thickness — it produced 1030 in the first version and 1055 in its correction, the same slip twice in a row. The measurement has to come from the same list the polygons come from, which is the general form of the frame-extent defect one level up: not a subset of the geometry this time, but a restatement of it. And the collection fills top-down, so at seventeen records the occupied shelf is at eye level and the empty ones below it — a shelf filled from the bottom would put the collection at the floor and the room at the top.

The sleeve is square, and getting that wrong is what produced the one real defect in the first version. A seat was 12 × 100 × 150 — a sleeve deeper than it is tall by nothing in particular — so the landed record grew 3× in depth and 2× in height to reach a square cover, and the growth read as a rule about covers rather than as an error in the seat. A 12″ sleeve is square, so depth equals height: the seat is 12 × 150 × 150 and the pull is a uniform 2×. The unit’s figures follow from it, which is why they moved.

Far view, 200 records — three units, 80 + 80 + 40. The wall gains units; no row lengthens.

At two hundred the object is a wall of three units and it reads as one thing, which is what the comb never did. The comb was 200 outlines at one pitch with nothing above them; here the repeated unit is the structure — you count units before you count records, and the part-filled third unit is where the collection currently ends. That is the far view’s whole job: how much there is and how it is arranged, answered without a single label.

Near view at true 1 : 1 — svg rendered at 482 × 453, its viewBox dimensions exactly, so nothing is scaled. The whole 441.7-unit shelf is inside the window. Labels at 10.39px, truncated at 21 characters.

An earlier version of this window was derived from two projected corners rather than from the min–max of the corner set, and neither of them was an x-extreme — those lie at x = −T, y = RD and x = ROW+T, y = 0, which the pair skipped — so the window came out 222 units wide against 441.7 of content and cut three records off the right while leaving 564px of the frame empty. That is §11.7’s frame-extent defect exactly, a bounding box taken over a subset of the geometry it bounds, recurring in the drawing code one round after being recorded in the prose. And the caption claimed the frame was cropping when the viewBox was; the frame crops nothing at either size.

The cap shown is 21, not 37, and that is §11.6’s proportions rule working rather than a conflict with it. The derivation is face less baseline inset over the measured advance, and this drawing’s face is 150 units against 5b’s 240 — so floor((150 − 14) / 6.235) = 21 here and floor(232 / 6.235) = 37 there, one rule and two numbers. The number of titles exceeding it is not stated here, and §11.15 says why: a truncation count is an artefact of which seventeen strings are in front of you, and the drawn list and the real collection give eleven and twelve for that reason alone. The advance measures 6.234 per character in the render, §11.6’s figure to three places — the type was always right, and an earlier version simply omitted the cap, so eleven labels overran into the paper above the shelf.

The pull — the landed record in the page’s drawing region, cover sheared onto its +x face, the unit behind it at rest with seat 10 of the top shelf empty.

The pull stays in the drawing, and the comparison is the point: the withdrawn square had no edge in common with anything beneath it. This one is bounded by the same two angles as every spine — its vertical edges are vertical and its horizontal edges run at 30° — and the cover is sheared onto the face rather than pasted over it. The empty seat is doing as much work as the scale: the unit behind is visibly short one record at seat 10, which is what says the object in front is that record and not a new one.

And the cover is no longer mirrored, which was a real drawing defect and the same one D2’s caption was removed for. The first matrix mapped the image’s x axis along +y and its determinant was negative, so the sleeve was flipped — seen from +x the in-plane right-hand direction is −y, not +y (right = up × view, with up = +z and the view direction −(1, 1, 1) from §11.20: ẑ × −(1, 1, 1) = (1, −1, 0), which projects to (1.73, 0) — screen-right, so the in-plane right is −y and the conclusion is unchanged under the corrected camera). The matrix now has determinant +0.866, and the check to keep is the sign of the determinant on any matrix that places artwork in the projection, since a mirrored sleeve is legible enough to pass a glance and wrong to anyone who knows the record.

The wrong-axis finding, stated generally, because this round is its fourth instance and the clearest. A parameter set over an axis that is not the one the property varies along cannot reach the property, however it is tuned — capacity is a count per row and a shelf reads as a shelf by the shape of its stack; the gate was set on total height when the bleed made visible height the quantity; the solid was sized by width in a band eleven times wider than tall; the archetype was derived from a proportion the real cells do not vary along. The tell is a parameter that keeps needing adjustment and keeps not converging, and the fix is never a better value — it is asking which axis the reading actually depends on.

11.12 · The route, and moving between the two views

Withdrawn above §11.26’s fork by §11.29: a bare route opens near, and the far view becomes a deliberate zoom-out. Below the fork this section stands as written, because there the near view is not a fixture. The withdrawn account: The route opens far. §11.10’s sequence is collection, shelf, record, and the far view is the only one of the three that answers a question the reader has before they have chosen anything — how much is here and how is it arranged. Opening near would land them mid-shelf with no account of where that shelf is, which is the state the row was in when it read as a queue.

Out is the same gesture reversed and it needs no control: the far view is where the near view zooms out to, so the way back is the way in. What it does need is a named target rather than a scroll — a zoom out returns the whole unit, centred, at the far scale, and never an intermediate. Two views means two, and a continuum between them is the third drawing §11.10 forbids.

At one unit the far view still exists, and that it is only 0.8 of the near view is the answer rather than the objection. The two views differ by job, not by magnification — labels absent against labels present — and §11.10 already rules that labels are absent in the far view rather than shrunk. A collection small enough that its overview is nearly its reading view is a small collection; the views still say different things about it, and suppressing one at seventeen records would mean the screen a reader learns changes under them as the collection grows.

The near view lands with the addressed shelf at the region’s top and the seat at the region’s left, not centred. Centring a seat puts half the region behind the reader’s target — records they have already passed — whereas the shelf reads left to right, so the useful half of the region is the half after the seat. That is also §11.9’s fill order applied to the viewport: the same direction the collection is written in.

A filter narrows the far view, and it narrows by emptying seats rather than by removing them. A filter that re-seats the collection changes every record’s position, and §11.1 leaves position carrying the collection’s order — so a filtered far view is the same unit with the non-matching seats empty, which makes the filter’s result a shape on the fixture rather than a new fixture. It also keeps the one thing the far view is for: the answer to how much there is stays comparable before and after.

And the landed record’s bottom corner over the empty shelves below is correct and is worth drawing at two hundred before it is trusted. §11.10 puts the record in front and the overlap is what front means; but every drawing of it so far has had three empty shelves behind that corner, and at two hundred records it will have three full ones — twenty spines and their labels behind a large paper face. That is the one place the pull has not been drawn against the case that will actually occur, and it is a composition question rather than a geometry one.

11.13 · The controls leave the horizontal band

The 260px header band is withdrawn: the wall starts directly under the app nav and takes the full height, and the page’s controls go down a 148px rail on the left. A third of a 900px viewport spent on chrome is a third the wall does not get, and the band was costing height in the one dimension the unit is measured in — §11.11 draws it at 1 : 2.37, so height is the axis the drawing needs and the axis the band was taking.

The page at 0.544 — nav, 148px rail, 420px facts column, 872px drawing region, all measured in page pixels rather than drawn ones. Rail type is drawn at its true 11px and therefore reads oversized at this scale.

Left, against the nav, and the drawing stays rightmost. Reading order is chrome, then facts, then drawing — which is also increasing specificity: the app, then the collection, then this record. And the drawing cannot move left, because the wall pans and its right edge is where the collection continues, so a rail on the right would put chrome in the path of the thing the view is for.

The duplicate resolves by deletion rather than by merging: the rail carries no identity and §11.9’s head keeps COLLECTION and the count. Two columns of chrome was the failure mode to avoid, and merging the header into the facts column would have produced it — a column that is page chrome at its head and the record’s facts below it is two things, and §11.9’s panel has to appear in that space. So the rail holds controls only and the facts column holds identity and then the panel, which is what §11.9 already ruled. The header’s Collection and 17 records were the duplicate, and they are the instance that goes.

The rail at 1 : 1 — 148 × 847, LABEL throughout: search, genre and sort at the head (§11.24), the three views stacked below a full-bleed rule at the type’s 42px pitch (§11.37), Add record at the foot below another.

Stacked, the switcher stops being buttons and becomes a list of views — and that is the honest object, because they are four representations of one set rather than three actions. So the current view is marked the way this page marks a current thing: ink against muted, with the 44 × 4 bar under it, and no box, pill or field around any of them. A row of three needs enclosure to read as a group; a column of three is already a group, so the enclosure would be drawing what the arrangement says.

Vertical stacking also shortens the names, and the shortening is a gain rather than a cost. Search and filter becomes SEARCH at the head — a ruled field, the same 34px control §9.3 specifies — and the views become SHELF, TABLE, GRID. A column has no room for a name that explains itself, so every name has to be the thing rather than a description of it, which is the same pressure that produced the spine label’s cap.

Add record sits at the foot, below a rule that bleeds to both edges of the rail. It is the only control here that changes the collection rather than the view of it, so it is separated by a rule rather than by a gap — §3’s distinction, applied to chrome. Putting it at the head would interrupt the view list with an action, and the list is what the rail is mostly for.

One drawing correction recorded because it is the same class three rounds running: the schematic’s scale was taken from the frame’s outer 826px when the frame’s content box is 784px — 826 less 40px of padding and 2px of border; the first version of this correction said 786 and subtracted the border once instead of on both sides, so it fixed 40 of the 42px and left 2 — so 42px of the page’s right edge was clipped and the drawing region rendered 799 of the 872 its caption claims. The nav band then read as bleeding off a page edge that was really the frame’s clip. Every other frame in §11.11 sizes to 786 or less; this one took the wrong width from the only place it was written down. The figures in the caption are page pixels and were always right; the drawing was the thing that disagreed.

What this does not settle: the rail at a narrow viewport. §11.8’s fork was withdrawn with its premise and §11.7’s stacking question is still deferred (§11.9) — a rail is the first element on this page that could plausibly become a horizontal strip when the columns stack, which would return the band this section just removed. Worth ruling with the stacking rather than before it.

11.14 · The pull has two phases, and the square is the second one’s end

Sequencing and every duration below are withdrawn by §11.19 and §11.21: the phases overlap, and the spans are 1600ms out and 860ms back with 1300ms of travel and rotation inside the first. What survives is this section’s reason for there being two phases at all — that a pull and a turn are different motions and the page needs both — which is what §11.19 kept while reversing how they are timed. What follows is the withdrawn account.
