Out, then round. The record leaves its slot in the projection, and once it is clear of the row it turns to face the reader and squares up. §11.10 and §11.9 were both right and both stated over the wrong subject: §11.10 ruled the record stays sheared and §11.9 ruled it lands square, and each wrote “the pull” when it meant one phase of it. A rule stated over a gesture when its subject is one phase of that gesture — which is the granularity shape again, now in time rather than in geometry.

§11.2 is not reversed. It is scoped, and the scope was always phase one. Its argument is that a gesture’s parts must not finish at different times — a scale completing before a shear reads as it turned when nothing turned. Here something does turn, so the reading that argument exists to prevent is the reading being asked for, and it is being produced by an actual rotation rather than by a timing artefact. A second gesture after the first completes is not a part finishing early. So the single ease-out, the 1000ms and the one curve driving translation, scale and shear together all stand, unchanged, for the pull.

The two phases abut with no hold, and the boundary is legible from the velocity rather than from a pause. The pull is ease-out, so it arrives at rest; the turn is ease-in-out, so it leaves from rest. Velocity returning to zero between them is what makes two motions read as two — a hold would make it read as a stall, and a shared curve would make it one motion with a kink in it. That is the same instrument §11.2 used, applied to the join rather than to the parts.

And the record ends genuinely on the page’s plane, not in the projection’s space. That is what makes the square legitimate where §11.9’s straightening was not: the straightening produced a square that shared no edge and no history with the drawing — it simply appeared — whereas this one shares the moment the reader watched it leave. The objection was never to a square; it was to a square with no account of how it got there. The turn is the transition between the two spaces, and it cannot be expressed in either — an isometric projection has no orientation at which a face is exactly face-on, so the turn is not a rotation inside the drawing, it is the record departing the drawing. That is the honest description and it is why the phase exists.

What the probe has to settle, since the shape is ruled and the timing is not. The split: 1000ms is fixed for phase one, and phase two is the open figure — faster than the pull is the hypothesis, since a turn covers less distance and a slow turn will read as a swivel. The boundary: whether zero hold reads as two motions or as one, which is the whole ruling above and the one thing a still cannot show. And the corner path: the four corners interpolate from the projected parallelogram to the page square, so the probe needs to show whether a straight interpolation reads as a turn or as a shape morphing — if it morphs, the corners need a rotation to follow rather than a line.

Three things that do not move during either phase. The wall does not pan, scale or dim — §11.9 refuses the lightness step and nothing here reopens it. The seat stays empty from the first frame of phase one through the landed state, because it is the record’s absence rather than an animation of it. And the facts panel arrives with phase two rather than phase one: it belongs to the record as a subject, and the record becomes a subject when it turns to face the reader. Put back is both phases reversed, in reverse order — round, then in.

11.15 · Which side the reader is on, and how units tile

Withdrawn by §11.20: this section’s sign is inverted, and the paragraph is kept because its reasoning about the test is what survives. P(1, 1, 1) = [0, 0], so the only viewpoints are ±(1, 1, 1), the visible faces are +x, +y and +z, y = 150 is the near edge and the spine is the +y face. What follows is the withdrawn derivation. y = 0 is the near edge, so the drawing shows the wall from the front and its labels are on the face the reader sees. The derivation is in the projection both files share: P(x,y,z) = [(x−y)·cos30, (x+y)·sin30 − z] makes the visible faces the ones with normals +x, −y and +z, which places the camera at (+∞, −∞, +∞) — negative y — so a smaller y is nearer. The spine is the −y face, thin and tall; the cover is the +x face; both are toward the reader, and the reference confirms it independently — its pulled cover faces right, which is +x. So if the build’s labelled face is at y = D, its labels are on the back of every record, and the drawing is not the file to change.

The test not catching it is the more useful half. Extents agree at 441.7 × 1047 and 1 : 2.37 for either orientation, because mirroring in y leaves the bounding box invariant — so a test comparing extents cannot distinguish front from back, and it passed on a property the question does not depend on. That is the same shape as the gate test that could not distinguish visible height from total: a test whose output is insensitive to the premise it is cited as checking. The check that does distinguish them is the sign convention itself, stated once and asserted at one place, rather than a comparison of two renderings.

Withdrawn by §11.23: the wall is one fixture and the row length grows — units do not tile at all. The paragraph below is right that a tiled wall must share one axis and wrong to conclude that tiling survives, and the drawing at 200 records settled it: three units along +x read as bookcases stepping away, with two uprights and a gap in mid-air at each seam. What survives is its reasoning about why the horizontal shift was wrong, and its own named alternative — a longer row — which §11.23 makes the ruling rather than a hypothetical. The withdrawn account: Units tile along +x, the wall’s own axis, and therefore project diagonally — the horizontal screen shift is withdrawn. A pure 596px shift is a step of +344 in x and −344 in depth, which arranges the units in echelon: a wall that steps backward as it goes right. Nobody designed that plan and no room contains it. A wall of records is against a wall, so the units share one axis, and in this projection one axis descends to the right. I drew the shift because it framed neatly, which is choosing the plan to suit the picture.

The cost, stated because it is real and it lands on the far view. A diagonal band grows on both screen axes, so at two hundred records the object is long and descending rather than a tidy row of three — and the far view frames the band rather than the unit, which is a different fit from the one §11.11 drew. It was unacceptable when drawn, and the alternative this sentence named — a longer row rather than a staggered plan — is now the ruling (§11.23): it reopens §11.10’s row length, which is a parameter, and not the tiling, which turned out to be a choice that read as furniture rather than a fact about where shelves go. The pan follows the same axis either way (§11.6).

And §11.12’s filter ruling reaches the producer, which is the correct consequence rather than an obstacle. Emptying seats means the query returns the whole collection with matches marked, not the matching subset — because a filter that returns only matches cannot preserve position, and §11.1 leaves position carrying the collection’s order. The cost is that the wall’s payload does not shrink with the filter; the gain is that the filter’s result is a shape on the fixture, and the answer to how much there is stays comparable before and after. That was ruled knowing it reached the data layer, and it is worth naming that the ruling is only true if the producer implements it.

The truncation count is withdrawn: eleven and twelve were counts of two different title lists, and neither is evidence about the cap. The cap is derived (§11.6) and the count is an artefact of whichever seventeen strings are in front of you — which is the shape §11.6 already records for Wall Density’s count, arriving again in a figure I wrote myself.

11.16 · The turn is a rotation, and phase one is bounded by it

The record rotates rigidly in three dimensions and is re-projected every frame; its projected corners are never interpolated. The probe answers this by watching: interpolating the four corners from sheared to square passes the face through intermediate quadrilaterals that are no rotation of any record, so the shape morphs instead of turning. A rigid rotation has a signature the morph cannot fake — the widths of the cover, spine and top face change together as one solid — and §11.17 replaces this paragraph’s account of the signature, which named a narrowing that belongs to the direction the record does not turn.

The axis is the cover’s near vertical edge, which under §11.20’s viewpoint is the one at y = 150, not its centre. This paragraph has been written three times and the third version restores the first: its original ground was that the cover advances throughout, that was withdrawn when §11.17 appeared to reverse the direction, and §11.20’s sign correction reinstates it — so the withdrawal is withdrawn rather than a third account invented. The opening rotation carries the cover normal from (1, 0, 0) to (0.707, 0.707, 0), and against the viewpoint (1, 1, 1) that is 1.414 against 1: the cover turns toward the reader and every point of it advances. The near edge is the point the turn plants — it does not move, and no point of the record ends further from the reader than it. A centre pivot sends the far half backward into the row the record has just left while the near half swings out, which reads as a turntable and spends part of the 151 units the pull just bought. So the turn and the pull agree in direction, which is the requirement the pull imposes.

The clearance term §11.14 was missing, and it is derived rather than chosen. A 12 × 150 footprint pivoting about its near vertical edge (y = 150) sweeps within √(12² + 150²) = 150.5 of that axis, so phase one must travel the full 151 units before phase two may begin — about the centre axis it would be √(6² + 75²) = 75.2, so 76, which is the cheaper number and the wrong pivot. Nothing is subtracted, and the first version of this paragraph subtracted the thickness: it wrote 151 − 12 = 139 as “the sweep less the thickness already clear of the seat”. The travel is along +y (§11.20) and the 12 is an extent along x, so it deducted a head start the record does not have — no part of it is forward of the shelf’s near plane at rest, and the quantity being cleared is the 150-unit depth swinging into the neighbouring seats. That is the wrong-axis shape again, in the one number the round exists to produce, and the two measurements from the probe — a band of roughly 150 to 190, a centre sweep of about 75 — match the unsubtracted figures exactly and rule out the subtracted ones. So phase one’s travel is not a free parameter: it is bounded below by what phase two needs, and the span is a duration for a distance the turn dictates — 1600ms per §11.21, §11.14’s 1000 being withdrawn.

Withdrawn by §11.19: the phases overlap, and the paragraph below argued against that from a scalar clearance. What survives is the zero-hold boundary’s reading — it does read as two motions rather than one with a kink, which is why there are two phases at all — and the principle that the clearance is satisfied by geometry rather than by scheduling, once the clearance is evaluated per angle instead of at 45°. The swing is legal because its eases are shaped to the angle-dependent requirement, not because it travels first. The withdrawn account: Sequential, not overlapped, and the probe already said why. The zero-hold boundary reads as two motions rather than one with a kink — which is what the split was for — and overlapping the phases to save distance would put the turn inside the travel, where the swept volume is exactly what is not yet clear. An overlap is only safe once the record is past 151 units, at which point it saves nothing.

What this reverses in §11.2, stated plainly: that section forbids a scale finishing before a shear because the result reads as it turned. Here it should read as it turned, so the prohibition is lifted for the pull and kept for everything else — §11.2’s single curve still governs any motion that is one motion, and the pull is now two. The argument was never that turning looks wrong; it was that a turn read where no turn was intended is a defect. A turn read where a turn is intended is the gesture.

And the record ends on the page’s plane, which settles the §11.9-versus-§11.10 question the drawing could not. How it gets there is §11.17’s, not this paragraph’s: a rotation about a vertical axis cannot end face-on under this projection, and the claim that it does is withdrawn there. So the landed record is square and flat, and it is in the projection’s space for the whole gesture and out of it only at rest. The paste-over objection is answered by the 151 units and by the spine closing 10.39 → 0 at the same 45° (§11.17): the reader has watched it leave the row and turn, so the square is where the record got to rather than a flat card laid over a drawing.

11.17 · Where the rotation stops and what finishes it

§11.16’s arrival claim is withdrawn: no rotation about a vertical axis ever squares the cover under this projection, and I ruled one that ends face-on two rounds after giving the reason it cannot. The measurement is exact — at 45° the cover’s horizontal edge projects to 183.7 against a constant vertical 150, which is 1.2247 : 1 and the best it ever reaches. The factor is √2 · cos 30, the amount by which a face diagonal projects longer than an axis edge, and it is the same constant that makes isometric drawings out of true projections. An isometric has no orientation at which a face is face-on because the projection, not the orientation, is what is oblique.

So the gesture is rigid to 45° and finishes with two terms, both of which are the projection being removed rather than shape being invented. At 45° the cover is an axis-aligned rectangle, upright and orthogonal on screen, and two things are still wrong with it: it is 22% too wide, and the body’s 12-unit thickness projects to an 8.49-unit sliver of edge below it — the rotated basis gives x̂ → [0, 8.49], ŷ → [−183.7, 0], ẑ → [0, −150], so the projected solid is 183.7 × 158.49 and not 183.7 × 150. So the finish is a horizontal compression of 0.8165 and the thickness term collapsing 8.49 → 0, and the second term is the one “taking the isometric out” actually names: the depth contribution (x + y) · sin 30 going to zero. An earlier version of this paragraph specified the compression alone and claimed width was the only fault, which would have landed the record at 150 × 158.49 — 1 : 1.057, a 5.7% band of edge under the cover — against §11.3’s cover at its own aspect, uncropped. 0.8165 is 1 / √2 · cos 30, the reciprocal of the factor that made it wide; and a face-on orthographic view of a box shows no thickness at all, so the sliver closing is the same event as the cover squaring rather than a separate flattening. Both terms reach zero together, which is why the finish reads as one move. The record does not leave the projection so much as the projection is undone on it, which is the account the paste-over objection asked for: the square is the 45° rectangle with the isometric taken out of it, and the reader has watched both halves happen.

The direction is the one that opens the face, and §11.16 had the signature backwards but not the direction. This clause said “backwards along with the signature” and it was wrong about the direction in a way worth tracing: §11.16 said the cover advances, this section appeared to reverse it, §11.16’s ground was withdrawn on that basis, and §11.20’s sign correction reinstated it — so §11.16 was right all along and this section’s apparent reversal was the withdrawn camera, not a disagreement. Away from the reader the cover’s horizontal edge runs 129.9 → 0 and shuts edge-on at 45°; toward the reader it runs 129.9 → 183.7 and opens — the figures are camera-independent and the toward/away labels were §11.15’s, so they swap under §11.20 and the conclusion below is unchanged. So the record turns toward the reader to show its cover — which is what the hand does: a record lifted spine-first has its cover facing along the row, and bringing it round is turning it to face you. This sentence read “turns away” until §11.20 fixed the viewpoint; the widening figures either side of it are camera-independent and unchanged, and this clause was the one part of the section that was not.

And the narrowing is withdrawn as the proof of rigidity, because it belongs to the direction that closes. The opening direction only widens, so it has no narrowing to show — but it has a better signature, and it is derived rather than chosen: the spine closes. The spine is the +y face (§11.20), 10.39 wide in projection at rest, and its normal turns exactly edge-on to the camera at 45° — the same angle at which the cover squares up. So spine width runs 10.39 → 0 and reaches zero precisely when the rotation ends.

That is the signature a corner interpolation cannot fake, and it is a stronger one than the narrowing was. A morph of the cover’s four corners has no spine and no top face to be consistent with; a rigid body shows three faces whose widths change together, and the reader reads rigidity from the agreement rather than from any one face. The cover widening while the spine closes at exactly the rate that keeps the solid solid is what says object. The 151-unit clearance stands unchanged — it is a fact about the swept volume and indifferent to which way the sweep runs (§11.16).

11.18 · Three clearances, and which one binds

Phase one travels 151 units, unchanged, and 363 is withdrawn as a requirement rather than adopted as a correction. The two figures answer different questions and there is a third that neither of them is: 151 is the sweep — the record can rotate without its volume touching a neighbour; 150 is the separating plane — the record is ordered in front of every record in the row; 363 is zero silhouette overlap — the record’s projected outline no longer touches the row’s at all. Only the first two are requirements.

The separating plane is the one the occlusion worry was really about, and it is satisfied at 150. Every neighbour spans y ∈ [0, 150]; travelling +y by d puts the pulled record at y ∈ [d, 150 + d], so at d ≥ 150 a plane on y separates it from all of them, and it is on the larger-y side, which under §11.20’s viewpoint is the near side — so it draws in front of the whole row regardless of x. This derivation ran along −y until §11.20 fixed the sign, which reached the right 150 by a route that sorted the record behind the row. The sort and the travel do different jobs and both are needed: at d < 150 the boxes still overlap in y, so the separating axis falls back to x — and a neighbour at larger x is genuinely nearer, so it correctly draws in front of the pulled record. The exact sort stops the order being wrong; it does not make the record front-most, and being in front of the whole row really is bought with 150 units of travel. An earlier version of this paragraph said the travel did not have to, which denies the requirement the same paragraph derives. What the sort does buy is that nothing is mis-drawn on the way there — and the 363 was measured without it, under centroid sorting, which is the moved-parameter shape again: a distance read off a defect in the paint order.

And zero overlap is not something to want. A record held out from the shelf it came from should cover part of that shelf — overlap is what depth looks like, and removing it puts the record beside the wall rather than in front of it, which is the composition §11.10 rejected when the square shared no edge with the drawing. At 363 the record has left the fixture; at 151 it is in front of it. The gesture is a record coming forward, not a record leaving.

One honest caveat about the margin, because this file has been caught by it three times: the two derived quantities are 150.48 and 150, which is 0.48 of a unit apart, and the shipped 151 clears the plane by a whole unit only because 150.48 rounds up. A gap of half a unit between two independently derived requirements is a coincidence rather than a margin, and a rounding is not a design decision. The sweep radius √(12² + 150²) and the plane’s 150 are both functions of the record’s depth, so they move together — but they are not the same function, and a thinner record or a shallower shelf separates them. Both are derived, so re-derive both whenever the box changes; do not treat 151 as covering the plane by construction.

The wrong-axis diagnosis does not apply here, and it is worth saying why the shape did not recur. 151 was derived over the rotation’s geometry and the rotation’s geometry is what it governs — it was never claimed to be the distance at which the row stops being drawn over the record, and that question splits in two: the sort answers whether anything is mis-drawn, and the plane’s 150 answers whether the record is front-most. Neither answer is 151, and neither is 363. The near miss was real though: had the order stayed centroid-based, the parameter would have been raised to 363 to fix a defect in the paint order, which is a distance standing in for a correctness bug and would have made the slide two and a half times longer for nothing.

11.19 · The phases overlap, and the landed composition

§11.14 and §11.16 are reversed on sequencing: the phases overlap, and the swing is the gesture. Sequential reads as slide, stop, pivot — three events for one action — which is what robotic meant, and it was never a judgement the stills could make. The numbers are the probe’s: 1300ms of travel and rotation, 290 units, the return being the whole gesture reversed on one clock — and §11.21 adds the finish after the rotation, so the spans are 1600ms out and 860ms back. The 1300 is what the probe measured and it is unchanged; what §11.21 changes is that it is no longer the whole span.

And the rule that forbade it was wrong in a way worth stating, because it is the wrong-axis shape in time rather than in geometry. §11.16 requires 151 units before any rotation, on the ground that the swept volume must be clear — but the clearance is a function of the angle, not a scalar: 151 is its value at 45°, and at 0.6° the sweep barely leaves the record’s own footprint. The correct statement is that the required travel at any instant is the sweep radius at that instant’s angle, which the sequential path satisfies trivially and the swing satisfies because its eases are shaped to. The parameter was evaluated at the gesture’s end and applied at its start.

The swing is legal at every point, measured rather than argued: rotation begins at 86 units, under 151; at 0.6° the record is already 149 units out; by 15° it is at 223 and entirely past the row in y; and its deepest reach back into the neighbours’ band is x = 13.5 against a nearest neighbour at 125. 290 exceeds the 150 that makes it front-most (§11.18) by a wide margin and was chosen for how it reads, not for clearance — which is the right relationship between the two: the constraint is a floor and the timing is a decision.

The landed state assembled at 1440 × 900, shown at 0.5444 — §11.13’s 148px rail, the 420px facts column carrying the panel, the record at 560 × 560 offset left, the empty seat clear to its right by the pan’s target (§11.26), arrows in their lanes at the region’s edges. Spines on the +y face, shelves painted in depth order. Rail and panel type drawn at true size.

The record lands at 560 × 560, offset to the left of the region, and neither number is the largest square that fits. This sentence said “right” until now — a survivor of the pre-§11.20 text, when travel was −y; the derivation below, the caption and the drawing were all corrected and the ruling sentence was not. An earlier version of this section centred the largest square the region holds — 779 — and the drawing falsified it: the unit projects to 324px wide, so a concentric 779 square covers the fixture entirely, which is total occlusion rather than the overlap §11.18 ruled and the composition §11.10 rejected. The horizontal offset is derived and the vertical placement is not, and the difference is worth stating because the derivation covers both axes while only one of them can obey it. The pull travels +y (§11.20), which projects to −cos 30 horizontally and +sin 30 vertically, so a record coming out of the wall moves down and to the left, and it lands left of the fixture with the empty seat clear to its right — by the pan’s target (§11.26), not by the construction. The 55px this sentence used to assert is withdrawn: 290 units of travel and a 560 cover do not produce that clearance for any seat in the row. An earlier version of this paragraph had it landing right, from a pull along −y that §11.20 withdraws. Vertically it cannot be: the cover is a fixed 560 in an 847 region, and seats span four shelves 198 units apart, so a cover tracking its seat’s height overruns the region for the top and bottom shelves and only middle seats would fit. A placement rule that works for two shelves of four is not a rule. So the cover is centred vertically in the region, and it is centred for a reason rather than by default — an earlier version of this paragraph claimed the offset on both axes and the drawing centred one of them silently.

The size is therefore bounded by what must stay visible, not by what fits: 560 leaves 264 of the unit’s 324px clear and the empty seat clears the cover’s right edge because §11.26 pans until it does — right, because §11.20’s sign puts the record left of the fixture; this sentence said left while the two either side of it said right. That is the binding constraint, and it is the same relationship as §11.18’s — a floor derived from what the composition has to show, with the size chosen above it.

No lightness step behind it, and the question §11.9 left open closes by construction. The panel is in the facts column and nothing is over the drawing but the record itself, so there is nothing for a scrim to separate — and the empty seat is the separation: it is drawn, legible and clear of the cover because the pan settles there (§11.26). That this argument rests on a clearance the construction does not give is why §11.26 gave the pan a target rather than leaving it to the numbers. A step would dim the one cue that says where the record came from, and a seat that is covered is not a cue at all — which is what the first drawing of this section did.

The panel’s order is the record screen’s, not a summary of it: artist, title, year, then the note, then the fact groups on their hairlines, then Open the full record and the two verbs. Turn over and Put back sit together at the foot because they are the two things you can do to the object, and Open the full record sits above them because it leaves this surface — §3’s rule, separating a departure from an interaction.

What the drawing does not settle, and should not: the cover is the panel’s subject and the panel is 420px wide, so a long title wraps. §4.2’s give order is the frame’s and does not transfer — there are no fixed bands here — but the title block growing downward pushes the fact groups toward the foot, and the foot is fixed because the two verbs are pinned to it. That is the same collision §4.2 resolved in the frame, in a column that has no ornament track to yield, so it needs its own answer before this is built.

11.20 · The viewpoint, the pull’s sign, and how the record grows

§11.15 is withdrawn on the camera and the derivation is closed rather than argued: P(1, 1, 1) = [0, 0], so this projection collapses that direction and admits exactly two viewpoints, ±(1, 1, 1). §11.15 named (+∞, −∞, +∞), which is neither — P(1, −1, 1) is [1.73, −1] and not zero, so it is a direction the projection still draws. Under the viewpoint that shows the tops, the visible faces are +x, +y and +z, and the −y face is a back face, which is the opposite of what §11.15 ruled.

The concrete check is the one to keep, because it is what the geometry costs in pixels: the spine point (6, 0, 650) and the right neighbour’s body point (17, 11, 661) land on the same pixel and the neighbour’s is nearer. So spines on the −y face vanish under any correct object order — they survived in the drawings only because their text paints last — which is also why the wall read as a fan of back faces and why the pull read as moving through the row. Three symptoms, one cause, and the cause was a sign.

What follows, all of it agreeing: the spine is the +y face as D2 had it, and the pull travels +y. §11.18’s separating plane keeps its 150 and inverts its side — a record travelled +y by 150 is on the larger-y side, which is the near side, so it is in front of the whole row. §11.17 needs no change at all: its figures are camera-independent, and the rotation that opens the cover carries its normal toward +y, which is toward this camera. That the three sections agree once the sign is fixed is the strongest evidence the sign was the only error.

Withdrawn by §11.25: growth rides the rotation’s window, because an orthographic projection has no size change on approach — the paragraph below reasons from a perspective intuition this drawing does not have. What survives is that growth is not a third term. And the growth is not a third term — it rides the travel, because it is the same fact. A record that comes toward the reader gets larger; that is what approach looks like, and the probe’s constant-size rotation is why it read as turning in place rather than coming out. So scale is on phase one’s curve and completes when the travel completes, from the seat’s 150 to the landed 560 — 3.73× — with the rotation overlapping it as §11.19 rules.

Which answers the growing-while-turning question by making it not a choice: the record grows while it turns because it travels while it turns. Putting growth on its own window would need a reason, and there is none — a record that finished travelling and then grew would read as a picture being zoomed, and one that grew before travelling would read as approaching without moving. Tying it to the travel is the only version where the size at every instant is the size the distance implies.

11.21 · The finish’s window, and what the growth scales about

The rotation keeps its 1300ms and the finish is added after it, so the out-span is 1600ms and the probe’s measurement is not re-interpreted. 1300 and 700 were read off a gesture with no finish in it, so the finish is additional to what read well rather than carved out of it — carving it would shorten the travel and rotation that were the thing being judged. The return reverses the whole gesture on one clock at the same ratio: 700 × 1600 / 1300, so 860ms back.

300ms for the finish, and it is chosen rather than derived — said plainly because two constraints bound it and neither fixes it. It must be long enough that a 22.5% change of width does not read as a cut, and short enough that it reads as the record settling rather than as a third phase, which means shorter than the rotation it follows by a clear margin. 300 against 1300 is a ratio of about 1 : 4.3. It is the one number in the gesture a probe should overrule, and the probe that measured 1300 could not have measured it, because the gesture it watched had no finish.

And the growth scales about the foot of the pivot edge — the bottom of the cover’s near vertical edge at y = 150 — which is Claude Code’s shelf end made exact. The reason to prefer that point over any other is that the rotation already fixes that edge, so using its foot makes one point of the record fixed by both transforms at once. Any other origin has the growth moving a point the rotation is holding still, and the two then fight over it: scaling about the record’s own centre grows it backward through the shelf, and scaling about the region’s centre detaches it from the seat entirely.

So the record keeps its foot on the shelf and grows forward and up, which is the same relationship the pivot has to the rotation and the same one the offset has to the travel. Three transforms, one fixed point, and the whole gesture is then describable as: that corner stays put while everything else leaves.

Worth recording as a class, because it is the third time it has cost a round: a transform’s origin is invisible to every still. The drawings show the growth’s start and its end, and every origin agrees at both ends and disagrees only in between — which is exactly the shape of the corner-path question, where interpolated and rotated corners matched at 0° and 45° and differed at every angle between. A still cannot be wrong about these; it simply has nothing to say, and the tell is a parameter whose two endpoints are both given.

11.22 · The view pans; the gesture does not move

The drift is withdrawn and replaced by a pan: the record’s transforms stay exactly as §11.21 rules them, and the drawing region pans so that the landing is in frame. The gap is real and Claude Code states it exactly — the gesture is authored in the wall’s coordinates and the landing is specified in the page’s, and nothing was converting between them. A drift converts by moving the object; a pan converts by moving the viewport, and the wall already pans (§11.6), so this needs no new mechanism and no new page room.

That is why the drift’s second consequence is the one that rules it out. §11.21’s argument is that three transforms share one fixed point; a drift leaves them sharing a point that is itself moving, which is not a weaker version of the argument but the negation of it — the foot stops tracing what the travel gives it. Under a pan the foot is fixed in the wall’s coordinates exactly as ruled, and §11.21’s claim narrows correctly rather than approximately: the point is fixed in the frame the gesture is authored in, and the whole frame translates.

And the pan is the better reading, not merely the cheaper fix. A record drifting to meet the composition is the object accommodating the page; a view panning to follow the record is the reader stepping across to look at it, which is what a person does at a shelf. The fixture moving on screen during the pull is the cost, and it is the correct cost: the wall stays still relative to itself and the record, and only the window over it moves.

Mechanically: the pan rides the swing’s own ease on the same clock, so the gesture and the framing are one motion rather than two. It resolves to zero when the landing is already in frame, which is the property the drift had and worth keeping. Vertically it answers the top-shelf case by the same means — a record whose foot sits high needs the view to show more above it, which is a pan and not a layout allowance, so no vertical room has to be found in §11.13’s bands.

Two consequences to keep, both honest under the pan: a neighbour reached by the arrows lands in the same screen position, because the pan differs by exactly the seat pitch and equalises it — the same outcome the drift produced, now derived rather than arranged. And §11.19’s composition becomes a statement about the framed view rather than about absolute page coordinates: 560 square, left of the fixture, the empty seat clear — all of it true of the frame the pan arrives at, which is what a landed composition always was. §11.26 makes the clearance the pan’s target rather than a figure: the 55px stated here was measured on one seat of the drawing, and the pan has to clear the seat for every one of them.

The timed-out navigation tests are the finding worth recording: the gesture was correct and the page could not contain it. Every ruling in §11.16 to §11.21 is a fact about the wall, and a fact about the wall cannot by itself put anything on the page — which is the class §11.19 nearly hit when it derived an offset on two axes and could implement one. The tell is a ruling whose terms are all in one coordinate system and whose obligation is in another.

11.23 · Tiling withdrawn, paint order separated from reading order

Two hundred records. Left: three units of 20 × 4 tiled along +x at 600 (§11.15). Right: one fixture of 50 × 4. Same seats, same projection, both at §11.11’s 198 pitch.

§11.15’s tiling is withdrawn: the wall is one fixture and the row length grows with the collection. The drawing is not close — tiled units read as three bookcases stepping away from the reader, and they do not even touch, because 600 of +x projects 520 right and 300 down and each unit carries its own uprights, so the seam between two units is two uprights and a gap in mid-air. The right-hand drawing is a wall of records; the left is furniture in a room. §11.15 named this alternative and called it a parameter — row length — against the tiling being a fact about where shelves go, and that framing is what makes the withdrawal cheap: nothing about the projection, the seating or the pull changes, only how many seats a shelf has.

The measurable difference is the aspect: 1481 × 1647 at 0.90 tiled against 883 × 1302 at 0.68 as one fixture. Both panes were first drawn at a 225 pitch — the pull drawings’ value, carried into a script whose only purpose was comparing at §11.11’s geometry — which gave 0.84 against 0.63 and, worse, drew rows at exactly zero overlap: the variant the next paragraph rejects, in the drawing arguing against it. Regenerated at 198; the gap widens. And both panes were then repainted: the generator emitted shelves in descending z, which is nearest-first, so every shelf plane painted before the row beneath it and masked nothing — the records’ top faces showed through the shelf above them. That is this section’s own rule failing in its own drawing: a shelf and the row below it are disjoint in z (records reach z + 150, the strip above starts at z + 190), so a separating plane exists and the order was simply inverted. The extents are unaffected — they are computed from corners — so the two aspect figures and the ruling stand, which is the one respect in which this was not the 363 case: a paint-order defect cannot move a bounding box. A tiled wall grows on both screen axes at once because its own axis descends, so it gets taller as the collection grows and the far view frames less of it per record; one fixture grows along a single axis and the far view frames a band. And the third unit is visibly part-empty at 200 while the first two are full, which is the fill order made into a silhouette — §11.12 rules seats empty rather than absent, and tiling turns that into a ragged third object.

Paint order and reading order separate, and §11.8’s argument does not reach the separation. The overlap is measured and structural: a record’s projected extent is 150 plus a 75px top face, 225 against the 198 pitch, so every lower row overlaps the row above by 27px and a correct paint order must interleave rows by column. Growing the pitch to 225 is the wrong repair — it changes §11.11’s unit for a reason that has nothing to do with how shelves are built, and it buys a DOM property at the cost of the fixture’s proportions. So the keyboard walk gets an explicit tabindex sequence in seat order. §11.8 preferred anchors to a parallel list because a list draws the identifying channel twice; a tab sequence draws nothing, so it is not a second representation and the argument is silent on it. §11.8’s assertion stands as written for document order within a row, and the cross-row case is now ruled rather than asserted.

And an interpenetrating object sorts by a reduced volume, stated as a rule because the next one will need it: where two objects share bounds, the sorted extent is the part that does not interpenetrate, and the drawn extent is unchanged. A shelf spans upright to upright and therefore shares bounds with both, so no plane separates them and the centroid fallback made a cycle — upright over shelf, records over upright, shelf over records — which painted a shelf over its own row and made every spine in it unclickable. Sorting the shelf as the span between the uprights resolves it. One object’s sorting bounds differing from its drawn bounds is sound and needs saying: the separating-plane order is exact only for disjoint boxes, so an object that interpenetrates has to be reduced to a disjoint proxy before it can be ordered at all, and a cycle in a painter’s order is the symptom that one was not.

The reframing dissolves into §11.22 rather than needing an answer: the probe refits its viewBox every frame, the build’s is fixed, and a record from the row’s left end travels 251px further left than the region holds. That is the same gap §11.22 closed — a gesture in the wall’s coordinates and a frame in the page’s — and the pan closes it here too, on the same clock and the same ease. No separate reframe, and no drift.

11.24 · The filter belongs in the rail; the narrow shelf is the far view

The rail gains the filter, directly under SEARCH and in the same vocabulary — and §11.12 is what forces it rather than making it a convenience. A filter that empties seats produces a shape on the fixture: that was the whole ruling, and it is the reason the query returns the collection with matches marked rather than the matching subset. A shape on the fixture is something you read on the shelf, so the control has to be on the shelf — arriving already filtered means the seats were empty when you got there, and an empty seat you did not watch empty is indistinguishable from a gap in the collection. Filtering elsewhere and landing on the shelf throws away exactly what §11.12 bought.

So: SEARCH, then GENRE and SORT beneath it, three lines of the rail’s 11px mono with the same ink underline, above the view switcher’s rule. ShelfControls’ behaviour survives and its form does not — it was a horizontal control strip, and §11.13 moved the page’s chrome into a column. The round trip through the table or grid chips stops being the only route, which is the defect: a behaviour reachable only from another view is a behaviour that view owns.

The fork is 1044 after all (§14): §11.26 moved it to the landing’s ~1280 because a fixed 560 cover could not fit below that, and §14 makes the cover elastic, which returns the binding constraint to this section’s own figure, because this section derives it from the fixture and so leaves a band where the wall is a fixture and the pull has nowhere to land. The ruling below stands in every respect but that constant. And the narrow shelf is the far view (§11.10), not a reflowed near one — which is a measured ruling rather than a fallback. §11.1 leaves the label as the only channel that identifies, and the label needs a 240 face to carry 37 characters; at 390px the near view holds about two seats, and two of two hundred is not a fixture. The shelf’s job is showing what the collection looks like, and at that width the near view cannot do it at any pitch. The far view can: labels are absent rather than shrunk, so it has no width floor at all, and it is the collection as an object, which is the one thing a 390px screen can still show.

Two consequences, both cheap because nothing new is drawn. A tap in the narrow far view goes to the record screen rather than to a pulled state — the pull needs a 560 cover and a 420 panel side by side, which 390px cannot hold, and §11.9’s two columns are the composition rather than a layout preference, so there is no narrow version of the landing to design. And the rail collapses to one row: search, the three view names, add record. §11.13 removed the horizontal band because the wall needed the height; at 390 the far view is bounded by width, so that argument does not hold and the band is correct there.

Which also closes what §11.8’s withdrawn fork left open, at a different place than it put it. The fork was at 820 and phrased as the record’s presentation — overlay or flank; the real fork is the shelf’s, it is at the width where the near view stops being a fixture, and below it the pulled state does not exist to be presented either way. That no mobile project runs the shelf specs is the finding worth keeping: the view had no narrow form and nothing was asserting that it did, so neither half of the gap could report the other.

11.25 · Growth rides the rotation, not the travel

§11.20’s reason for putting growth on the travel is wrong, and wrong in a way that decides where growth goes — §11.21 is untouched by this ruling, and the distinction matters: §11.20 schedules the growth, §11.21 says what it scales about. §11.20 rules that a record coming toward the reader gets larger and that this is what approach looks like — but this is an orthographic projection, where approach produces no size change at all, by definition. A record travelling toward the viewer in isometric is exactly the same size at every distance; that is what makes the projection isometric. So growth is not approach. It is the record leaving the projection — which is precisely what the rotation is.

Growth therefore rides the rotation’s window, joining at 0.42, and the cause is shared rather than the schedule being convenient. Two transforms with one cause, one window and one fixed point, with the travel underneath — which makes §11.21’s shared-fixed-point argument sharper rather than weaker. Size does not change through the first third: the travel establishes the motion as a motion, and then the growth and the turn arrive together as one departure from the drawing.

The measurement is why the old distribution could not be tuned into working: 410px of growth against 290px of travel on one ease is a ratio of 1.41 at every instant. The size change is always half again the position change, everywhere along the curve — so it read as scaling rather than travelling structurally, not because the numbers were off. A constant ratio is the signature of two quantities sharing a curve when only one of them belongs on it.

The two alternatives, both weighed and both declined. Growing entirely after the travel would read as a zoom, which §11.20 rejected correctly — the section whose scheduling is withdrawn here got that much right — and this is not that, because the rotation’s window still overlaps most of the travel. And the finish is the other candidate with a real claim, being literally where the projection is removed; but 410px over 300ms is abrupt, and it would separate the size from the turn that shares its cause, which is the one relationship this ruling exists to establish.

Built as an adjustable window rather than a constant, like the finish’s 300ms — and for the same stated reason. The 0.42 join is a motion parameter, and this is the second one in the gesture that no still can judge (§11.21): the endpoints agree under every distribution and only the frames between them differ. What a still cannot judge, a ruling should not fix.

11.26 · The pan clears the seat; the fork is the landing’s

The landing moves, and neither the travel nor the cover does — because the mechanism that moves it is already ruled. §11.22 pans the view precisely to reconcile a gesture in the wall’s coordinates with a frame in the page’s, and the seat’s occlusion is that same mismatch one more time: 290 units and 560px are both right in their own space and collide in the frame. So the pan gains a target it did not have — it settles where the empty seat clears the cover’s trailing edge — and the gesture is untouched.

The other two options each spend something that was settled by a method the composition cannot overrule. 290 was watched, on a probe, against the thing §11.25 calls unjudgeable from stills; shortening it to fix a static overlap is a still overruling a motion. And 560 was bounded below by the fixture and the seat staying visible, so shrinking the cover satisfies that bound by retreating from it rather than meeting it. The pan costs nothing already ruled, which is what makes it the answer rather than the compromise.

And the seat stays load-bearing, which is the whole point of not solving this with a lightness step. §11.10 makes the empty seat the mark that says which record is out and §11.22 makes it the separation that replaces a scrim — both fail silently if the cover covers it, and a cover that hides the seat would have sent the next round looking for a scrim to fix a symptom the pan owns.

The fork is the landing’s width, not the fixture’s: about 1280 rather than 1044. §11.24 derives it from the fixture, which is the right method and the wrong subject — the fork exists to separate the width where the pull works from the width where a tap goes to the record screen instead, so it has to be derived from the pull. Deriving it from the fixture leaves a band from 1044 to about 1280 where the wall is a fixture and the pull has nowhere to land, which is exactly the failure the fork was written to prevent, surviving inside the fork itself. One constant either way, and the correct one is max(fixture, landing).

Add record does not wrap: in the band it is one row item, not a column item at a column’s width. §11.13 set it at the foot of a column and §11.24 collapsed the rail to a band; the wrap is the column’s width rule arriving in a layout that has horizontal room and no vertical room — the same granularity shape, in the smallest thing on the page. And one thing worth recording rather than ruling: the far view arrives after a client measurement, so a phone paints the near view once first. That is a flash of a view §11.24 says does not exist at that width, and it is a build concern rather than a drawing one.

11.27 · The chrome on the drawn paper

The generic hairlines take §3’s value — 0.72 — and stop being a second scale. --border at 1.08:1 and --input at 1.15:1 are not rules a reader can follow; §3’s hairline is 0.72 on this paper and was chosen against it, and the app has been carrying two hairline values the whole time — one derived on the drawn ground and one on a ground nothing painted. §11.5 did not lower them, it made them measurable, which is the same shape as the 11px label at 3.88: a defect that predates every ruling and surfaces when the measurement moves to the ground the app paints.

And §3 already forbids the outcome, which is why this is a correction rather than a new rule: it spends its argument keeping a rule at the threshold of visible, and a rule at 1.08:1 is past that threshold on the wrong side. A hairline that cannot be seen is not a quiet rule, it is an absent one — the table’s rules and the search box’s edge are the structure those views are built from.

The chip surfaces invert rather than retune: a hover must sink, so it steps toward ink, not away from it. At 0.945–0.955 against a 0.925 ground they are lighter than the paper, so the gesture reads as lifting — and that is a behaviour reversing, not a ratio drifting, which is the more serious of the two. A number that drifts is wrong by a margin; a surface that was meant to depress and now rises is telling the reader the opposite of what it means, and no amount of tuning inside those values fixes the direction.

The value is the ladder’s shade step applied from paper: 26% toward ink, which is 0.731. §5.5’s steps are proportional — tint at 34% toward paper, shade at 26% toward ink — so borrowing the step means borrowing the proportion, not a lightness delta, and the proportion applied against paper is what a surface one step below paper means.

An earlier version of this ruling said 0.90 and called it the ladder’s step, and the figure disproves itself against this section’s own standard: 0.90 on a 0.925 paper is 1.08:1 — the exact ratio the hairline paragraph two above disqualifies --border for. It was a flat delta of 0.025 wearing a proportional step’s justification, which matched neither the 34% nor the 26%, and it would have inverted the direction while leaving the surface as invisible as the one it replaced. 0.731 reads 1.91:1 against paper — a surface a reader can see sink.

The general form, because it is what let a wrong number pass a paragraph arguing for the right principle: a proportional step and a fixed delta are not interchangeable, and a value quoted as “one step” has to name which. The chrome borrows the drawing’s steps rather than inventing its own, which is the whole content of this ruling — and a borrowed step is only borrowed if it is recomputed against its new ground. Both changes are one-line token edits and neither touches a drawing.

What this does not do is make the chrome part of the composition. §11.5 makes every ratio measurable against one paper and nothing more — the table, the grid and the search box stay the app’s chrome, ruled only where they contradict a value the drawings depend on. The two here contradict §3 and the ladder respectively, which is why they are ruled and the rest is not.

11.28 · The far view’s fit, and what the reader clicks

The count moves beside the drawing and the fit stays to height — option 4 with option 1, and it does enlarge the drawing, which is the one measurement in the brief that is wrong. Code reads the region’s height as the screen’s already; it is not — the COLLECTION band is eating 281px of the 847 available, which is why the region is 1240 × 566. Moving the count into a column returns that height: at 17 records the fixture goes from 239px wide to 311, and at 200 from 384 to 531 — 30% and 38%. Not a large drawing, but it is not nothing, and it comes from deleting a band rather than from any change to the fixture.

Those are the measured figures; this section first said 337 and 542, computed against the region’s 847px of height when the drawing’s box is 779 — the 34px padding on both edges, omitted. It is the content-box error from §11.19’s frame, arriving in the section that argues about how much height a band was eating, and the padding is the same quantity the argument is made of. The padding stays: recovering the last 8% would put the fixture against the region’s rule, and §11.28’s whole case is that the drawing wants room rather than that it wants to be large.

The far view at 17 records under this ruling. The count beside the drawing rather than above it; the occupied run hovered, sunk to §11.27’s 0.731, its hairlines recomputed to 0.588 against that ground, its count beside it. Fixture 311px wide against 239 now — the measured fit, padding included.

The same at 200 records — 531px wide, four shelves of fifty, one fixture per §11.23. The composition does not change; the object does.

Fit to width is rejected for the reason Code gives and fit-with-scroll for a sharper one: it changes axis partway up the range. Vertical below about 400 records and horizontal above, so the same gesture would mean two different things depending on how many records you own — a control whose direction is a function of collection size is not a control the reader can learn.

And the fixture’s shape does not follow the collection (option 5), for the reason §8.1 already gives: three empty shelves are constant because unfilled, not because abandoned. They are the room the collection grows into, and a fixture that resized itself as records arrived would mean the wall never looks the same twice — which spends the fixed frame that makes position readable at all (§11.1). The emptiness is honest. What was wrong was spending the region on emptiness too, and that is the band, not the shelves.

The click target is the occupied run, not the fixture and not the region. A region-sized target that does one thing is not a control, it is a page that responds anywhere; and the fixture includes three empty shelves, so half the fixture as a target promises a view of nothing. The run is the only part of the drawing that has something to zoom to. Clicking it opens the near view at that shelf — which is what makes the target mean something rather than being a button drawn in the shape of a shelf.

It signals with the hover §11.27 just ruled: the run sinks to 0.731, its hairlines take 0.588, and its count appears beside it in 11px mono. The hairline moves because the ground moved — §5.5’s shade step from 0.731 rather than from paper — and the first version of this drawing left it at 0.72, which reads 1.04:1 on the hover surface against 1.99:1 on paper. That is worse than the 1.08:1 §11.27 refused 0.90 for, one section after that section’s closing sentence says a borrowed value is only borrowed if it is recomputed against its new ground — and it erased the only channel separating one spine from another, so the hover said one object at the moment it meant seventeen records. 0.588 restores the separation at 1.74:1 — close to the 1.99:1 the run has at rest, and deliberately not equal to it. Matching rest would put the hairline near 0.556, which is a number tuned to a target; 0.588 is §5.5’s shade step and the derivation wins. This sentence first claimed 1.91:1 and a match, and 1.91 is §11.27’s figure for 0.731 against paper — a different pair, carried onto a hairline-against-surface measurement, which is the cited-for-a-quantity-it-was-not-measured-on class landing inside the sentence that repairs a ground mismatch. Two things at once — the sink says pressable in the vocabulary the chips already use, and the count says what is there, which is the one fact the far view withholds by design. No cursor change carries this on its own and no caption is added: a caption explaining a drawing is the admission that the drawing does not work.

Adam’s error is the finding worth keeping, because it is not an affordance problem. He read the far view as a broken near view — reasonably, since it is the same drawing smaller, and §11.10’s “labels absent rather than shrunk” is indistinguishable from labels that failed to draw. The fix is not a hint; it is that the count beside the object makes the pair read as the collection, as a number and as a shape, which a near view never shows. The composition tells him which view he is in; the hover only tells him what to do in it.

11.29 · The desktop route opens near

§11.12’s “the route opens far” is withdrawn on the desktop: a bare / opens the near view, and the far view becomes a deliberate zoom-out. Code’s case is right and its strongest part is the one that uses this file’s own standard against an earlier ruling of mine: §11.28 spent a whole band to buy the drawing 30% more width, on the ground that 30% is not nothing — and by that standard a first screen that answers neither of its questions at the common case is a worse buy than a click. At 17 records the far view is a 311px object with no labels; the near view is seventeen records you can read and pull.

And opening far below a size while opening near above it is rejected on §11.28’s own ground, harder: behaviour changing partway up the range. Worse here, because the threshold is invisible — a reader cannot see why their collection opened differently from someone else’s, and crossing 80 records would silently change what the app does on load. A fork the reader can see (§11.26’s viewport width) is a different object from one they cannot.

What opening near costs, stated because §11.28 refused to let the far view hide its emptiness and this must not hide its own: the fixture is 442 × 1047 at 1:1 in a 968 × 799 region, so it does not fit. Height is short by 248px — the arrival shows about three shelves of four — and width leaves 526px of the region empty at 20 seats. The first is answered by where it lands; the second is real and is the near view’s standing condition, not a defect of this ruling: a fixture narrower than its region is what a 20-seat shelf looks like, and §11.28 already refused to resize the fixture to fill space.

So the arrival lands on the occupied shelf rather than at the fixture’s top corner — the same target §11.28 gives a click on a run, and for the same reason: the empty shelves are the room the collection grows into, and a view that opens on them opens on nothing. The pan (§11.22) does the positioning; no new mechanism.

Nothing else moves. The far view keeps §11.24’s narrow shelf — below the fork the route still opens far, because there the near view is not a fixture — and keeps §11.12’s filter shape, stays reachable from the count, and Escape still reaches it. §11.28’s fit, click target and hover are untouched: this rules when the far view is entered, not what it is.

And the remembered-or-linked view composes rather than competing, once the view is in the URL: a bare / opens near, a linked view opens where it says. That is one constant now (DEFAULT_ROUTE_VIEW) and a URL parameter later; build the constant first, because a default is what a link is an exception to.

11.30 · Reaching the run by keyboard

The run is focusable, and it is a button rather than an anchor — which is where the parallel to §11.23 breaks and has to. A spine is an anchor because a record has a route; a run has none, and §11.29 makes the near view the default rather than a destination, so “the shelf” is a camera position and not an address. An anchor with no href is a link to nowhere announced as a link, which is worse for the reader it exists to serve than a control announced as what it is. It is a button labelled by what the hover says in ink: 17 records — zoom to this shelf.

Order: after the rail, before nothing — it is the last stop on the far view because it is the only one. The rail is the page’s chrome and the run is its content, and §11.24 put the filter in the rail precisely so the shape on the fixture is read after it is set. Tab order follows that sequence rather than reversing it. At more than one occupied run — any collection over a shelf’s worth — runs take document order, which is §11.23’s seat order one level up: top shelf first, because that is the order they filled.

Focus is the hover’s sink and count plus a 2px ink rule along the run’s front edge, and the addition is the point. Hover and focus must not be the same state: hover follows a pointer that is already where the reader is looking, and focus has to be findable by someone who cannot see where it went. The sink alone is a 1.74:1 change in a drawing made of 1.99:1 hairlines — legible as a response, not as a location. The rule is 0.18 on the 0.731 surface, which is 7.89:1, and it lies along the front edge because that edge is the run’s longest continuous line and the only one no spine interrupts.

2px because §3 already owns this: it is the weight reserved for a mark that is not a rule about type, and §11.27 has just spent the round making sure the app has one hairline value rather than two. A focus ring at any other weight would be the second tier §3 forbids. And the value is recomputed against its ground rather than borrowed: 0.18 reads 7.89:1 on the hover surface and 15.07:1 on paper, so it clears on both — which is the check §11.27’s closing sentence asks for, run before the value was chosen rather than after it failed.

This paragraph first shipped 8.12 and 9.48, so the sentence making the check’s case was the one that failed it — and the two errors are different in kind, which is the part worth keeping. 7.89 against 8.12 is a rounding-grade slip; 15.07 against 9.48 is not reachable by rounding from this pair at all, so it was computed against some other ground and carried in — the cited-for-a-quantity-it-was-not-measured-on class, twice in three sections (§11.28). The tell is cheap and general: a figure that cannot be reached from its stated pair by rounding was measured on a different pair, and that is checkable without knowing which. The value is unaffected: 0.18 clears both grounds by a wide margin, so only the figures moved.

What this does not do is give the far view a second control. §11.28 rules the run is the only target because the fixture is half empty shelves; keyboard access does not widen that — it reaches the same target by another route, which is the whole of §11.23’s argument for a tab sequence over a parallel list. Escape still returns, and the count in the facts column is text rather than a control, so nothing new enters the order.

11.31 · Which lines the page carries

Adam is right that nothing rules them and right to have looked — the drawings carry the structure and the rulings describe only its parts. §11.19 rules the panel’s order, §11.13 the rail’s bleed, §11.27 what value a hairline takes; none of them says the page is divided by drawn lines, and every drawing in §11.19, §11.28 and §11.29 divides it by drawn lines. That is the drawing-ahead-of-the-ruling case rather than the reverse, so the lines are stated here rather than removed.

Six lines, and no others: two verticals — rail to facts column, facts column to drawing region — each full-bleed from the nav to the page foot; two horizontals in the rail, above the view switcher and above Add record; and two in the facts column, under the count and above the two verbs. The facts column’s two are present when the panel is: the far view carries four and the landed state six, because a rule under the count with nothing below it separates nothing — the far view’s count sits in the column unruled, which is what §11.28’s drawings show. This enumeration said four, omitting the rail’s pair, and then said six as a flat count of every state — the same class twice in one sentence: the first miscount read the rulings instead of the drawings, the second read one drawing as though it were all of them, and §11.13 gives the rail its pair explicitly in both — counting the lines in a drawing by reading the rulings rather than the drawing, in the section written to close exactly that gap. Both verticals run the page’s full height because §11.13’s argument was that a column is a region rather than a box, and a rule that stops short of the foot draws a box. The horizontals close the panel’s ends: the count is the collection and everything below it is one record, and the verbs are what you do rather than what is true.

The fact groups’ separators bleed across the facts column too, exactly as the panel’s two horizontals do — they are not inset. A separator that stopped at the type’s measure would be a rule about type (§3), and these divide a region; an earlier draft of this paragraph called them inset and the next paragraph called them bleeding, which the drawings settle in favour of bleeding. What distinguishes them from the six is what they divide, not where they stop.

Two weights, and the drawings have been corrected to it rather than the rule bent to them: 1px for every rule on this page, 2px reserved for §3’s non-type marks — §11.30’s focus edge, the journal edge, and the rail’s set bar. That bar was drawn at 4px and is now 2: it is a non-type mark, so §3 gives it the same weight as the focus edge, and at 4 it was a third tier inside the sweep that claims there are two. Its length, 44, is what distinguishes it from a rule — a mark that stops is not a rule that failed to reach. All six structural lines were drawn at 2px and the separators at 1, which is precisely the structural-weight-plus-divider-weight split this paragraph says §3 forbids — three weights counting the focus edge. The 2px was never a decision: it was reach for visibility at a reduced drawing scale, which is a property of the drawing and not of the page, and it hardened into an apparent tier. The ruled fields’ ink underlines stay at 2px, because §9.3 rules those and they are not rules.

Value: 0.72 on the 0.925 paper, 1.99:1 — §3’s hairline against the ground the app paints (§11.5), which is the same correction §11.27 applies to --border. The app’s 1.08:1 is not a lighter version of this line, it is an absent one, and the structure Adam could not find in the rulings is also the structure he cannot currently see on the screen — the same defect reported twice, once against the file and once against the build.

And what aligns: everything in the facts column aligns to one left edge, and every horizontal in it bleeds across the column rather than stopping at that edge. The type has a measure and the rules have a region — §3’s inset-hairline distinction, which is about type, against the full-bleed rule, which is about structure. The drawing region carries no rules at all: it holds one drawing, and a rule inside it would be a line the projection did not put there.

11.32 · The oxblood accent

The accent does not survive on the shelf, and it survives unchanged everywhere else. §11 rests on one premise — the wall at rest is line, ink and paper, and colour arrives with the pull — and an oxblood Add record in the rail would be a second colour on a surface that has exactly one, arriving before the gesture that is supposed to introduce it. The pull would then be colour joining colour rather than colour arriving, which is the whole of what the rest state buys.

So the rule is the rest state’s, not the accent’s: on the shelf view nothing is oxblood, and the rail’s Add record stays ink on §11.13’s LABEL, as drawn. On the table and the grid the accent is untouched — those views have no rest state to protect and no pull to spend it on, and globals.css’ intent (actions only, never headers, borders or decoration) is a good rule that §11 has no quarrel with.

Which makes the inconsistency real and acceptable, and worth saying so rather than resolving it flat. The same action is ink in the rail and oxblood in the table’s header — but the two are not the same object: one sits in a drawing whose rest state is a premise, the other in a chrome view that is a table. §11.27 already sets the terms: the chrome borrows the drawing’s values where they contradict it and keeps its own elsewhere. An accent that must disappear on one view is not a broken accent; an accent applied where it contradicts a view’s premise is a broken view.

And the active filter chips are the case that decides it, because they are the one place the accent would land on the shelf: §11.24 puts GENRE and SORT in the rail, so an active chip in oxblood would sit beside a monochrome fixture. Active takes the rail’s own set-mark: the short ink bar under the label that §11.13 gives the active view name — 44 wide, and 2px rather than the 4 it was drawn at. This paragraph first said “the 2px ink underline §11.13 gives a set control”, which was wrong twice: the rail’s underline is the field’s rule (§9.3), present on GENRE and SORT whether or not a filter is set — so the named replacement encoded no state at all, which is the one thing the paragraph exists to specify — and §11.13’s actual set mark is the bar, not an underline. A value borrowed by name without checking what it does on the ground it lands on, one section after §11.31 and two after §11.30 record that class.

One consequence stated so it is not discovered: a filter set on the table and carried to the shelf changes appearance, oxblood chip to ink underline. That is correct rather than a seam — §11.12 rules the filter’s result is a shape on the fixture, so on the shelf the filter’s expression is the empty seats, and the chip only says which filter made them. A chip competing with the shape it caused would be the defect.

11.33 · Hover and focus on a spine

No, a spine does not pull out on hover — and the reason is the one Adam’s question already contains. A small version of the pull is still the pull: §11.19’s gesture is the transition from the collection to a record, and a hover that performs 10% of it says that transition is underway when nothing has been chosen. §11.25 made the point in the other direction — growth is the record leaving the projection — and a hover cannot mean a transition that has not been chosen. Motion of a record is the channel this page reserves for the pull, and a preview spends it — the view’s own motions are untouched, since §11.22’s pan and §11.28’s zoom move the camera rather than anything in the drawing.

A spine hovers exactly as a run does: it sinks to §11.27’s 0.731 with hairlines at 0.588, and nothing else. No lift, no offset, no shadow. The far view’s run also shows a count on hover because the far view withholds counts by design; the near view withholds nothing — the spine’s label is already set on its face, so there is nothing to reveal and a tooltip would repeat the drawing. Same vocabulary, and the difference between the two is a fact about each view rather than a decision about hovers.

Focus takes the sink plus an ink mark, as §11.30 rules — but on the spine’s top face, not its front edge, and 2px does not fit on the front. A spine’s face projects to 10.4 units wide, so a 2px rule is 19% of it: at that proportion the mark stops reading as an edge and starts reading as a spine of a different colour, which is the channel §11.28 spent the hover hairline correction protecting. The top face is 130 units deep and no spine’s label crosses it, so the mark has room and interrupts nothing.

Value unchanged: 0.18, 7.89:1 on the sunk surface and 15.07:1 on paper (§11.30, recomputed rather than assumed). And the ruling is the same shape as §11.30’s own: hover and focus must differ, because hover follows a pointer already where the reader is looking. What changes between run and spine is where the mark can physically go, which is geometry, not vocabulary.

The app’s oxblood focus ring goes, on the shelf only, per §11.32 — and this is the case that shows why that ruling had to reach past Add record. A focus ring is chrome the app applies everywhere without asking what it lands on; on a monochrome fixture it is the only colour on the page, arriving on whatever the reader happens to tab to. §11.32 rules colour off the shelf, and a default that paints colour onto the shelf defeats it more thoroughly than a button would, because it can land anywhere.

11.34 · An emptied seat is drawn

The first option: an emptied seat draws its footprint — the seat’s own rectangle on the shelf’s top face, 12 × 150, one hairline at 0.72. Nothing else changes. Six matches then read as six records and eleven empty berths rather than as a shorter shelf, because the berths are drawn and a short shelf has none.

The measurement is the finding and it is sharper than the fix: position invariance was necessary and not sufficient, and §11.12 tested the property rather than what the property was for. The seats hold to the pixel, exactly as ruled — and a shape made of absences is only a shape if the absences are drawn. An undrawn seat is not an empty seat, it is no seat; the layout was right and the drawing had nothing in it to read. Same class as the extent test that could not see a front/back flip: the thing asserted was true and was not the thing that mattered.

The other two are declined on their own terms. Reordering under a filter fights §11.1’s fixed frame, which is the whole reason position can carry the collection’s order at all — and it would make the filter’s result a different wall rather than this wall, filtered. And accepting “a run that stops early” gives up §11.12’s premise while keeping its language: if the genre filter — the filter the rail actually has — produces no readable shape, the ruling is not serving the case it was written for.

Footprints are drawn only where a record was displaced, never where one has not yet been shelved — which is §8.1’s test again: a seat emptied by a filter is a fact about the filter, and a never-filled seat is a fact about the backlog. Drawing both would put sixty-three footprints on a seventeen-record fixture — the never-filled seats, not the eighty the fixture has, since seventeen of those hold records and cannot carry one and turn the room-to-grow into a grid of vacancies, which is option 5’s defect arriving from the other side. The three empty shelves stay blank.

1px, and it does not contradict §11.31’s “the drawing region carries no rules” — a footprint is projected geometry rather than a page rule. §11.31 forbids a line the projection did not put there; the footprint is a seat’s own rectangle in the wall’s coordinates, drawn by the same projection as the shelf under it and moving with the pan, which no rule in §11.31 does. Weight follows from that: it is not one of the three named 2px non-type marks, so it takes 1px like everything else drawn at hairline.

And the footprint is a hairline rather than a tint, so §11.32 is untouched: the shelf at rest stays line, ink and paper. It reads as the shelf’s own marking — the outline a record leaves on a surface it has been standing on — which is what an empty berth in a real fixture looks like, and it needs no legend.

11.35 · The count’s mark, and what a sort moves

The count carries the arrow — THE WHOLE COLLECTION → in 11px mono beneath the figure — and the set bar is refused. §11.13’s 44-wide bar means this is the current state: it marks the active view name and, under §11.32, a set filter. Putting it under the count would say the count is set, not that it is pressable, and a state mark on a control is worse than no mark because it reads as an answer rather than an offer.

The arrow is already this page’s departure mark and it is already in both views: §11.19’s panel ends OPEN THE FULL RECORD → and §11.28’s run hover reads 17 RECORDS →. So the mark is the same in both views and only its timing differs — at rest on the near view’s count, on hover on the far view’s run. The far view’s own count does not carry it: there is nowhere to go, since you are already looking at the whole collection — because the far view’s run is the whole drawing and its count is the thing withheld, while the near view’s count is already on screen and only its pressability is not.

And this is not the caption §11.28 refused. That refusal was about explaining a drawing — a label on a control is the control’s name, not a gloss on a picture, and the page has carried arrow-labels since §11.19 without any of them explaining anything. Adam reporting the far view as missing is the measure of the defect: a pointer cursor and an accessible name are not marks, and 72px of ink that does nothing else on this page is a display figure until something says otherwise.

The sort reordering the wall is intended, and §11.1 already licenses it: position carries the collection’s order, not a record’s address. The sort chooses which order, so moving everything is what position-carries-order means rather than a violation of it. The fixed frame §11.1 protects is the fixture — seats, pitch, row length — and none of that moves under a sort; what moves is which record sits in which seat, and the label is the identifying channel precisely so that position does not have to be.

§11.34’s footprint is unaffected, because it is read within one arrangement rather than across two. A footprint says a record was displaced from this seat, in this order — it is a statement about the filter, not a memory of where something used to live, and re-sorting redraws both the records and their vacancies together. The one thing a reader loses is positional recall across sorts, which §11.1 already declined to sell them.

Section order remains the tie-break under a chosen sort, as built. A sort names one key and the collection is full of ties — a shelf of records that share a year would otherwise arrange themselves differently on each load, which is the determinism §11.1 depends on and the same reason spineWidth hashes rather than randomises. The tie-break is not a second sort; it is what makes the first one a function.

11.36 · The set bar leaves the flow

The bar comes out of flow: it is drawn against the label’s baseline and occupies no height, so the switcher’s pitch is one number whether a view is set or not — 42, per §11.37.
