Not a fixed row height — that would absorb the bar by reserving space for it on every row, which is the same 8px spent invisibly instead of visibly, and it would make the rail’s rhythm a consequence of the widest possible state rather than of the type.

The reason is what the bar is: §11.31 settles that a mark that stops is not a rule that failed to reach, and this is the other half of it — a mark is not content, so it cannot push. A bar that displaces its neighbours makes the rail’s spacing encode state, so GRID sits 8px lower when SHELF is active than when it is not, and a set filter moves the switcher. Position in the rail is the reader’s map of the page’s controls; a map that shifts when you use it is not one.

And it generalises to §11.32’s reuse, which is why this is worth a ruling rather than a build note: the same bar marks a set filter, and GENRE and SORT sit above the switcher — in flow, a set filter would push every view name down, so choosing a genre would move the control you choose the view with. Out of flow, setting anything moves nothing.

One correction to accept from the build: a rail without GENRE is legitimate — §11.24 renders the facet only where facets exist — so omitting it is a claim rather than a gap. It asserts a collection with no genres. The four drawings were nonetheless stale rather than deliberate, since each draws a seventeen-record collection whose panel sets PRESSING, PROVENANCE and MATRIX, and §11.28’s pair predate the ruling by generation order. But the distinction stands for the next reader: an absent control in a drawing says the state that hides it, and a drawing cannot abstain.

11.37 · The type governs the pitch

42, and the specimen is corrected — which reverses last round’s tie-break without contradicting it. That ruling chose the specimen’s 44 over a page drawing’s 38 on the ground that the 1:1 drawing is the true-size one; both figures were hand-set, so it was a choice between two drawings and the specimen was rightly the authority. 42 is not a third drawing: it is the measured advance of the rail’s own type at an 18px gap. A drawing’s figure is authoritative over another drawing, not over the type it depicts.

And §11.36’s reasoning settles it rather than merely favouring it. That section took the bar out of flow so the rhythm would follow the type instead of the widest state — reaching 44 now means padding the gap to 20px to hit a number, which is the same defect in the other direction: a figure chosen first and the spacing bent to reach it. The 44 was never derived; it was the value the in-flow rail happened to average.

All five rails are redrawn at 42 and the specimen with them, so the file states one pitch. The general form, since this is the second tie-break between a drawing and a measurement in two rounds: a drawing is evidence about composition and a build is evidence about type metrics, and when they disagree about a number that type produces, the drawing is the thing that moves — which is what §4.2’s 69px stack and §8.1’s acquisition date each settled one instance of.

12 · The reference pass on /records/[id]

The order is: finish the shelf, make this page sound, style the remaining six against it, then the image viewer. Of the shelf’s three opens, two are closed — §11.27 is in build step 10 and the pitch is 42 (§11.37) — and the third, §11.19’s title-wrap collision, stays with the shelf. An earlier version of this paragraph moved it here as “also this page’s”, which it is not: §11.19’s collision is between a 420px panel’s title block and a foot pinned by Turn over and Put back, and this page has neither — its identity cell is a 480px band with a 412px measure. This page’s own title question is closed, by text-wrap: balance (§4.2): the worst case fits at 498 of 500 and the defect was the shape, not the height. Two different questions sharing the phrase a long title in a narrow column.

The pass has one job and it is not improvement: make every value on this page one that another screen can be measured against. A reference page with two hairline values or an undecided collision does not export a vocabulary — it exports the ambiguity, six times. Nothing here is a redesign; each item is a value this page states differently from a ruling that now exists.

Two of the three reconciliations were done before the pass began, and the list is corrected rather than left as work: the paper is painted at globals.css:124 with a repo test holding it, and the hairline is 0.72 at globals.css:167. Measured on the route, all 39 border edges at 1440 conform — 20 page rules at 1px, 13 control edges, 4 on one boxed element, AppHeader’s own, and one 2px mark which is the journal edge, one of §11.31’s three named ones — so the page already conforms on weight and value and the pass’s reconciliation is the line set alone. The withdrawn list follows, kept because the ordering argument still holds for any screen that has not had the pass. What it reconciles, in order of blast radius. The paper: the page predates the 0.925 token, so every ratio on it was measured on a ground the app no longer paints (§11.5) — this must go first, because the next two items are ratios. The hairlines: §11.27’s 0.72 replaces whatever --border was giving, and §11.31’s weights apply — 1px for every rule, 2px only for the named non-type marks. The lines: §11.31 rules which lines a page carries and this page has never been enumerated against it, so the pass states its set rather than inheriting one.

What it decides: the oxblood accent on this page. §11.32 rules it off the shelf because the shelf has a rest state to protect, and this page has the opposite premise — it is where the record’s colour lives — so the shelf’s answer does not transfer and no section has asked the question here. It cannot be deferred, and the reason is the one that was misapplied above: every screen styled against this page has buttons, so whatever an accent does beside a derived colour here is what six screens inherit. That inheritance argument is true of the accent and was not true of the shelf panel’s collision, which no other screen’s structure reproduces.

What it fixes, from Adam’s screenshots — four, all of them the build departing from a ruling this file already carries, none needing a new one: the construction block sitting outside its bar; the clipped journal field; the region’s isometric solids rendered grey, where §5.5 and §9.2 give them the ladder’s three tones — the matrix still excepted, which §5 rules record-independent; and the 10px ← Collection link, deleted by §8.1 and still drawn. The buttons are not among them — they are the pass’s decision rather than its repairs, since what they need is the ruling above and not a correction to one.

What the pass does not touch: the composition. §1 through §10 are settled and the frame is closed (§8). A reference page is authoritative because it is stable, so the pass reconciles values and decides the accent, and any wish to improve the drawing is out of scope by construction.

13 · The record’s controls, and what the ornament is made of (placement superseded by §24; ornament clause stands)

Superseded by §24: both verbs sit together at AppHeader’s far right, in a slot empty on every other screen. The placement argued below is withdrawn; the band deletion stands. Edit moves to the right end of the frame’s eyebrow line, level with COLLECTION. Delete does not go with it — it goes to the foot of the scrolling region. And the ← Collection band is deleted entirely. Three moves, one reason each, and §3 supplies all three: a departure, an interaction and an ending are three things, not two.

Withdrawn by §27: the eyebrow row below is undone. It cost no height only while Edit shared the line; §24 moved Edit to AppHeader, and the row outlived its reason and began charging about 19px.

Edit belongs on the eyebrow line because that line is already the record’s own header rather than the app’s. Not in AppHeader: that is chrome shared with six screens, and a control that acts on this record cannot live in a bar that is identical on all of them. The eyebrow is the frame’s top line, it is 11px mono, and Edit is 11px mono — so the control joins a line it already matches and costs no height. The structure, because “costs no height” is a claim about it: the eyebrow was the first child of the identity cell’s column flex, and it is now wrapped in a row of its own — justify-content: space-between, baseline-aligned, the eyebrow first and Edit second, so the row’s height is the line’s and Edit is at the cell’s right edge rather than absolutely positioned against it. All three identity-cell drawings carry it, and all five region drawings carry Delete as their last row — drawn rather than ruled in prose, per §11.35. The ← Collection band needs no drawing: it is in none of them, having only ever been built.

Delete goes to the foot, alone in its own row, and the reason is not caution about mis-clicks — it is that deletion is the record’s end and the page is the record. §11.19 put Open the full record above Turn over and Put back on exactly this ground: a departure separates from the verbs that act on the object. Delete is neither — it is the departure that takes the record with it — so it sits after everything the record is, which is the last row of §9’s region. Keeping the two verbs together would put the app’s only irreversible act in its chrome line, where every other screen’s chrome is safe.

And the band goes with them — the container, because §8.1 already deleted its only other occupant: “Navigation is constant across records (§3), so it lives in AppHeader and nowhere else; the 10px ← Collection is deleted.” That the build still draws the link is a build defect against §8.1 and it is in §12’s fixes; what §13 adds is only that the band has nothing left to hold once Edit and Delete move out. Deleting it gives §9’s region its height back, which is §11.28’s move on the shelf arriving here.

Flat solid colour is admitted on this screen, and it does not contradict §11: §11’s rest state is the wall’s. The shelf withholds colour so the pull can introduce it, and §11.32 kept the accent off the shelf on exactly that ground — this page is where the pull arrives, so colour here is the arrival rather than a preview of it. A record screen that withheld colour would leave the gesture arriving nowhere.

The values are the ladder’s and nothing else: tint, base and shade of the record’s own derived colour (§5.5). No new hue enters as ornament — a flat shape in any colour the cover did not produce would be decoration that means something it cannot know, and the oxblood question is §12’s separate decision about controls. Flat shapes take tint where they are ground and base where they are a mark; shade stays a face of a solid, because a shade with no object to belong to is just a darker rectangle.

The isometric solids already take the ladder on their three faces — top tint, left base, right shade — in every drawing in this file, so §13 rules nothing new about them and the forms and geometry stand as §9.2 has them (four archetypes fixed per section, height at 0.62 of the section, the two-thirds visible gate, half a column of clearance from a control). An earlier version of this paragraph diagnosed them as drawn grey and called the three tones the fix — which was read off Adam’s screenshot rather than the file: the drawings carry the clamped ladder on all seventy-four faces and the build does not. So the dullness is a build defect against §5.5 and §9.2, and it is in §12’s fixes. The matrix still is excluded: §5 captions it record-independent, so its three grey faces are the one place the ladder must not reach — and a fix stated as “the solids stop being grey” would have coloured exactly that one.

And two flat shapes per region, no more: one tint field as ground in the last section’s widest cell (§9.4) and one base rectangle as a mark in an empty cell above it. Two rather than “a few”, because §9.4’s floor and the one-mark-per-section rule are what stop ornament becoming pattern, and a third flat shape makes the region read as a layout with colour blocks rather than a page with marks in it. This is the app’s ornament vocabulary from here: isometric solids in the record’s three tones, flat fields in tint, flat marks in base, and no hue that was not sampled.

14 · The landing is elastic, and the fork returns to the fixture

Not intended, and the contradiction is inside the file rather than in Adam’s machine: §11.29 rules that the desktop opens near because the far view answers neither of its questions at a typical collection, and §11.26’s fork then withholds the near view from most desktops. A thirteen-inch laptop is a desktop. The gesture the design is built around cannot be unreachable on the commonest machine that runs it.

So the landing shrinks: the cover is the region’s width less the 24px gutters, capped at 560. The cover is min(560, W − 616) — the viewport less the 148 rail, the 420 panel and the 24px gutters — so it is 560 from 1440 all the way down to 1176, and elastic only from 1176 to 1044: 512 at 1128, 428 at 1044, which is where it stops. This paragraph first gave 658 as the cover’s width at 1274, which is the uncapped term written as the result — the cap was in the rule and not applied to the worked figures, so the elastic range was stated 98px too wide at its top. The panel, the rail and the gutters are as assumed; only the middle figure was wrong — and 428 is still wider than the 420 panel, so the cover remains the largest thing on the page, which is what §11.19 sized it to be. 560 was never a floor: §11.19 bounded it below by the fixture and the empty seat staying visible and then chose a number above that bound, so shrinking it spends a choice rather than a constraint.

And the fork returns to 1044 — §11.24’s figure, restored for a different reason than it was first given. §11.26 moved the fork to the landing because deriving it from the fixture left a band where the wall was readable and the pull had nowhere to land; with the landing elastic that band closes from the other side, so the binding constraint is the fixture again: one shelf of twenty, the rail, the panel and the region’s pad. §11.26’s rule survives verbatim — max(fixture, landing) — and its maximum has changed which term wins.

The two alternatives are declined, and one of them is barred by a ruling rather than a preference. Stacking the panel under the drawing buys 420px and contradicts §11.9, which §11.24 quotes as “the composition rather than a layout preference” — and it would put the panel below the fold while the cover is above it, so the landed state becomes a scroll and the two things the pull delivers stop being one view. A near view without the pull is §11.24’s narrow mechanism, and it is right below the fork and wrong above it: it answers the layout problem by removing the feature, which is the cheapest fix and the one that costs the most.

What Adam saw was the ruled behaviour, so there is no build defect here — and that is the finding. The fork measured where a fixed landing fits, and nothing in §11.26 says the landing has to be fixed; the parameter it was derived over was a constant only because nobody had made it a variable. Same shape as §11.36’s pitch: a figure that looked like a constraint turned out to be a value, and the rule derived over it inherited the stiffness rather than the requirement.

15 · No, and where the sampled colour does belong

No — and the decisive objection is not the premise, it is that hover would make the pull redundant on its own subject. §11.19’s gesture means this record is now itself, and its content is the colour arriving. If the colour has already arrived by the time you press, the pull delivers a cover you have seen the colour of and a panel — it stops being a transition and becomes a zoom, which is the thing §11.20 refused and §11.25 reasoned about from the other side.

And the case for it does not survive §11.1, which is the part worth stating because it is where the argument sounds strongest. The claim is that a sampled colour identifies rather than decorates — but §11.1 already rules that the label identifies, and the label is on the spine’s face at rest. Hover reveals nothing the reader cannot already read, so colour on hover is decoration wearing identification’s justification. A channel that only appears on demand, on the element that already names itself, adds a second answer to a question that was answered.

§11.33 stands unchanged: sink to 0.731, hairlines 0.588, nothing else, and §11.32’s exclusion of even the app’s own accent stands with it. A hover that painted would also break what §11.28’s hairline correction protects — 0.588 was derived as §5.5’s shade step from 0.731, and against a sampled ground of any lightness it is no longer a step from anything, so every spine’s separation would become a function of its own cover.

So the boundary, stated once so the question does not return: the sampled colour belongs to a record that is out of its seat, and to nothing that is in one. Not per view and not per element — per state of the record. A seated spine is line, ink and paper whether hovered, focused, filtered or sorted; a record in flight and a record landed carry their colour, and so does the record screen, because §13 rules that page the place the pull arrives.

That is why the landed cover’s field is legitimate on the same page the hover is not — both are on the shelf, and one of them is a record that has left its seat. And it answers the version of this question that will come next: a selected spine, a recently-viewed spine, a spine matching a search — all seated, all line and ink. The far view’s run is the same rule applied to twenty records at once, so it does not colour either.

One thing confirmed rather than ruled: the record screen using the sampled value is correct and not a leak from an earlier build. §5.2 derives it, §5.5 makes the ladder from it, and §13 admits flat colour there on the ground that the page is the pull’s destination. What the app had at some point was this value on a seated spine, which is the one place it has never been ruled to belong.

16 · The count does not transfer; §3’s module test does

Confirmed: §11.31’s six is a count of one page’s structure and not a budget. Its six name the rail, the facts column and the drawing region — regions that exist only on the shelf — so reading six as a target here would mean deleting 14 of 20 rules to reach a number counted on another structure. What transfers is the two weights, the 0.72 value, and the bleed distinction; each page states its own set, and §11.31’s number is evidence that the set is finite rather than a figure to hit. That is the derived-from-the-set defect refused before it was committed: a count taken over one composition describes that composition.

And the 372px horizontal stays inset at 372, as §3 already rules — this section first said it bleeds, which is the failure mode §3 names by name. §3: “an inset hairline separates two things inside one module, a full-bleed one separates modules”, and the failure is “an implementer extending either to the cell edge, which silently promotes a paragraph break into a division”. The title stack and the pressing block are both inside the identity cell, so the line separates two things within one module and 372 is deliberate. No drawing changes; the three identity cells already carry it.

And my test was the wrong axis, which is why it produced the wrong answer: marks type or separates type sorts lines by their relation to the nearest run of text, when the question is what the two divided things are. Both sides of the 372 are type, so the test had nothing to read and defaulted to separates. §3’s axis is the module: two things inside one module take an inset line, two modules take a bleeding one — which is the rule stated over the signal rather than over something correlated with it, and it decides every case including the ones mine could not see.

The 220px over Images is the other inset hairline §3 names, and it stays inset for the same reason: the note and the Images N Manage → line are both inside the About cell, so it too separates two things within one module. Both of §3’s insets are now decided and neither moves, which is what §12 requires of a reference page — one decided line and one undecided one is the ambiguity it says must not be exported. And one thing §11.31 left implicit, which survives from the withdrawn ruling: when a line does bleed, it bleeds to the container that owns it and never to the viewport — §11.31’s verticals bleed to the page because the page owns them, and the facts column’s horizontals bleed to the column.

17 · The arrangement takes the cell’s aspect (withdrawn by §20)

Withdrawn by §20 — the drawing is width-bound, so matching the cell’s aspect lowers the scale and takes the floor from six failures to nine. The account below is kept for its diagnosis of the dead height, which is real, and not for its remedy. None of the four: the frame’s aspect changes, because the arrangement was composed without reference to the box it lives in and that is the whole defect. 0.903 against a 0.659 cell is not a fitting problem — it is a composition that was laid out in free space and then posted into a box, so 147px of dead height and 73% occupancy are what a mismatch of that size looks like. The generator arranges forms into a box of the cell’s proportion; the drawing then fills its cell in both directions, nothing spills, nothing is cropped, and the scale that clears §5.5’s floor comes free.

And this is available where the other three are not, because the arrangement is not the page’s composition. §8 closes the frame — the bands and the cells — and §12 keeps the pass off it; the construction’s internal arrangement is the generator’s — §5.1 makes it one of the eight marks derived per record, and this section supersedes §5.4’s “same image on all seventeen” for the identity still (its matrix clauses stand) — so re-proportioning its bounding box changes no cell, no band and no projection. An earlier version of this sentence cited §5.4 as licence, which is the section that forbids it: §5.4 was written when both stills were placeholders, and the generator that replaced the large one arrived without it being marked. Placement was always the hash’s business; this constrains the space it places into.

The box alone does not deliver this — §19 supplies the missing term, a rotation of the arrangement in plan — and with it the reasoning below holds. The floor clears by scale alone, at or above Code’s figures: filling height gave a 0.600% minimum and a 1.091% median, and filling both directions cannot be smaller than filling one. Which also explains why §5.5’s own remedy failed — the sweep from 1.05 to 1.45 reached 0.494% and left two records failing: growing a face inside a drawing that occupies 73% of its cell is spending the wrong term. The area was short because the drawing was small, and the drawing was small because its aspect was wrong.

The other three are refused on named grounds rather than on preference. Cropping puts a cut object in a cell — the Edge Marks ruling is that a cropped object reads as a mistake where a cropped field reads as a plane, and this is an object. Widening the cell is a band change §8 closes. And changing the archetype set to make the cube-coloured records clear a number is the derived-from-the-set defect exactly: the cube is small by design (§5.5, stating the 6:1 band as a fact about the generator’s set), so resizing it to satisfy a floor would tune the vocabulary to the measurement it is measured by.

Two things are preserved and must survive the re-proportioning, because each was a fix for a defect this file already paid for. The spread — six slots ringing one origin gave a centre-weighted cluster, and a narrower box is exactly the condition that re-clusters it, so the 6:1 size band and two forms breaking the disc’s edge stay as stated. And the per-record offset within the shared frame is the signal, not drift: fitting per arrangement is what once made six records look like one drawing, so 35 units of vertical variation is the hash showing through a frame that does not normalise it away.

18 · What the identity cell does when the artist does not fit

The type never moves. The grid does. §4.2 names the sizes and forbids 16 to 39, and a remedy that gives the artist a smaller size below some width adds the tier §4.2 exists to prevent — it would not be a responsive rule, it would be a fourth size with a media query for a justification. So the answer is not a size and not a clip: the content track floors at 412, §4.2’s give order runs as it already rules — its ordering is that section’s and is not restated here — and below the width where 412 plus its chrome no longer fits, the page is one column.

The floor is derived rather than picked, which is what makes it a rule: 412 is the measure §4.2 already sets the type to. A track narrower than its own measure is not a squeezed composition, it is a different one — which is why the build’s collapse-to-min-content test wrapped titles at 196: it let the track find a width from the content instead of giving the content the width the type was designed for. The track’s floor and the type’s measure are the same number because they are the same decision.

And the grid is fixed, so the fork is 1440 and needs no new figure: the bands are repeat(12, 120px), not fractions. This page has never reflowed — §7 says nothing below 1440 is specified, and what the narrow cell is actually reporting is that a fixed composition was being asked to be a fluid one. Below 1440 the twelve columns become one and the identity cell spans it. The two-track grid does not exist in that state — there is no corner field to reserve, which is a different claim from the give order having zeroed it (§4.2 ties the reserve to title lines, so at 1200 with a two-line title the order leaves it at 140). And the artist has the full measure at 40px down to 480 — 412 + 2 × 34. Below 480 the measure yields, and that is the give order’s fourth term rather than an exception: §4.2’s three, unchanged and not re-listed here — the gap, the reserve, the genres run — then the measure itself to the column’s inner width, 322 at 390. An earlier version of this sentence re-enumerated the three from memory and got two of them wrong, dropping the gap and splitting the reserve into “ornament” and “the corner reserve”, which are one track. The type still does not move, because a narrower measure is a worse setting of the same sizes and not a new size; what it costs is the shape §4.2’s text-wrap: balance was protecting, so titles take more lines and the even measure goes. An earlier version of this sentence claimed a single column is wider than 412 at every supported width, which is false at 390 — the width the defect was reported at and the one §11.24 rules the shelf for. A give order that stops before the last term will always be closed by asserting the last case cannot arise.

Clipping a fact is never the answer, and §9.2’s rule does not license it. That rule makes cells clip so §5.1’s edge marks stay inside the cell that owns them — it is about ornament, and ornament carries no data. A clipped fact is worse than an absent one: §6 requires an absence to be visible, and a silently cut artist name is a fact rendered as a shorter fact, which is the same shape as an empty state that said no images yet on a record that had one.

What six screens inherit is therefore a rule about grids and not about strings: when a fixed composition runs out of width, the columns collapse and the type holds. §12 could not let the title question be deferred because every screen inherits it; this is the general form of that answer — the scale is the constant and the layout is the variable, which is also why §14’s cover shrank and §14’s cap held.

19 · The ring rotates in plan, then the forms rise

Superseded by §20 on the first term and on the curve’s shape, which are separate withdrawals. The first term: rotation is exhausted on this ring (b/a 0.919 against a 0.38 threshold) and the aspect is no longer the target. The curve: the monotonic fall on 0°–45°, the symmetry about 45° and the unique root there are all properties of a centrally symmetric ring, and §20 establishes this ring is not one — the measured sweep peaks at 1.830 at 21.8° and falls to 1.633 at 37.9°, so it is not monotonic, not symmetric, and a target can have more roots than one on the interval. Read the three sentences below as the symmetric case, which is the case this arrangement is not. And the floor: the paragraph below saying the floor clears once the arrangement is turned, and crediting §17’s mechanism, is withdrawn too — §20 measures the drawing as width-bound, so turning it never makes it height-bound in a way that clears the floor, and §17’s mechanism reading was wrong rather than merely incomplete. What survives unwithdrawn: the feasibility test, the isometry guarantee, and the second term — the forms rise — which is carried into §20. This marker was extended three times, once per claim as each was reported, when one reading of §19 against §20 would have found all three. Two terms in order: the ring turns in plan until the projected box matches the cell, and where rotation cannot reach it the forms rise. So not the first option and not the third — the ring is never re-proportioned and the floor is never reconsidered — and the second only as the second term, when the feasibility test below fails. The ring keeps its shape and its spread exactly under both. Re-proportioning the ring cannot reach the target and would not have worked — shrinking its footprint reduces screen width and screen height together, since both x and y feed the vertical term, so a squeezed ring is a smaller arrangement at the same aspect. That is why §17’s “arrange into a box of the cell’s proportion” looked unsatisfiable: the lever everyone reached for moves both axes at once.

What moves one axis is orientation. A ring elongated along the x − y diagonal projects wide; the same ring along x + y projects narrow and tall, because that diagonal is the one the projection sends vertically. Between them the projected aspect falls monotonically, and the interval on which it does is 0° to 45° — an eighth turn, not a quarter. The curve is symmetric about 45°, so over a quarter turn every target has two roots, the second being the mirrored plan, which flips which forms break the disc’s edge. The generator solves on 0°–45°, where the root is unique.

The two endpoints are different kinds of thing: the upper is a constant of the projection and the lower is the generator’s to measure — an earlier version of this paragraph had both moving. At 0° the x − y and x + y ranges are equal for any centrally symmetric ring, so the aspect there is cos 30 / sin 30 = 1.732 at every width; at 45° the width term is the ring’s own width, so the minimum is about 1.732 · b/a and rises with it. Which leaves one open question rather than a correction: the build’s ring measures 1.804, and no width can lift the 0° aspect above √3 — so that figure was taken on something other than the bare ring, the ring plus the forms’ z-extent being the obvious candidate, or the ring is not centrally symmetric. The generator must say which, because the feasibility test below is derived from the upper endpoint being that constant.

And the lower endpoint rising is a feasibility condition, testable before any rotation: the minimum over the interval is about 1.732 · b/a, so a target of 0.658 is reachable only while the ring’s width-to-length ratio is under 0.38. At 0.4 the whole interval bottoms out at 0.693 and at 0.6 it never falls below 1.0 — so rotation is exhausted at any appreciable width, and this is the likely case rather than the remote one. When it fails the next term is the forms’ own height, ruled here rather than mentioned: z enters the vertical term alone, so raising the forms lowers the aspect at every heading and does it without touching the plan — which keeps the isometry guarantee below intact, since the spread is a property of the plan. Rotate first because it costs nothing; raise second because it changes the silhouette. 24.2° is the root for the bare ring and is a sighting shot, not the answer.

And this is the protection §17 asked for, stated rather than assumed: a rotation is an isometry, so every pairwise distance in the spread is preserved by construction. The centre-weighted cluster was a spacing defect and spacing is exactly what a rotation cannot change — the 6:1 size band, the slots’ separations and the two forms breaking the disc’s edge all survive because none of them is a property of the plan’s heading. Re-proportioning would have had to be argued; rotating is guaranteed.

The floor is not reconsidered, and the third option is refused on §17’s own ground. §5.5’s 0.5% was set on a drawing whose aspect was wrong, which makes it worth re-checking and does not make it wrong — changing the measurement because the thing measured fails it is the defect this file has refused twice, at the archetype set and at the withdrawn ceiling. With the arrangement turned, the scale binds on height rather than width and the dead third goes, so the floor clears for the reason §17 gave — that reasoning was right about the mechanism and wrong that the box alone delivered it. Both halves of that sentence are withdrawn by §20: the drawing is width-bound, and §17’s mechanism was wrong.

Which is §18’s shape once more and worth naming as a pair: a rule that fixes a container and expects its contents to follow is one term short. §17 set the box and left the arrangement free; the box then constrained nothing, because a nearly square arrangement fits a tall box by leaving air. Both rulings needed their last term supplied by measurement rather than by argument, and in both the missing term was the one the earlier text had assumed would take care of itself.

20 · The plan narrows on one axis; the aspect is a result, not a target (squeeze withdrawn by §22)

§17 is withdrawn. Matching the cell’s aspect is not merely insufficient — it is harmful, and the measurement says so: the drawing is width-bound at 360 of 360 with 386 of 547 in height, so equalising the two ratios pulls the slack one down to the binding one and never lifts the binding one. A uniform lift reaching 0.658 takes the scale from 1.307 to 1.221 and the floor from six failures to nine. §17 read 73% occupancy as dead space convertible into area; it is saturation in one direction and slack in the other, and only the saturated direction pays.

Withdrawn by §22: k returns to 1, because at the factor that clears the floor the squeeze leaves two forms 3.9px apart — the colour assignment clears it instead. The account below is kept for its mechanism, which is correct. The lever is a third operation, and it was missed because the options were framed as shape against orientation: scale the plan anisotropically along the axis that projects horizontally. §19 proved a uniform shrink moves both screen axes together and that rotation trades one against the other until exhausted — neither result covers squeezing u − v alone, which reduces projected width and leaves projected height untouched. The squeeze carries the slot positions and not the forms. Scaling the forms with them narrows each base face in one direction, so area goes as scale² · k rather than scale² — 0.387% would reach 0.461% and fail the floor outright — and it would make a cube stop being a cube, which is the archetype change this section refuses below.

And the target is a clearance rather than the floor itself: the worst record goes to 0.55%, ten per cent above 0.5%. That is area × 1.421, scale × 1.192, so the arrangement’s projected width must fall 16.1%. An earlier version of this paragraph solved to the floor exactly and landed under it — 12.500 to 11.0 is 12.00% where 12.02% is needed, putting the worst record at 0.4997% — and even the 13.7% figure cleared by 0.0003 points, which is the coincidence-for-a-margin shape §7 records at the 498-of-500 title and the 1px year cell, arriving a third time in a figure derived here rather than inherited.

The 16.1% is of the projected extent, and the slot span must narrow by more than that, because the end forms’ own widths sit inside the extent and do not shrink. With the extent as S + F — the projected slot span plus the end forms’ contribution — the generator solves (kS + F) / (S + F) = 0.839 for k, and F is a measurement this file does not hold. So the ruling gives the clearance and the extent; the span follows from the arrangement, which is the only place F is known.

The spread survives this in the sense §17 protected it, and the difference is worth stating because the concession is real. §17 was written against the centre-weighted cluster — a squeeze along one axis moves slots toward that axis, not toward the centroid, so it cannot re-cluster; ordering, the 6:1 size band and the two forms breaking the disc’s edge are all preserved. What is conceded is at least 16.1% of one axis’s distances — strictly more of the slot span itself, since the end forms’ widths sit in the extent and do not shrink — which is still a smaller thing than the defect the rule exists to prevent and is less small than it sounds. This paragraph quoted 12% until now, the figure the section withdrew above, so the honesty it exists for was costed low.

Then the forms rise, as §19’s second term, and it now has a purpose it lacked: not to reach an aspect but to fill the height the narrowing leaves. After the squeeze the drawing is still width-bound, so height slack persists at roughly 108 of 547; z enters the vertical term alone, so raising the forms spends that slack at no cost in width and no cost to the plan. The cell’s aspect is then a result of the two operations rather than a target imposed on the arrangement — which is the whole correction to §17.

The floor is refused a third time, on the ground it was refused twice: the six failures are the records whose colour lands on the cube, and §5.5 records the cube as small by design — the 6:1 band, a fact about the generator’s set. A floor re-measured so that the small form stops failing it is a floor tuned to the thing it measures. And the archetype set is not the lever either — growing the forms while the plan holds is the tuning refused at §17, distinct from the z rise, which changes height rather than the size relationship the set encodes.

One finding closed: §19’s open question about the 1.804 is answered by elimination, and the answer is that the ring is not centrally symmetric. Measured on the bare ring at z = 0 with no forms it is already 1.8042, and z can only lower the aspect; the spans are u − v 12.500 against u + v 12.000, and 1.0417 × √3 is 1.8042 exactly. That also explains the non-monotonic sweep — the aspect rises to 1.830 at 21.8° before falling — so §19’s monotonic interval holds for a symmetric ring and not for this one, and the uniqueness it claims on 0°–45° is a property the arrangement does not have.

21 · The ornament library

One vocabulary, and the library is the frame generator’s archetype set — licensed by §5.1 as one of eight marks derived per record, counted at six in §9.2, its arrangement ruled by §20 — with no new forms. What the library holds is arrangements: the solo figure and the pair. The six are the beam, the slab, the cube, the plate, the panel and the line, and this is the file’s canonical list — every other section cites it rather than naming them. §9.2 gives two proportion triples — beam 0.8 × 0.8 × 7.6 and plate 2.8 × 2.8 × 0.28 — and describes the panel as upright without dimensions; §5.5 names the slab in passing. This section states the remaining proportions as its own rather than quoting them: cube 1 × 1 × 1, panel 2.4 × 0.3 × 3.2, slab and line to be measured off the generator. An earlier version of this sentence attributed all four to §9.2, which holds two, and the cube and panel figures were recalled from the generator script rather than read from the file — the inherited-not-measured class (§11.28, §11.30, §20), committed inside the paragraph correcting an enumeration from memory. Until now no section listed all six, so the earlier remedy here — cite rather than re-list, borrowed from §18 — pointed at an enumeration that did not exist and steered a reader away from the only section naming the slab. Citation replaces re-listing only where a canonical list exists; where none does, the governing section becomes it. They span the shape space the projection can express, and adding figures so ornament is more interesting is the same move as widening the archetype set to clear a floor, which §17 and §20 each refused. A second set could not read as a second system in any case: an isometric cube in a construction and an isometric cube in a library are the same object, so the only thing a parallel vocabulary would add is two names for one thing.

So the unit of the library is the grouping, not the shape. A solo figure is one archetype at the section’s height (§9.2); a pair is two archetypes whose footprints do not overlap in plan and whose silhouettes do overlap in projection — that overlap is the whole reason a pair is a different mark from two solos, because it is what makes the two read as one object in space. §9.2’s 0.62 governs the pair’s combined box, not each form, so the two are correspondingly smaller and the pair passes the same gate a solo does — 0.627 of the cell against a two-thirds ceiling, the figure §9.2 already measures. Applying 0.62 to each form instead makes every pair illegal by construction: disjoint footprints project to a vertical offset, so two 0.62 forms exceed the ceiling whatever their heading. A pair therefore trades size for structure — each form is smaller than a solo would be — which is the honest cost of spending one mark’s allowance on two objects. Three is not in the library, and the file has already refused it once: §10.3 rules that three marks at the drawn size read as a row of specks rather than as one mark — it converts a presence problem into a pattern — so this is §10.3 applied to the library rather than a new ceiling. What limits repetition is §9.4’s one-mark-per-section rule, paired with its floor as §13 states the pair; an earlier version of this sentence cited the floor alone, which is a minimum area and cannot bound a count — only a count or a ceiling can, and §13’s sentence names both halves where this one had dropped the operative one. A third form also turns a mark into a composition that competes with the construction.

Curved forms are admitted and free-drawn ones are not, and the line between them is construction. The disc is not an archetype — it is the ground the construction stands on (§5.4), which is why it takes tint and why it is not a figure a page may place solo or paired — but it is precedent for curvature in the drawing: a circle in plan, projected to an ellipse, drawn by the same projection as the solids. So the rule rests on a construction test rather than on the disc’s membership: a curved ornament is a primitive in plan — circle, arc, annulus — laid on the ground plane or on a face and projected with everything else. What is refused is the free silhouette, because it has no construction and therefore no answer to why it is that shape rather than another, and a mark whose shape is arbitrary is decoration in the sense §5.4 forbids. Organic, here, means curved in plan; it does not mean drawn by hand.

An isometric figure never crosses a page edge. A flat field always may. That is not a new rule — it is the Edge Marks ruling, and §19 and §20 are its consequence rather than a separate prohibition: a cropped object reads as a mistake and a cropped field reads as a plane extending past the view. So Adam’s masked mode belongs to the flat shapes and not to the figures, which is also why §13 gives the flat pair their own count.

A figure may be clipped by the cell that owns it, and §9.2 depends on it: the gate measures visible height precisely because the region solid’s bottom bleed is deliberate, and no one-column solid could pass a total-box test. That is occlusion rather than cutting — a cell edge has the next section behind it, so a figure running under it reads as continuing; a page edge has nothing behind it, so a figure crossing one reads as severed. An earlier version of this section said a figure never bleeds and never crosses a cell edge, which made §9.2’s drawn solids defects and its gate unsatisfiable at once.

The flat field’s test is the one that needs a threshold, statable so a build can check it: a field bleeds at a page edge, never at a cell edge, and at least a third of it lies outside the frame. The first clause is load-bearing — a field cut by an internal boundary is a field that did not fit its cell, and nothing about its geometry says otherwise — and the second stops a mark that merely touches the edge from reading as a near miss. The asymmetry is the point: a figure may be occluded and may not be severed, and a field may be severed because a severed plane is what a plane from outside looks like. A third is a threshold, not a measurement, and it is stated as one; what it has to be is large enough that no reader wonders whether the shape was meant to end there.

A page’s ornament is fixed per screen and written down, never hashed. §9.2 settled this for the region and the reason generalises: a hash makes ornament encode which record or which page you are on, and §5.4 rules that ornament carries no data. The construction is the sole exception in the app because it is the record rather than a mark about it — the frame’s ornament is the record’s, everything else’s is the screen’s — and a second hashed mark would undo that distinction by making two things vary for different reasons in the same drawing.

Narrowed by §26: a pair is available in a §9 region’s air column, because an air column is a section carrying no construction — the condition this section gives the six screens. It stays unavailable in any section with content.

Two units, and they are not the same: figures are counted per section and flat shapes per region. At most one figure per section, which is §9.2’s unit — and §9.2 caps solids at one per section, so a pair is not available inside a §9 region. The withdrawn version of this cap said two solids per section and rested the pair on it; §9.2 says “one per section”, so the pair’s whole permission was a miscount of the section it cites by number in the same clause. Where the pair is available is the six screens the library exists for: a section that carries no construction has nothing for a second solid to compete with, and the pair takes §9.2’s obligations on its combined box — the gate on visible height, and the clearance from a control measured from the pair’s outer extent rather than from either form. Plus §13’s two flat shapes per region, one tint field as ground in the last section’s widest cell and one base rectangle above it. A screen may have fewer of either. The withdrawn version of the unit rule counted figures per region, which capped them four times too low and made §9.2’s four drawn solids — beam, plate, cube, panel, one to a section — defects. The ceiling is not a target; §11.28 refused to resize a fixture to fill space and the same holds here, so a screen with nothing to decorate decorates nothing. And each screen names its own figures in its own spec rather than drawing from the library at random, which is what makes six screens share a vocabulary instead of sharing a random number generator.

What keeps this one system rather than two is that the library adds no form and no value. The forms are the frame generator’s, enumerated in this section, the values are §13’s and the ladder they step on is §5.5’s, the bleed rule is Edge Marks’, the count is §9.4’s, the per-screen fixing is §9.2’s. The forms were attributed to §5.5 here through three rounds of correcting the same misattribution elsewhere in this section — §5.5 owns the ladder and not the set. The library’s original content is four things: the pair, the plan-primitive rule for curves, and the bleed test’s two clauses — page edge not cell edge, and a third of the shape outside. Edge Marks rules which marks may bleed; where and how much are new here, and the one-third is a threshold this section chooses, as it says of itself above. All four are constraints on how the existing set is used rather than additions to it, which is the claim that survives; this paragraph opened with “nothing in it is new” until now, which was true of the forms and the values and overstated for the rest. A vocabulary that grows to meet each new screen is not a vocabulary; it is a record of what each screen wanted.

22 · The colour lands on a form that can carry it

The assignment varies and the archetypes, the plan and the floor do not: the base step lands only on a form whose largest visible face, at the drawn scale, clears §5.5’s floor. The hash still chooses the arrangement and still chooses among the eligible forms; it no longer chooses among all of them. That is the one term in this problem nothing had varied, and it is the only remedy that changes neither what is measured nor the thing measuring it.

It is not the refused option, and the distinction is exact. Resizing the cube tunes the vocabulary to the measurement; re-measuring the floor tunes the measurement to the vocabulary. Choosing where the colour lands tunes neither — it is a property of the assignment, and the assignment is the generator’s. The cube stays small, keeps its grey faces, and still appears in arrangements; it stops being eligible to carry the record’s colour, which is the one job it was too small to do.

§21 is what makes this legitimate rather than merely available: it rules ornament fixed per screen and never hashed, because a hash makes ornament encode something — with the construction as the one exception, since it is the record. So the construction’s assignment is already the single place this file intends a hash to carry meaning, and which form carries the colour is part of that assignment, not a property of the vocabulary. Constraining the hash to legal outcomes is what a hash that carries meaning should always have been.

Determinism is kept by construction, not by luck: the hash orders the forms and colour takes the first eligible ones in that order, so a record’s colour placement is as stable as its arrangement — and depends only on the id, per §5.1’s rule never to feed it anything mutable. If an arrangement has no eligible form it is illegal and the hash advances to its next arrangement, deterministically, the same way; that case has not been observed and the test asserts it across the full list. §5.1’s traced-path check between the two coloured forms is re-run by the same test, since moving the colour can change which two forms the eye travels between.

§20’s squeeze is withdrawn: k returns to 1. Its only purpose was the floor, and the measurement says what it costs to buy it that way — at the first factor that clears all seventeen, 62 overlapping pairs against 37 and two forms 3.9px apart, which is coincident. §20 was right that a one-axis squeeze moves slots toward the axis rather than the centroid, and wrong that this protects the spread: it protects the spread from the centroid and not the forms from each other. That is the granularity shape in plan — a guarantee stated over the wrong pair.

And §20’s input is recorded as the fixture-list defect, not a slip: it solved from 0.387% when the worst of the seventeen is 0.320%, because the first test carried twelve ids and the five it omitted were the five worst. A sample that drops its tail reports its median as its minimum. The list now lives in one shared file and every floor figure in this document is measured against it.

Where the cube’s smallness lives, stated rather than moved: §5.5 owns the ladder, and the archetype set belongs to the frame generator (§5.1, §17, counted in §9.2) — but §5.5 is where the file states the 6:1 band, as a fact about that set: it is what stopped the probe’s compositions reading as orderly. So §17’s and §20’s refusals cite the right sentence, and that sentence reports the generator’s set rather than ruling it. A citation to where a fact is stated is sound; it is only the claim of ownership that would be wrong.

23 · The construction cell is four columns: the floor was failing a cell the drawing does not have

The gap is a build-versus-drawing defect, and it is in the cell, not the archetypes. Measured off both rasters with one threshold, the construction’s bounding box against its own cell: the supplied render occupies 73% of its cell’s width and 88% of its height; the build occupies 82% and 46%. The render’s cell is 693 × 704 — aspect 0.98. The build’s is 694 × 1069 — aspect 0.65. The forms are not smaller in the build; the box is a different shape, so a nearly square arrangement fits a nearly square cell and a tall one leaves half its height dead. The render is not a drawing of mine — it is the supplied composition §0 makes the specification — and at the cell it depicts the arrangement is height-filling, which is what §17 through §22 were trying to produce by other means.

Two departures in §2.1 compound to make the difference, and both are the file’s, not the drawing’s. The width: §2.1 measures the upper dividers at 451 and 888 and snaps them to 480 and 840, which takes the construction cell from 437 to 360 — 18% narrower than drawn. §2.1 states the rounding as the identity cell gaining 29 and “the figures cell” losing 51; the construction cell loses 77, and nothing in §2.1 names it. The height: the band grew to 547 when the tail’s 47px moved in, where the raster’s band is about 452. 0.97 in the drawing, rounded narrow and grown tall, is 0.658 in the build — exactly the aspect §17 was built on.

So the upper band is 4 / 4 / 4, and the construction takes the fourth column from the cover. Every cell moves toward the drawing rather than away from it: identity 480 against a drawn 451, construction 480 against 437. The identity cell cannot give the column: its 412px title measure (§4) needs the 480.

The cover cell’s geometry, ruled rather than left to the span: the cover is 414 square, and the sleeve bar and the black square share one 30px column at the cell’s right edge — bar above, black below — which is how the supplied render draws them. The file had drawn them side by side, bar at right 38 and black at right 0, which needed 58px of width beside the cover that a 480 cell does not have. So: 26 left padding, 414 cover, 10 gap, 30 column = 480. The band is 547 and §23 does not change it — it is the denominator for §9.2’s gate and step 16’s floor re-measurement, so it is stated here rather than implied. The bar runs 26 → 398 and the black 398 → 547, the band’s foot; both are positioned against the cell, not its padding, so the 26 applies to their top and not their bottom. The drawings first ended the black at 544, 3px short of the foot, which the render does not do and which read as a fourth dimension nobody had named. The bar still runs its full edge — the cell’s, which is what §5.1 meant.

The costs, named, because §23 is correcting exactly an unnamed loss: the cover goes 448 → 414 in the drawings, 8% linear — and to 414 from the build’s 547, 24%, the build’s cover having grown with the band; the render’s cover measures 422 at 1440, so 414 is within 2% of the supplied composition. The bar goes 30 × 430 → 30 × 372, 13% of its area; it is §5.5’s floor-exempt mark, bounded by the sleeve it sits beside, so the floor does not bind on it, and it remains one of the band’s two base marks — the count is unchanged. The paper below the cover is the band’s, as in the render, and carries nothing. An earlier version of this paragraph gave the cover as 480 square and the render’s cover as about 452; the first left no width for the bar and the second was the band’s height, not the cover’s.

The floor clears by the correction alone. At 480 × 547 the cell’s aspect is 0.88 and the arrangement’s is 1.02, so the drawing stays width-bound and its scale rises with the width: ×1.33, area ×1.78. The worst record goes from 0.320% to 0.569%, and all seventeen clear 0.5% with no change to the archetypes, the plan, the floor or the assignment. §22 stays as the guard it was ruled as — colour lands only on an eligible form — and is now expected to bind on no record; its test still asserts that across the shared list, so if it ever binds it says so.

What this does to §17–§22: their mechanisms stand and their shared premise falls. Each took the cell’s 0.659 as given and tried to make the drawing fit it; the 0.659 was itself a rounding of the drawing, so five rulings were solving a problem the file had introduced one section earlier. The refusals they made — not tuning the archetypes to the floor, not re-measuring the floor — were right, and that is why the answer was elsewhere: when every lever that honours the rules is exhausted, check whether the constraint is itself a reading of the drawing, and re-read it. The drawing was on the table the whole time; nobody measured the cell against it.

One further difference the render shows, recorded and not ruled: its beam rests on top of the tall slab, so forms there stack as well as spread. That is part of why its arrangement is 0.82 tall where the generator’s is 1.02. It is not needed for the floor after the span correction, and adding a tier is a change to the generator’s vocabulary that should be judged by looking, on the corrected cell, before it is ruled.

24 · Edit and Delete record go in the top nav, at its far right

§13’s placement is superseded: Edit and Delete record sit together at the far right of AppHeader, in line with the nav, on this screen only. §13 refused AppHeader because a bar identical on six screens cannot hold a per-record control. That objection is to the bar’s contents being per-record, and a named slot answers it: AppHeader gains one actions slot at its right end, empty on every screen but this one, filled by the page rather than by AppHeader. The component stays identical everywhere; only this page puts something in it. No other screen changes, and none renders anything there.

The two verbs stay together, in that order, and after the app’s own right-hand glyphs, separated from them by a 1px, 16px-tall hairline at 0.72. The hairline marks the slot’s boundary: what is left of it is the app’s, what is right of it is this record’s. Both are 11px mono uppercase in ink, the nav’s own type, so they cost no height and add no weight.

What §13 was protecting is kept by a different mechanism: its worry was the app’s only irreversible act sitting in chrome. Delete record asks before it acts — a confirmation naming the record — so its place in the nav makes it findable without making it one click from gone. §3’s departure/interaction/ending distinction is not re-argued: the owner has weighed it and placed the controls, and the file’s job is to make that placement sound.

What moves with it: the eyebrow line returns to Collection alone, and the foot row that held Delete record is deleted from all five region drawings. The three frame drawings now show both verbs in the nav. §13’s deletion of the ← Collection band stands.

§13’s ornament clause is independent of this and stands unchanged — two flat shapes per region, the ladder’s values. Nothing in it depends on where the controls are, so it can be built now.

25 · The ornament specimen, the size rule raised, and distribution

To Adam, plainly: free organic outlines are refused. Every ornament is built from a plan and raised into the projection — that is what gives it three faces and lets it sit in front of or behind other forms. A free outline has no plan, so it cannot be drawn in this projection, and it is the one shape that depicts nothing and comes from nothing. What “organic” means here is the curve primitives — cylinder, ring, quarter ring — raised from circles and arcs, drawn above at the ruled size.

The size rule is raised from 0.62 to 0.855 of the section’s height, which is the gate itself. At 0.62 a figure showed 78 of an allowed 107 — conservative by a quarter for no stated reason, and Adam’s “boring” is that quarter. At 0.855 the visible height equals the two-thirds ceiling exactly; the gate now binds, and every solo and pair above is drawn touching it.

Superseded by §26 for a solid’s top face: it is 0.773, not tint, because tint is the ground a construction’s disc paints and a tint top vanishes on it. The sheet below this is drawn on paper with the superseded tint top, which is why it could not show the collision. The ladder’s three values, stated: tint 0.83, base 0.66 (the record’s sampled colour, clamped), shade 0.535 — 26% toward ink. A solid’s faces are tint on top, base on the left, shade on the right. Flat marks take tint or base, never shade. Base crossing the boundary is deliberate — it is the record’s colour, and both kinds of mark carry the record; the exclusivity was only ever shade’s. The earlier sheet’s 0.69 was a probe face value mislabelled as shade, which is why shade read lighter than base. Ornament always takes the record’s sampled hue: the pairs above are drawn in a second record’s hue to show it.

A pair must earn its box, measured in model units: footprints disjoint, silhouettes overlapping, and the combined projected box at least 1.2× the area of the larger solo’s. Each pair above states that ratio. Drawn widths are not the measure: every figure is drawn to the same height, so a pair — taller than either form — is drawn at a smaller scale, and its drawn width compared with a solo’s compares two scales. The first sheet printed drawn widths and all three pairs appeared to fail. Width alone is not the measure either: a beam lying past a slab adds nothing to the beam’s width, yet the pair is plainly larger than the beam — so the box is compared by area.

Minimum width: no face narrower than 6px as drawn. Below that a solid reads as a rule, within reach of §11.31’s 2px weight. The rod passes at 12px at the ruled size and is ineligible at any smaller one.

Distribution: fewer figures, all at full size — no half-size tier. In the lower region, at most one figure per three sections, never in consecutive sections, only where a section leaves an empty area. The two flat shapes sit on opposite page edges. Weight lightens down the page. The ceiling is not a target, and the balance comes from the gaps: a figure in every legal section is even, and even is what reads as monotonous.

26 · The page as a whole: section shape and ornament together

records/[id] at 1440, the whole scroll. Above the dashed line is the ruled frame at §23’s 4 / 4 / 4, with §24’s Edit and Delete record at the nav’s far right and the construction at the build’s own fit — forms and disc together, inside the cell’s 24px margin; below it, the lower region with varied spans and §25's distribution.

A solid’s top face moves; the disc stays tint. §13 makes tint the ground, and the disc is ground, so the face gives way: a solid’s top is 0.773, one third of the way from tint to base, and is used only as a face — never a flat mark. The construction cell above is the test, drawn on its tint disc rather than on paper: the plate and the beam read against it. §25’s “three values” is corrected to four face steps: tint (ground and flat), top (face only), base (face and flat), shade (face only).

Section shape is ruled here, with the ornament, because the ornament cannot be judged on a field that has not been decided. Eight sections of one width is what read as monotonous; figures placed into it were decoration on a flat field. The lower region runs as five rows: a wide section beside air (7 + 5), three tight columns carrying nothing (4 / 4 / 4), a full-width strip (12), two halves (6 / 6), and a last row that begins with air (3 + 9). The air columns are where the figures and flats go, so the rhythm makes the air rather than finding it.

The left page edge is made, not found: the last row is ordered air first. Every other row starts with content at x = 0, so “flats on opposite page edges” needs one cleared column on the left, and this ruling makes it. The tint triangle bleeds off the left edge in that column; the base quarter-disc bleeds off the right edge beside About this record — the lighter value lower, per the paragraph on weight below. Two figures in eight sections, never consecutive: the pair in Pressing detail’s air, the solo in Price history’s strip.

The construction is drawn at its fitted size, not smaller. An earlier draft of this drawing showed it at 0.78 because it spilled past the cell’s left edge. The spill came from fitting the forms’ box without the disc, which is larger: fitted with the disc included it sits inside the cell at 432 × 371, with no scale factor. 0.78 was never a ruling on the build — it would have cut the base-face area to 0.608 of itself and put §23’s worst record at 0.346%, below the floor. This record’s drawing measures 0.910% at the fit. The rule, since the construction drawing is the one a build copies: the fit box includes the disc.

Clipping is a boundary, not a treatment: each figure’s clip is its own cell, so it can never enter another. A figure may be cut by at most one of its cell’s edges — its foot, per §9.2’s bleed. Two cut edges read as a figure too big for its box rather than as masking, which §17 records as reading like a mistake. An earlier sentence here said every figure is clipped, which is stronger than §21’s “may” and was never meant.

The top face holds on the disc, and the drawing is the test. 0.773 on 0.83 is the tightest step in the ladder — about 1.21:1 against 1.84 for base on the disc — but the top face does not carry the form alone: its base and shade faces draw its edges against the ground, so the top only needs to read as a different surface, and in the construction cell above the plate’s top does. If a build shows the plate losing its top, the step widens toward base; the number is ruled against this drawing.

Weight lightens down the page, as §25’s draft said: the flats are the other way round from the first drawing. Base goes to the quarter-disc on the right beside About this record, and tint to the triangle on the left edge in the last row. The pair in Pressing detail’s air extends §21: §21 makes pairs available where a section carries no construction, and an air column is exactly that.

27 · The eyebrow returns to the flow; the band stays 547; fixtures come from the collection

Deletion, not a fifth term: §13’s eyebrow row is undone and COLLECTION returns to the content flow. The row existed to let Edit share the eyebrow’s line; §24 removed Edit and left the row carrying one label. A mechanism kept after its reason is the defect, and a give-order term added to absorb it would be a second mechanism serving the first. What the deletion recovers is the row’s own overhead — its gap and its grid track — not the label’s line, which the eyebrow still occupies.

If the worst title still exceeds the cell once that is measured, §4.2’s existing third term fires: the genres run collapses to its count. That is the ruled response to a shortfall, not a clip, so §18’s “clipping a fact is never the answer” holds whichever way the measurement lands. overflow-hidden must not be the thing that resolves this cell, and the test asserts that no pressing fact is clipped on the collection’s worst title.

The band stays 547: delta 0. The 570 is inferred from the cover column’s bar and square, which are positioned against the cell, not against its padding — 26 is the bar’s top offset, not the band’s top padding. The square’s 544 was the 3px defect corrected to 398 → 547 in all three drawings. Raising the band would clear the overflow by spending height the frame budgets to its bands (§2.1), which is the unnamed change that cost §17–§22; the deletion clears it without spending any.

Standing rule: a fixture is derived from the real collection’s extremes, never hand-written to look plausible. Two fixtures have now produced a false pass on the exact quantity they existed to test. §20’s id list dropped the five worst records, so its minimum was a median. The identity-cell probe’s five-line case needs 462 where the collection’s real worst needs 495 — 33px short, more than the eyebrow costs, so it could never have caught this. Every test of a bound takes its case from one shared file generated from the collection, with the extremes selected by measurement.

Procedural, seventh instance: the repo’s build target ends at §10, so §11 exists only in this file and in an excerpt deferring to a section its reader cannot consult. Re-exported this round, and the rule is the handoff rule one level up: an excerpt naming a source of truth is only sound if the source is reachable. The extended-grid handoff’s pointer discipline assumed a repo copy that was never there.
